why: Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Composite Bowman. Renamed with the Classical Armenian word for archer (ałełnawor, from ałełn, “bow”: Bedrossian's Armenian-English dictionary; modern spelling աղեղնավոր, romanized agheghnavor, since ղ is gh both times). Archery is the oldest image of Armenian warfare: in the founding myth Hayk kills Bel with an arrow (Movses Khorenatsi I.11), and the Arsacid-era sources count the nobles' horsemen as lancers and bowmen (Buzandaran). No source of 884–1045 singles out Armenian foot archers, so the unit is an abstraction resting on that tradition; Armenian troops in the Fatimid army of Badr al-Jamali (from the 1070s) fall after the window. “Composite Bowman” named nothing Armenian, since the composite bow was common to the whole Near East, and it was not adopted in the 11th century as the original history text claims. Ignoring armor remains a game abstraction.

Renamed from Elite Composite Bowman. Follows the rename of the unique unit (Composite Bowman → Agheghnavor).

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Fereters (Infantry (except Spearman-line) +30 HP; Warrior Priests heal +100% faster). Ashot III made Ani the royal seat in 961, was crowned there and walled it; Smbat II (977–989/990) built its outer double walls; the catholicos, resident at nearby Argina since the mid-10th century, moved the see into Ani in 992; and under Gagik I (989/990–1017/1020) the kingdom and its capital reached their height, Ani becoming one of the great cities of the Christian East, until Byzantium annexed it (1045) and the Seljuks took it (1064) (Stepanos Taronetsi; Aristakes Lastivertsi; N. Garsoïan in Hovannisian, 1997; Hewsen, 2001). Fereters is a Latin-English church word (feretory, from feretrum) with no Armenian institution behind it.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Cilician Fleet (Demolition Ships +20% blast radius; Galley-line and Dromons +1 range). The sparapet was the commander-in-chief of the Armenian host, an office hereditary in the Mamikonian house from the 4th to the 8th century and held by the Bagratids in the 9th (Smbat the Confessor, sparapet 826–855); his son Ashot I held it too and rose, with the caliph's title of prince of princes (862), to the crown in 884/885 (Toumanoff, 1963). Within the window, Vahram Pahlavuni, sparapet of Ani, led the nakharars against the Byzantine army in 1042 and had Gagik II crowned (Matthew of Edessa); the Imperial Age placement follows him. The armour effect abstracts the noble host the sparapet commanded; with Plate Barding Armor left out, the Paladin with Sparapet reaches 5/7 armour, the armour of a fully upgraded Paladin without civ bonuses, within the ceiling of its class (RULES 6.16.11). Cilician Fleet belongs to the Cilician kingdom, which leaves the core of the civ and had no significant war fleet.
A Byzantine ship type; Greater Armenia had no war fleet, and Cilicia, which leaves the core, relied on Genoese, Venetian and Cypriot ships.

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret that Constantine VII told his son never to give to any other nation (De Administrando Imperio 13); Greater Armenia had no fleet, and the tech was a leftover of the Cilician naval identity. Fire Ships stay as the generic fire ship.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

No war fleet of its own, on a landlocked plateau: the basic navy only (RULES 6.16.1: Galley and War Galley, Fire Galley and Fire Ship, Hulk and War Hulk, demolition ships and the Dock techs), with no substitute siege warship (see Dromon).
As Galleon.

The counterweight trebuchet appears only in the 12th century: in Byzantine use by 1165 on P. E. Chevedden's reading of the great stone-throwers at Zeugminon in Niketas Choniates (Dumbarton Oaks Papers 54, 2000), or only at the end of the century according to M. S. Fulton (Artillery in the Era of the Crusades, 2018), and certainly in use in the region by c. 1187 (al-Tarsusi's treatise for Saladin); even Chevedden's case for an earlier Byzantine invention points to the Komnenian emperors (from 1081), after the window and its epilogue. The Mangonel line is the light stone-thrower (RULES 6.16.5), and the Traction Trebuchet replaces the counterweight engine as the heavy one (see that entry).
No gunpowder before 1045; even Cilicia fell (1375) before gunpowder mattered in the region.
No gunpowder before 1045; even Cilicia fell (1375) before gunpowder mattered in the region.

There is no evidence of crossbows in Greater Armenia before 1045, and the hand crossbow was still a Latin novelty to Byzantium in the 1090s (Anna Komnene calls the tzangra a barbarian bow unknown to the Greeks, Alexiad X.8). The Crossbowman stays as the generic Castle Age bow tier (RULES 6.16.3); the Arbalester, which needs crossbow evidence in the window, is withheld, and the Agheghnavor fills the elite foot-archer role.
No printing in the window: the first Armenian printed book, Hakob Meghapart's Urbatagirk, appeared in Venice in 1512.

The noble heavy cavalry was the main arm of Armenian armies, recruited as such by the Sasanians and the Byzantines (Garsoïan, 1985; Hovannisian, 1997), and still mustered in 1042 (see the gold discount bonus); denying the top of the Knight-line was the main inversion in the game's civ.

The azat horsemen fought with lance and bow (Buzandaran); the civ had Cavalry Archer without its upgrade. The equipment is extrapolated into the Bagratid period from the Arsacid–Sasanian sources, since in-window sources give musters and battles, rarely equipment.

The Parthian-Sasanian horse-archery tradition of the Armenian nobility, whose kings were an Arsacid branch until 428 (Garsoïan, 1985); extrapolated into the Bagratid period, like the rest of the cavalry equipment.
Needed for the Masonry, Architecture free bonus: Zvartnots (643–652), the church of Aghtamar (915–921) and the cathedral of Ani by Trdat (989–1001) (see that bonus).
Mountain fortresses such as Amberd, fortified by Vahram Pahlavuni, who built its church in 1026, and Bjni, and the walled cities of Ani and Kars (Hewsen, 2001).
Mountain fortresses such as Amberd, fortified by Vahram Pahlavuni, who built its church in 1026, and Bjni, and the walled cities of Ani and Kars (Hewsen, 2001).
Building in dressed tuff and the carving of khachkars (cross-stones, the earliest dated example at Garni, 879) made stone working central to Armenian culture (Hovannisian, 1997).

Historical call by the traction test (RULES 6.16.5), on the Vietnamese standard: an inference with a stated basis. The rope-pulled heavy stone-thrower (Arabic manjaniq, Greek manganikon) was the standard heavy engine of the powers that fought in and over Armenia throughout the window: Byzantium, in whose 10th-century armies Armenians served in large numbers, and the Caliphate's emirates around Armenia, among them the Sajids of Yusuf. The wars of the window were wars of fortresses (Yusuf's sieges of Kapuyt and Ernjak, 913–914, in Draskhanakerttsi; the double walls Smbat II built round Ani), and in the epilogue the Seljuks battered Manzikert with a great stone-thrower, which a Frankish soldier of the garrison burned (1054; Aristakes Lastivertsi; Matthew of Edessa). The counterweight engine came only after the window (see Trebuchet). No 884–1045 Armenian source consulted for this design names a stone-thrower, so the inference is flagged (civ-level contested list); it is comparable to the Vietnamese one, though it rests on the engines of the neighbouring powers and of the armies in which Armenians served rather than on an Armenian-led siege. It replaces the counterweight Trebuchet as the long-range siege weapon (RULES 6.11), trained at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age.

Kept from the game (level 1). The ocelomeh were, with the eagle warriors (cuauhmeh), one of the two great military orders, ranked below only the otontin and the cuachicqueh; entry depended above all on taking captives, and many members were nobles. The Codex Mendoza shows warriors rising in rank and insignia with each captive. The extra damage after defeating enemies evokes this promotion, although merit came from capturing, not killing (Hassig 1988). The regional Eagle Warrior line also stays in the Aztec tree. Decision: the generic unit lines keep their game names (no Macuahuitl Warrior or Tequihua for the Two-Handed Swordsman and Champion), since neither is a period term for the same function, the first being a modern coinage and the second a rank (RULES 6.16.15). The regional Eagle line is shared with the Maya, and its upper tiers stand for the eagle order; renaming its scout tier alone, for instance after the quimichtin (Sahagún's ‘mice’, the scouts and spies of Mexica armies), would split the line. So the misfit of the Eagle Scout, which turns a noble order into a cheap scout (rated stretched), is flagged for the site, and quimichtin scouts are an N2 idea.

Kept from the game (level 1). The spear-thrower (ahtlatl) with its darts (tlacochtli) was a feared weapon, used mostly by elite warriors as the armies closed, after the bow and sling volleys (Hassig 1988). It was pan-Mesoamerican and far older than the Mexica (already at Teotihuacan), which is why the Maya keep their own atlatl tech (Hul'che Javelineers) with a different effect (intended overlap, RULES 6.7). As a long weapon tradition it is not a datable moment (RULES 6.2, 6.3): it is a kept existing tech, held as a tech rather than a passive by the effect-size tie-break (RULES 6.2.4), since a strong effect suits the brake of cost and delay. Decision: it stays as a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19 b), for its fame and as the game's own Aztec tech. The datable alternatives, Itzcoatl's grants of conquered land to the nobles and warriors who fought Azcapotzalco (1428) and Moctezuma I's laws tying noble privilege and dress to deeds in war (Durán), would be new level-2 techs and are not used.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Garland Wars. Renamed to the standard English rendering of xochiyaoyotl (‘flower war’). The Triple Alliance fought recurrent wars against Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco and Cholula, which the sources present as prearranged, in which picked warriors displayed their skill and took captives. Durán credits the arrangement to Tlacaelel under Moctezuma I (1440–1469); the story that the wars began during the famine of 1450–54 is Ixtlilxóchitl's, and Hicks (1979) doubts it (see contested). Both accounts place the arrangement under Moctezuma I, after the ancient atlatl in the civ's own chronology (RULES 6.4). The attack bonus stands for the battle experience of these veterans (Durán; Hassig 1988).

New in the codex (level 1). After the Triple Alliance of 1428 the conquered provinces paid tribute on a fixed schedule: staple foods from the nearer provinces; cotton mantles, cacao, feathers, warrior suits and gold from the distant ones, recorded province by province in the Codex Mendoza and collected by the stewards (calpixqueh) installed in each province (Berdan & Anawalt 1992; Berdan, Smith et al. 1996). Farm output turning into gold renders tribute in kind becoming the wealth of the state. Tribute is a datable institution, so it is the Town Center tech rather than a passive bonus (RULES 6.2). The effect is Burgundian Vineyards, kept by the Burgundians and shared in the Persians', Berbers', Tatars' and Rus' designs, and the Bengalis' design has it as a passive: seven civs in all (RULES 6.7; reuse is accepted in N1, RULES 6.16.12).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: there were no rams and no wheeled vehicles in pre-Hispanic Mesoamerica.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Battering Ram).
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Battering Ram).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: no torsion or traction artillery existed in the Americas.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Mangonel).
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Mangonel).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: no bolt-throwers existed in the Americas.
Removed with the Siege Workshop: a wheeled assault tower; Mesoamerican assaults used no such engines.
Counterweight artillery never existed in the Americas; the only trebuchet seen at Tenochtitlan was built by the Spaniards in 1521 and failed at its first shot (Bernal Díaz; Cortés, third letter).
No siege engines are left to improve.

The crossbow was unknown in the pre-Hispanic Americas, which have neither crossbow tier (RULES 6.16.3); Aztec missile troops were archers, slingers and atlatl dart-throwers (Hassig 1988). Archers, Slingers and Skirmishers with Atlatl cover the role. In the current game the Bulgarians also lack crossbows (so do the current Spanish; the Castilian and Bulgarian designs restore the Crossbowman).
Removed with the Crossbowman (see there).

High-castled sailing warships were unknown; the Mexica navy was thousands of dugout canoes (acalli) on Lake Texcoco (Cortés, third letter). The Aztecs already lack the Galleon. Boat tier (RULES 6.16.1), resting on the acalli: the high-seas sailing ships (Galleon, Carrack) are removed and the siege ship goes with the siege engines, while the Galley (renamed Canoe), Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines stay with their tiers as a generic abstraction of canoe fleets for water maps; the demolition ships are generic post-1500 items kept as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.2).
A sailing ship carrying a catapult: both a European ship type and a siege engine.
There was no printing: Mexica books (amoxtli) were painted by hand. With no equivalent for the function the tech is removed (18 of the game's 56 civs already lack it).

The pochteca were professional long-distance merchants organised in hereditary, self-governing corporations with their own courts, who also served the state as spies (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, book 9). The current game gives Guilds to the Incas but not to the Aztecs; here it is added and renamed Pochteca (agreed rename).
Renamed from Guilds. Agreed rename: the guild-like corporations of the pochteca, the professional merchants of Tenochtitlan, Tlatelolco and other cities (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, book 9).

The Mexica and their allies built in stone and lime: the Templo Mayor, the causeways across the lake, the Chapultepec aqueduct and Nezahualcoyotl's dike (1449). The civ already had Fortified Wall without Masonry or Architecture, which was incoherent.

Same basis as Masonry: monumental and hydraulic engineering on the scale of the Templo Mayor and the dike of Nezahualcoyotl. Decision: the Keep, which the Aztecs lack in the game, is not added, since the region gives it only where defensive stone towers are documented (the Inca); the temple-pyramid as a town's last stronghold (the burning-temple glyph of the Codex Mendoza; Cortés's ‘torres’ at Cholula) is a reading the design declines, and the Guard Tower and Fortified Wall stay as abstractions.

Slingers fought beside archers as standard Aztec missile troops (Hassig 1988), and Bernal Díaz repeatedly describes showers of sling stones. The regional Slinger, which the Inca, Muisca and Mapuche keep and the Maya also receive, takes over part of the role of the removed crossbows.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no siege engine of any kind existed in the pre-contact Americas (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice. The Siege Workshop stays in the tree for this engine alone. For its other units the design’s reading stands: No Mesoamerican people built siege engines: towns fell to assault, fire and blockade. Infantry with the anti-building bonus, Arson, Sappers and Petards replace them (owner's decision, RULES 6.16.5; RULES 6.11 and section 10). Before the heavy-engine floor every Castle had to be taken by units standing in its arrow fire; the Traction Trebuchet now does it from range, as a game convention, until an N2/N3 assault unit exists (ideas), with no compensating bonus (RULES 6.16.13). The Petard, a 16th-century gunpowder charge, stays unrenamed as a flagged generic abstraction of assault parties with fire, outside the one-late-element limit (RULES 6.16.2).

Renamed from Horse Collar. Agreed rename. Chinampas, raised beds of lake mud between canals, fed Tenochtitlan; the freshwater southern lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco were turned into vast chinampa districts under the Triple Alliance in the 15th century (Smith 2012). The farm bonus renders their scale; this rename gives the generic farm upgrade its local name.

Renamed from Heavy Plow. There was no plough (farmers used the digging stick, huictli). Hillside terraces (metepantli), often edged with maguey, intensified farming around the Basin, notably in the Texcoco piedmont (Donkin 1979). Same effect; the same rename is used for the Maya.

Renamed from Crop Rotation. Agreed rename. The milpa, intercropping maize, beans and squash, kept fields productive: the Mesoamerican equivalent of rotation. The word is Nahuatl (mīlli, ‘field’, with -pan, ‘on’); the same rename is used for the Maya as the standard term. The tier order is a game convention: historically the milpa came first, and chinampas and terraces intensified it later.

Renamed from Gambesons. Same effect as Gambesons (Militia-line +1 pierce armor): the ichcahuipilli was a quilted cotton jacket, the standard body armour of Mesoamerican warriors, which the Spaniards adopted as the escaupil. The Maya get the same tech under an English name.

Renamed from Iron Casting. There was no iron. Prismatic obsidian blades struck from prepared cores, much of it the green obsidian of the Sierra de las Navajas near Pachuca, edged the macuahuitl and tipped darts and spears (Hassig 1988; Smith 2012). Same effect as Iron Casting. The Maya counterpart is Flint Points and the Inca one Tin Bronze. The other Blacksmith tiers keep their generic names as a flagged generic equipment level (RULES 6.16.6): Forging and Blast Furnace, although there was no iron metallurgy (metals, copper, gold and silver, were mostly ornamental); Bodkin Arrow, although arrowheads were of obsidian and flint, not forged iron; and Scale Mail, Chain Mail and Plate Mail Armor, although there was no metal armour. The quilted cotton ichcahuipilli already renames Gambesons and cannot stand for three tiers more. The feathered warrior suits (tlahuiztli) that veterans wore over it are documented above all as insignia granted by the number of captives taken (Codex Mendoza, fols. 64r–67r); how much protection they added beyond the cotton armour is uncertain, so they do not pass the same-function test for an armour tier (RULES 6.16.15), and regional armour names stay an N2 idea. Chemistry stays for its +1 ranged attack as a flagged abstraction, although the Mexica had no gunpowder. The Aztecs lack Ring Archer Armor in the game, and the design leaves it so.

Renamed from Wheelbarrow. There were no wheeled vehicles: loads were carried with the tumpline (mecapalli), a strap passing over the forehead, the basic tool of Mesoamerican porters (Hassig 1985). Same rename for the Maya.

Renamed from Hand Cart. Porters used a wooden carrying frame (cacaxtli) slung from the tumpline, shown in the Codex Mendoza (Hassig 1985). Parallel to the agreed Hand Cart → Llama Caravans for the Incas; same rename for the Maya. The Trade Cart keeps its generic name and look as a flagged abstraction of the pochteca's porter trains (RULES 6.16.6), since there were no wheeled vehicles.

Renamed from Coinage. There were no coins: cacao beans served as small change and standard cotton mantles (quachtli) as larger units of value in markets and tribute (Berdan, Smith et al. 1996). Same rename for the Maya, where Landa also records cacao as money. Banking (tributes to other players are free) keeps its generic name as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.6), since no Mesoamerican equivalent with a period term was found.

Renamed from Treadmill Crane. There were no cranes or treadwheels: temples, causeways and dikes were raised by the coatequitl, the rotational labour draft for public works that each calpolli owed to its city and ruler (Hassig 1985; Smith 2012). Same effect as Treadmill Crane (Villagers construct buildings +20% faster): organised labour is the Mexica equivalent of faster building, as the tumpline is of the Wheelbarrow. A rename beyond the agreed list, applied under RULES 6.16.6. The Inca design renames it Mit'a, after the Andean rotating labour service; the Maya keep Treadmill Crane under its generic name as a flagged abstraction, since the term is Nahuatl (see the Maya design).

Renamed from Galley, with the look of the Canoe. The Mexica fought on the lake in dugout canoes (acalli): thousands of them defended Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Cortés had thirteen brigantines built to break them (Cortés, third letter; Bernal Díaz). The Scenario Editor Canoe, a small warship introduced in The Forgotten (RULES section 5), gives the Galley the look of a dugout war canoe; the Galley keeps its stats, and the Canoe's look, scale, attack and role must be checked in game. Same rename for the Maya, Mapuche and Tupi, and outside the Americas in the Malians' and Avars' designs; the acalli war-canoe line proper is an N3 idea.
Renamed from War Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Upgrade tier of the renamed Galley, with the same Canoe look (see Galley).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Ratha (Mounted Archer). Paik (from Sanskrit padatika, merged with Persian payk) was the foot soldier of Bengal and Orissa, armed with bow, sword, shield and spear and later the matchlock, and the backbone of the Sultanate's armies and of the later Baro-Bhuyans (Banglapedia, ‘Paik’ and ‘Military’; Sarkar (ed.) 1948). Besides the levies the sultans kept a palace guard of paiks: it killed Jalaluddin Fath Shah in 1487, opening the Habshi period, and Alauddin Husain Shah (1494–1519) disbanded it (Riyaz-us-Salatin; Sarkar (ed.) 1948). Most paiks were archers, so the model is the Rattan Archer, a shielded foot archer, rather than a spear infantry such as the game's Ghulam (the model of the Tamils' Velaikkarar); both would be placeholders until new art (see ideas).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Ratha (Mounted Archer). Paik (from Sanskrit padatika, merged with Persian payk) was the foot soldier of Bengal and Orissa, armed with bow, sword, shield and spear and later the matchlock, and the backbone of the Sultanate's armies and of the later Baro-Bhuyans (Banglapedia, ‘Paik’ and ‘Military’; Sarkar (ed.) 1948). Besides the levies the sultans kept a palace guard of paiks: it killed Jalaluddin Fath Shah in 1487, opening the Habshi period, and Alauddin Husain Shah (1494–1519) disbanded it (Riyaz-us-Salatin; Sarkar (ed.) 1948). Most paiks were archers, so the model is the Rattan Archer, a shielded foot archer, rather than a spear infantry such as the game's Ghulam (the model of the Tamils' Velaikkarar); both would be placeholders until new art (see ideas).
Renamed from Elite Rattan Archer. Follows the unique unit (Rattan Archer → Paik), for the Bengalis only.

New in the codex (level 2). By 1352 Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah had united Lakhnauti, Satgaon and Sonargaon under one ruler, and Delhi chroniclers called him Shah-i Bangalah, ‘king of Bengal’ (Shams Siraj Afif); the name Bangalah, until then that of the eastern delta, came to mean the whole region (Eaton 1993, ch. 2). The new kingdom held out twice in the fort of Ekdala against Firuz Shah Tughluq (1353–54, 1358–59), which secured nearly two centuries of independence, and built a new capital at Pandua, whose Adina mosque (1373–75) was the largest in the subcontinent. Sturdier, busier Town Centers render a united kingdom that held its centres. Decision: the Town Center slot goes to the union of 1352, which gave the civ its name, rather than to a Pala moment such as the prakriti's choice of Gopala (c. 750) that ended the ‘law of the fish’, recorded in Dharmapala's Khalimpur plate, whose reading is itself contested (see contested).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Paiks (Rathas and Elephant Units attack +20% faster). In the Indian tradition Bengal and Bihar were the land of the best war elephants: the Arthashastra (2.2) ranks those of Kalinga and Anga first (Trautmann 2015), and the Hastyayurveda, the Sanskrit treatise on elephant medicine attributed to the sage Palakapya, is set at Champa in Anga, near modern Bhagalpur, in the Pala heartland. The Pala kings kept royal herds under their own officers: the stock list of officials in their land grants, from Dharmapala's Khalimpur plate (c. 800) onwards, includes a superintendent of elephants and horses (and of cattle, buffaloes, goats and sheep) (Majumdar (ed.) 1943); the Akhbar (851) credits the king of ‘Rahma’ with some 50,000 elephants, and Lakhnauti later sent elephants to Delhi as tribute (Minhaj; Digby 1971). The tech stands for the keeping and healing of these royal herds, while the elephant passive renders their place in battle and the Hindustanis' elephant passive the Delhi stables that Bengal helped to fill. It renames the game's Dravidian Medical Corps (a 19th-century military name) with the same effect; the Tamils' design gives that tech up. It replaces Paiks, which named the foot soldier but sped up chariots and elephants; the paik becomes the unique unit. Decision: the level-1 rename stands rather than a new level-2 tech for one of the civ's datable royal and military moments, none of which has a fitting existing effect: Dharmapala's Kanyakubja assembly (c. 800), where he installed Chakrayudha with the assent of the northern kings; Ramapala's recovery of Varendri with the help of his samantas (late 11th century, Ramacharita); and Ekdala (1353–59).

Changed by the codex (level 1). The Palas, who styled themselves paramasaugata (‘devout Buddhists’), were the last great royal patrons of Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism in India; they endowed monasteries, shrines and images across Bengal and Bihar, and the Vajrayana of their age, carried to Tibet by masters such as Atisha (who left Vikramashila c. 1040), shaped Tibetan Buddhism. The effect is an arbitrary abstraction of a large, cheaply sustained monastic and lay population.

No secure evidence of guns on the Sultanate's boats: the gun-armed river flotilla (nawara) is Mughal, of the 17th century. The Galley and Fire Ship lines keep the anti-ship role at sea and the single-use Demolition Ship the anti-building role; no substitute siege warship is added (RULES 6.16.1). Navy tier: see Galleon.
Same basis.

Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): the boat tier, by the vessels the sources name. The war fleets of the delta's own states are well attested, but only as fleets of boats (Sanskrit nau in the Pala and Sena records): the fleet of boats on the Ganges by Devapala's camp at Mudgagiri (Monghyr plate); Vijayasena's fleet sent up the Ganges against the kings of the west (Deopara prashasti); the war fleet that Iwaz Khalji (c. 1212–27) organised at Lakhnauti, the first of Bengal's Muslim rulers credited with one (Banglapedia, ‘Iwaz Khalji’); the war-boats with which Fakhr al-Din of Sonargaon fought Lakhnauti in the rainy seasons (Ibn Battuta, 1340s); the Bengali boats on the Ghaghra in 1529 (Baburnama); and Turbak's fleet, beaten by the Ahoms in 1533 (the Buranjis, via Gait 1906). None of these sources describes the hulls, and the known names of Bengali war-boats (kosa, ghurab) belong to the Mughal flotilla of the 17th century, so nothing inside the window shows planked war galleys (see contested); the design applies the boat tier, as for the Burmese river fleets. The high-seas sailing warships (Galleon, Carrack) are removed, while the Galley, Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines stay with their tiers as an abstraction of the river fleets for water maps, with the Dock techs and the ‘Galleon, Fast Fire Ship and Carrack’ upgrade kept for the Fast Fire Ship. Bengal's sea-going ships, which carried its rice and cloth to Malacca (Tomé Pires), were merchant shipping, not a war fleet. The ship-regeneration passive and the N2 river war-boat idea carry the delta's naval weight. The Scenario Editor's Canoe (RULES section 5), which the Avar, Aztec, Maya, Mapuche, Tupi and Malian designs use as the Galley's look (the Avars for the Slav dugouts of 626), is not adopted: the sources describe no hulls for the delta's war-boats, so a dugout look would claim a vessel type they do not attest, and in the game the Canoe is a light boat (70 HP; codex/tools/scenario-units-stats.md), lighter than fleets that fought on the rivers and carried armies; the Burmese design declines it on the same ground for the Irrawaddy fleets. The Galley keeps its look.
See Galleon.

No crossbows are attested in Pala, Sena or Sultanate armies, whose archers used bamboo bows; in South Asia the crossbow belongs mainly to the hill peoples of the north-east. The Arbalester needs crossbow evidence, so the crossbow tier goes and the Crossbowman stays as the generic Castle Age bow upgrade until the N2 bow/crossbow split (RULES 6.16.3); the Paik and the Elephant Archer carry the archery.

Bengal's wars turned on boats, elephants and foot archers, and the counterweight trebuchet is not attested in Pala, Sena or Sultanate Bengal in the sources used here, nor are the maghribi engines of Alauddin Khalji's sieges in Rajasthan and the Deccan, on which the Hindustanis keep the Trebuchet. Removed as an engine that never reached the civ (RULES 6.16.5). The traction test of the same rule fails as well, so no Traction Trebuchet is given: no heavy stone-throwing engine of any kind is recorded in Pala, Sena or Sultanate hands in these sources, from the Pala wars to the defence of Ekdala (1353–59) and the Husain Shahi conquest of Kamata (c. 1498). The Mangonel-line stays as the generic stone-thrower, and with the Siege and Armored Elephants and the Petard it keeps the civ able to break buildings, while the Bombard Cannon gives the late Sultanate a long-range weapon in the Imperial Age (see there). Decision (power budget): the kit stands as designed. The cash-crop passive, cheaper University technologies, Shah-i Bangalah and the Bombard Cannon come in; the Arbalester, the Cannon Galleons, the Galleon and Carrack (boat tier), the Trebuchet, the Ratha, Siphons and Block Printing go, and the archers still get no Thumb Ring (no thumb draw is attested in Bengal, RULES 6.16.4). The Bombard Cannon, the one late element, gives the Imperial Age its long-range weapon against buildings, and no further compensation is added (RULES 6.16.13).
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
No printing in the window: Sanskrit, Bengali and Persian texts were copied by hand, and the first book in Bengali type, Halhed's grammar, was printed at Hooghly in 1778.

An abstraction of faster building: no treadwheel cranes are attested in Bengal, and the tech stands for the scale of its brick building, from the mahavihara of Somapura, among the largest monasteries of South Asia, to the Adina mosque (1373–75), the largest mosque of the subcontinent in its day. Stone Shaft Mining stays absent, which fits a delta without stone.

The civ's one late element (RULES section 2), in the Imperial Age, its game age. Bengal's guns are firmly attested only from the 1510s (see contested), and contemporary witnesses, Portuguese, Mughal and Ahom, supply the clear fame the rule asks for: João de Barros credits artillery with Bengal's edge over Arakan and Tripura (via Banglapedia, ‘Military’); Babur, who fought Nusrat Shah's army on the Ghaghra in 1529, says the Bengalis were famous for their artillery, though he found that they fired at random (Baburnama); and the Ahom Buranjis record the guns of Turbak's invasion (1532–33) and their capture by the Ahoms (Gait 1906). Cast copper-alloy cannon of the Husain Shahi period also survive (Naher, Lahiri and Chattopadhyay 2014), among them a piece from Nariya (Shariatpur) in the Bangladesh National Museum whose inscription the authors read as dated 945 AH and assign to Ghiyath al-Din Mahmud Shah, the last Husain Shahi sultan; but 945 AH began on 30 May 1538, around or just after Sher Shah's capture of Gaur, which closes the window, so the reading or the attribution is uncertain, and the piece confirms the arm rather than standing as evidence inside the window. Relevance (RULES 6.9): the guns gave the late Sultanate its edge over its eastern neighbours (Barros) and armed its army against Babur on the Ghaghra (1529) and its invasion of the Ahom kingdom (1532–33). Only the bombard comes in: a Hand Cannoneer for the paiks' later matchlocks would be a second late element, and gun-armed boats are not attested inside the window (see Cannon Galleon). It also gives the civ, which loses the counterweight Trebuchet, a long-range weapon against buildings from the Imperial Age (RULES 6.16.5).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Camel Archer. al-Bakri (1068) describes the early Almoravids fighting on foot in close ranks, the front rank with long spears and the ranks behind with javelins; in a separate passage he records the prized lamt shields of antelope hide made at Nul Lamta and sought in the Maghreb and al-Andalus, the shield this infantry carried. The Inca Kamayuk, a spearman with long reach strong against cavalry, is the nearest existing unit; the Mapuche Colihue Lancer and the Ethiopians' Chewa Spearman use it too. Named after the al-murabitun, ‘the people of the ribat’, who gave the Almoravids their name. It replaces the Camel Archer: no camel-mounted archer is attested as a Maghrebi troop type (camels served the Saharan Sanhaja and the army's baggage, and combat relied on spears, javelins and swords).

Renamed from Elite Kamayuk. Follows the unique unit (Kamayuk → Murabit) for the Berbers only.

New in the codex (level 1). In 1159–1160 Abd al-Mu'min had the Maghreb surveyed (taksir) from Barqa to the Sus, deducted a third for mountains, rivers and wasteland, and assessed the rest for the land tax (kharaj), payable in grain and coin (Ibn Abi Zar, Rawd al-qirtas, year 555 AH); it gave the Almohad caliphate its fiscal base (Bennison, 2016). Farmers whose fields yield coin to the treasury translate the assessment, as for the Persians' Kharaj, the same land tax. It takes Kasbah's slot (see dropped). The shared tech is kept rather than a new fiscal tech (level 2) with ‘All gold income +10% faster’, the gold half of Grand Trunk Road, which the Arabs' design now uses for Abd al-Malik's coinage.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Maghrebi Camels (Camel Units regenerate 15 HP per minute). Yusuf ibn Tashfin kept a royal guard of black slaves (ʿabīd), and in the 14th-century narratives of Zallaqa/Sagrajas (1086) the Almoravid vanguard held while Yusuf took the Castilian camp and committed this black guard, whose attack broke Alfonso VI's knights; one of its men wounded the king (Rawd al-qirtas; al-Hulal al-mawshiyya; Huici Miranda, 1956). The Almohad and Marinid sultans kept black slave guards beside their tribal troops (Bennison, 2016). Infantry stronger against cavalry translates foot soldiers who broke a charge of armoured knights. Maghrebi Camels, an abstraction of the dromedary's hardiness, gives way to this royal institution.

No Maghrebi hand firearms are documented before the early 16th century, when Moroccan and Hafsid troops met the Portuguese enclaves with them (the earliest dates are contested), and the famous Moroccan arquebusiers of Alcácer Quibir (1578) and Tondibi (1591) were Saadian, after the window and outside the civ's dynasties: the unit would be a late element without clear Berber fame (RULES section 2). The Bombard Cannon stays on secure in-window evidence: the Marinid defenders of Algeciras fired iron balls with ‘truenos’ against Alfonso XI (1342–1344; Crónica de Alfonso XI).

No Maghrebi gun-armed sailing fleet is documented inside the window; the gun-carrying corsair fleets of Algiers and Tunis came with the Barbarossa brothers and the Ottomans after 1516. The galleys and fire ships keep the fleet-of-ships tier (RULES 6.16.1; see the Ships bonus), the Galleon as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2).
As Cannon Galleon.
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
The Almoravid infantry fought as a phalanx with long spears in the front rank (al-Bakri, 1068); stopping at the Pikeman contradicted their best-documented tactic.

Fortification by Berber dynasties (see the tabiya bonus): the Almoravid walls of Marrakesh, raised in rammed earth (tabiya) by Ali ibn Yusuf in 1126–1127; the Almohad walls and gates of Rabat (Bab er-Rouah) and the Kasbah of the Udayas (c. 1150–1197); the Almohad rebuilding of the Alcazaba of Badajoz (1169) with its albarrana towers; the Torre del Oro in Seville (1220–1221); and the Marinid siege-city of al-Mansura outside Tlemcen (1299–1307).

Fortification by Berber dynasties (see the tabiya bonus): the Almoravid walls of Marrakesh, raised in rammed earth (tabiya) by Ali ibn Yusuf in 1126–1127; the Almohad walls and gates of Rabat (Bab er-Rouah) and the Kasbah of the Udayas (c. 1150–1197); the Almohad rebuilding of the Alcazaba of Badajoz (1169) with its albarrana towers; the Torre del Oro in Seville (1220–1221); and the Marinid siege-city of al-Mansura outside Tlemcen (1299–1307).

Almohad monuments such as the Kutubiyya in Marrakesh, the Hassan Tower in Rabat and the Giralda in Seville; the analysis notes the absence contradicted the civ's own history text. Treadmill Crane stays in the tree under the region's one reading of the tech (see the Arabs' design): no treadwheel crane is attested at Maghrebi building sites in the sources used here, so it is kept as a generic abstraction of faster building, resting on these Almoravid and Almohad programmes.

Kept from the game (level 1). The Hussite wagon fort (vozová hradba): reinforced wagons with boards, chained together, crewed by crossbowmen, handgunners and flailmen, behind which the infantry was safe from missiles and cavalry. Žižka’s Military Ordinance (1423) is mainly a code of discipline and march; the crews are known from later sources and reconstructions (Durdík 1953). The real fort worked as a closed, static formation, not as single vehicles; Wagenburg Tactics’ armour stands for the closed fort. Shared with the Magyars through their Black Army tech.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Houfnice (upgrade of the Bombard Cannon: long-range anti-building gun that cannot attack at close range). In the Hussite wagon fort the houfnice and the lighter tarasnice fired stones or scattershot at close range into massed troops (houf, ‘crowd’) (Durdík 1953); through German Haubitze and Dutch houwitser the name gave English ‘howitzer’. The game made it a super-bombard with long range and a minimum range, the opposite of its role; the Organ Gun profile (a gunpowder piece firing volleys at groups of units) is the closest existing match, though the Organ Gun is multi-barrelled and weak against cavalry, while the houfnice was a single short barrel used from the wagon fort against both infantry and horse (own art is N3). Trained at the Siege Workshop from the Imperial Age, where the old Houfnice upgrade stood, with its Elite upgrade at the Castle as for the Organ Gun. The Bombard Cannon stays as the siege gun. The name also belongs to a different game unit, the Houfnice (its own model), the Bombard Cannon upgrade this design replaces: a reused name, allowed with a note on the site (RULES 6.16.15); the site keys units by model. Decision: the unit is rebuilt in N1 rather than left for N2, since the game’s long-range super-bombard inverts the houfnice’s role; a Castle Age Houfnice beside the Castle Age Hand Cannoneer would be too large a power shift, so it keeps the Imperial Age.

Renamed from Elite Organ Gun. Follows the unique unit (Organ Gun → Houfnice), for the Bohemians only; the Portuguese design drops the Organ Gun.

Changed by the codex (level 2); replaces Wagenburg Tactics (Gunpowder Units move +10% faster). Hussite field armies marched in parallel wagon columns that could close into a fort quickly (reconstructed from later 15th-century sources by Durdík 1953; the 1423 Ordinance sets the order and discipline of the march) and ranged far on their raids (the ‘spanilé jízdy’ of 1427–33 reached the Baltic). Once closed, the chained, boarded wagons held off cavalry and storming infantry, as at Ústí nad Labem (1426). The old effect kept only the march; the added armour gives the static fort, which is worth a new tech (level 2) rather than the game’s speed-only effect. The name stays Wagenburg, the German term of the Hussites’ enemies and of modern scholarship, which the game already uses; the Czech is vozová hradba.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Hussite Reforms (Castle unique tech, same effect). The Four Articles of Prague (1420) demanded free preaching, the chalice for the laity, apostolic poverty for the clergy and the punishment of public sins by the secular power; the Diet of Čáslav (1421) adopted them as the programme of the land, and Church estates passed largely to the nobility and the towns (Kaminsky 1967; Šmahel 1993). Three of the four articles are religious demands, so the tech belongs at the Monastery (RULES 6.2); a clergy that costs no gold is a neat translation of the apostolic poverty the Articles demanded. The label keeps the game’s ‘Gunpowder and Monk’: priests such as Prokop the Great led the Hussite armies and the lay chalice was the movement’s symbol, although the Taborites sacked many monasteries in 1419–21.

New in the codex (level 2). On 8 March 1348 Charles IV founded the New Town of Prague, a planned town of broad streets and great markets (the Horse and Cattle Markets) with its own walls beside the Old Town; with the castle, the Old Town and the Lesser Town it made Prague the imperial residence and one of the largest cities of Central Europe, and the defenestration at its town hall on 30 July 1419 began the Hussite revolution (Kaminsky 1967; Šmahel 1993). The same programme of 1348 founded the University (see the University bonus) and defined the Lands of the Bohemian Crown. Town Centers that are sturdier and work faster stand for the walled, growing capital. A new tech (level 2): no existing unique tech represents a planned capital, and the Four Articles cannot be split into a second tech (RULES 6.3). Chosen over Wenceslas II’s mining code (Ius regale montanorum, c. 1300) and groschen reform, which would add a second silver element beside the mining passive, which already carries the groschen.
Bohemia was landlocked: no gun-armed warships.
As Cannon Galleon.

Navy (RULES 6.16.1): Bohemia was landlocked and had no war fleet of its own, so the civ keeps the basic navy (Galley-line to War Galley, Fire Galley and Fire Ship, Hulk and War Hulk, demolition ships and the generic Dock techs), with no substitute siege warship.
As Galleon.
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. The Hussite crossbowmen fought from the wagons (see the Hussite Wagon), and the sources consulted record no Bohemian mounted crossbowmen as a troop type, before or after the Hussite wars. Removed; the crossbowmen stay as the foot Crossbowman and Arbalester.

Before the Hussites, Bohemia fielded first-rate armoured cavalry: Ottokar II won at Kressenbrunn (1260) with his heavy horse and fell at the Marchfeld (1278), and John the Blind died charging with his knights at Crécy (1346). The last cavalry armour upgrade (held by 36 of the game’s 56 civs) restores part of that kingdom without changing the Hussite profile. Bloodlines is not added: the evidence is about armour, not horse breeding.
Charles IV was a great builder: Karlštejn (from 1348), the New Town of Prague, the Charles Bridge (from 1357) and St Vitus’ cathedral under Peter Parler.

Kept from the game (level 1). The emblematic soldier of English armies from Edward I’s Welsh wars to Castillon (1277–1453). Bows recovered from the Mary Rose (sunk 1545) suggest very heavy draw weights (estimates of c. 100–180 lbf, debated). English archers also carried swords or bucklers and stakes and were decisive only alongside dismounted men-at-arms (Strickland and Hardy 2005).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Yeomen (Castle unique tech, same effect). The Crown’s arms legislation supplied the archers: Henry III’s writs of 1242 and 1252 extended Henry II’s Assize of Arms (1181) to bows and arrows for the poorer free men; Edward I’s Statute of Winchester (1285) fixed the arms every man had to keep by his wealth and ordered a watch at the town gates from sunset to sunrise (‘watch and ward’); and Edward III’s proclamation of 1363 ordered archery practice on holidays, an order repeated in the Statute of Cambridge (1388) and later, which suggests it was not always obeyed (Strickland and Hardy 2005). With a culture of archery among free men of modest means (later called yeomen), it fed armies whose archers were increasingly recruited as professionals by indenture (Bell, Curry, King and Simpkin, The Soldier in Later Medieval England, 2013). At the Town Center because it rests on the Crown’s legislation, a state matter (RULES 6.2); the tower half fits the Statute’s watch. This is now the civ’s only range bonus: the passive renders rate of shooting instead (level-1 review, section 9).

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Warwolf (Trebuchets deal blast damage and are more accurate). The chevauchée, the great mounted raid that burned and plundered across enemy country, was the core of Edward III’s strategy: the Cambrésis (1339), Normandy on the way to Crécy (1346), the Black Prince’s raids from Bordeaux to Narbonne (1355) and towards the Loire before Poitiers (1356), and Reims (1359–60) (Rogers, War Cruel and Sharp, 2000; Sumption). The later raids of Knolles (1370), John of Gaunt (1373, from Calais to Bordeaux) and Buckingham (1380–81) failed to bring the French to battle, and Henry V’s war (1415–22) was one of sieges and occupation instead. The whole army rode. The Knight-line stands for the men-at-arms, and the Scout Cavalry-line for the hobelars, light horsemen raised first in the English lordship of Ireland (the first of them came to Edward I’s Scottish campaign of 1296) and then in England, who rode with Edward III’s armies in the 1330s and 1340s until the mounted archers replaced them (Morris 1914; Lydon 1954; Prestwich 1996; see the Gaels’ contested note on the hobelar); the mounted archers, who rode with the raids and shot on foot, are the foot archers. The loot applies to every enemy building destroyed, as in the Danes’ bonus, since the engine ties no loot to a unit class. Replaces Warwolf, dropped under the relevance test (see [[dropped]]); the analysis proposed this tech.

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. Crossbowmen, many of them foreign (Gascon, Brabançon, Genoese), were important in Angevin and early Edwardian armies, among them mounted crossbowmen (balistarii equites) in the pay of John and Henry III, but they belong before the civ’s core period: after c. 1300 the longbow displaced the crossbow in English field armies, the crossbow survived mainly in garrisons and at sea, and the ‘mounted archers’ of the Hundred Years War rode to battle and shot on foot with the longbow (Strickland and Hardy 2005; Prestwich 1996; Ayton 1994). Removed; no substitute is needed, since the archers are the foot Archer line and the Longbowman (see the N2 idea of a dismounting mounted archer). The designs of the Franks, Burgundians, Italians, Castilians, Portuguese, Poles and Germans keep the line on the same test.
Same reason as the Mounted Crossbowman.
The cranequin (rack-and-pinion spanning device) is a 15th-century continental crossbow fitting; it has no place in an army built on the longbow.

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, the projector of Greek fire, a state secret that Constantine VII ordered never to be given to another nation (De Administrando Imperio 13); its game effect, an explosive charge for fire ships, has no medieval English equivalent. The fire-ship line itself stays as the engine’s convention for close-range incendiary warships.

English armies besieged with gunpowder artillery: guns at the siege of Calais (1346–47), Henry V’s train of great guns at Harfleur (1415) and the artillery of the conquest of Normandy (Caen 1417, Rouen 1418–19) (Sumption, vol. IV). The civ already had the Cannon Galleon; land artillery removes that incoherence. The Hand Cannoneer is not added: handgunners in English armies are documented mainly in the Wars of the Roses (Edward IV’s Flemish handgunners in 1471; the Bosworth shot of 1485), after the design core (see contested).

Genoese carracks captured at the battle of the Seine (1416) were taken into Henry V’s navy, which also built its own ‘great ships’, the largest being the Grace Dieu (launched 1418); the Mary Rose (1511), built just after the window, shows the type in English service (Rodger, The Safeguard of the Sea, 1997). In the game the Britons were the only civ of the region without it. Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, from the royal cogs of Edward III’s war (Sluys, 1340) to Henry V’s great ships, with the Galleon as the skeleton’s flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2); the Cannon Galleon rests on guns aboard English warships from the 1330s (the cog Christopher is reported with three guns and a handgun when the French took her at Arnemuiden, 1338).

The open fields of the Midland system were worked in two- and three-course rotations, with the fallow course grazed by the village’s livestock (David Hall, The Open Fields of England, 2014). The game gives the tech to the Saxons (now the Anglo-Saxons’ design, which ends in 1066) but not to the Britons, who stand for later medieval England, a reversed chronology (RULES 6.12).

Kept from the game (level 1). The mounted aristocracy (boilas, later bolyars) was the elite core of Bulgarian armies from the khanate to the Second Empire, armoured in part from the khan's stores (the inventory inscriptions cited for the Blacksmith half of the siege passive); konnik is the ordinary Bulgarian word for horseman. The name stays: “Bolyar”, which the analysis proposes, would clash with the Boyar of the Rus' and the Lithuanians. Fighting on as infantry when unhorsed is a game mechanic, not a documented Bulgarian speciality.
