New in the codex (level 1); replaces Stirrups (Cavalry attacks +33% faster), the game's Castle Age Castle tech, dropped (see [[dropped]]). Krum (khan c. 803–814) gave the Bulgars a siege train: an Arab engineer stationed at Adrianople, unpaid by Nikephoros I, deserted to him and taught the Bulgars to build engines, with which Krum took Mesembria (812), capturing siphons and Greek fire (Theophanes); he took Adrianople after a siege (813) and deported its people beyond the Danube. For the campaign of 814 against Constantinople he gathered a great train of engines of every kind, which the Scriptor incertus says was to be carried on 5,000 iron-bound wagons drawn by 10,000 oxen; he died on 13 April 814, before it set out. The armour of the game's Ironclad renders the iron-bound train; the tech is the First Empire's datable military moment, at the Castle in the Castle Age, before Cuman Alliance (RULES 6.4).

New in the codex (level 2). Byzantine payments repeatedly bought peace with Bulgaria: tribute to Asparuh after 680/681 (Theophanes), gifts and the title of kaisar for Tervel (705), garments and red skins worth 30 lb of gold under the treaty of 716, which Krum demanded to renew in 812 (Theophanes), and the annual tribute that Leo VI agreed to pay Simeon after Bulgarophygon (896; Fine, 1983). The peace of 927 crowned this policy: after Simeon's death Romanos I Lekapenos recognised Peter as basileus (tsar) of the Bulgarians and the head of the Bulgarian church as patriarch, gave him his granddaughter Maria, renamed Irene (“peace”), and resumed yearly payments (Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes). The gold-income effect abstracts these payments, although the sums were modest (the 30 lb of gold of 716 equal some 2,160 nomismata, against the 80,000–200,000 solidi a year paid to the Avars) and the Second Empire received no comparable tribute; the treaty is a datable act of state, so it sits at the Town Center (RULES 6.2).

New in the codex (level 1). In 893 a council of the realm deposed Boris I's son Vladimir-Rasate, enthroned Simeon, moved the capital from Pliska to Preslav and made Slavonic the language of the Bulgarian church, with clergy trained by Clement and Naum replacing the Greek clergy; Clement is said to have taught some 3,500 pupils in his district of Kutmichevitsa before 893 (Theophylact of Ohrid, Life of Clement). The Preslav and Ohrid schools translated and copied Greek religious texts into Slavonic, and Chernorizets Hrabar's On the Letters defended Constantine-Cyril's Slavonic letters against those who held that only Hebrew, Greek and Latin were fit for scripture (Curta, 2006; Obolensky, 1971). Its effect and its weight are religious, so it sits at the Monastery (RULES 6.2), as Clerical Recruitment does in the Anglo-Saxons' design; Greek remained the language of state inscriptions and seals (the Narash boundary stone of 904, the seals of Simeon and Peter).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Bagains (Militia-line +5 melee armor), the game's Imperial Age Castle tech, dropped (see [[dropped]]). The Cumans were allies of the Asen dynasty, bound to it by marriage and paid in plunder: Peter and Asen brought Cuman troops from beyond the Danube in 1186 (Choniates); Cuman horse archers and a feigned retreat won Kaloyan's victory over the Latin Empire at Adrianople (14 April 1205), where Emperor Baldwin I was captured, after which the Cumans went home with their booty (Villehardouin; Robert de Clari); Kaloyan's wife was a Cuman (Akropolites), and the Terter dynasty (1280–1323) was of Cuman origin (Vásáry, 2005; Madgearu, 2016). Renamed because “alliance” fits the relationship better than “mercenaries”. The team-wide reach is a game convention: the only Bulgarian parallels are the alliance with the Greek archontes of Thrace in 1205 and the joint Bulgarian–Nicaean siege of Constantinople (1235–1236). Identical team-wide effects count once per team (RULES 6.16.12), so a team with Bulgarians and Cumans gets 5 free Elite Kipchaks per Castle, not 10; the reuse of the Kipchak (also the Cumans', Georgians', Hindustanis' and Arabs' model) is accepted under the same rule.
Bulgaria had neither a war navy nor gunpowder before its fall (Tarnovo 1393, Vidin 1396); only the Dobruja despotate kept a small Black Sea fleet in the 1360s–1370s.

No war fleet of its own (see Cannon Galleon): the basic navy only (RULES 6.16.1: Galley and War Galley, Fire Galley and Fire Ship, Hulk and War Hulk, demolition ships and the Dock techs), with no substitute siege warship. Siphons stays out too: Krum captured siphons and liquid fire at Mesembria in 812 (Theophanes), but no source records Bulgarian use.
As Galleon: no ocean-going ships.

Added as the generic Castle Age bow upgrade that every civ whose world knew the crossbow keeps until the N2 bow/crossbow split (RULES 6.16.3): it stands for the Archer's Castle Age tier, not for Bulgarian crossbowmen. The Arbalester, which needs crossbow evidence in the window, stays out, since crossbow use by Bulgarian troops is not established (see the N2 idea).

Christianisation under Boris I (864/865), a patriarchate (927, restored 1235) and great monasteries such as Rila (10th century): the monastery tree should not be cut down for the civ whose history centres on its Christian and literary culture (Heresy stays, for the Bogomils).
As for Faith: a full monastic tradition, from Preslav and Ohrid to the Tarnovo school of Patriarch Euthymius (14th century).
As for Faith: the cult of St John of Rila and the monastic centres of the Second Empire.
Pliska's inner citadel had stone walls over 2 m thick and Preslav was walled in stone; the First Empire also built the Erkesia earthwork across Thrace.
Pliska's inner citadel had stone walls over 2 m thick and Preslav was walled in stone; the First Empire also built the Erkesia earthwork across Thrace.

Kept from the game (level 1). The coustillier (coutilier), named after his coustille (long knife or short sword), was the armed attendant of the man-at-arms in each lance of Charles the Bold’s ordinances (1471–73); the post already existed in the French companies of 1445.

Kept from the game (level 1). The coustillier (coutilier), named after his coustille (long knife or short sword), was the armed attendant of the man-at-arms in each lance of Charles the Bold’s ordinances (1471–73); the post already existed in the French companies of 1445.

Kept from the game (level 1). The urban militias of Flanders with goedendag and pike defeated the French knights at Courtrai (1302), before the Burgundian period. The dukes called up town contingents, as for the siege of Calais (1436), which the men of Ghent and Bruges abandoned; the pikemen of the 1471 lances were professional ordinance troops, not militia.

New in the codex (level 1). Philip the Good’s monetary ordinance of 1433 gave Flanders, Brabant, Hainaut and Holland-Zeeland a common coinage from 1434, struck to one standard in the mints of the four lands, whose silver pieces were known as vierlanders, ‘four-lands’ coins (Spufford, Monetary Problems and Policies in the Burgundian Netherlands 1433–1496, 1970). With the Chambres des comptes of Dijon and Lille (1386), the first States General (1464) and the Parlement of Mechelen (1473), it was one of the institutions that bound the Burgundian Netherlands together (Blockmans and Prevenier 1999). Gold income renders the mint profits and the revenues of a richer, more integrated state, the lower trading fee one trusted coin across the markets of the Low Countries. A state reform, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2). The coinage takes the slot rather than the Chambres des comptes or the Parlement, which would need a new (level-2) tech with an effect no one uses, or Burgundian Vineyards, which moves to the Mill; the civ thus has three techs (four passives and three techs, within the cap of RULES 6.1).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Burgundian Vineyards (Castle unique tech, same effect). Philip the Bold’s ordinance of 31 July 1395 banned the ‘disloyal’ Gamay grape in favour of Pinot Noir to protect the quality and name of Burgundy wine (Dion 1959); Cistercian viticulture (Clos de Vougeot) had made it a prestige export, and the dukes used it as a diplomatic gift. At the Mill because the ordinance and the effect concern farming (RULES 6.2); the Town Center slot goes to the common coinage, a weightier act of the state.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Flemish Revolution (All existing Villagers are transformed to Flemish Militia). Philip the Good founded the Order at Bruges on 10 January 1430, during the festivities for his marriage to Isabella of Portugal, daughter of John I. Its knights (24 under the statutes of 1431, 30 from 1433) swore loyalty to the duke as sovereign of the Order, could not belong to another order without his consent, had their conduct examined at each chapter and could be expelled for treason (Boulton 1987; Vaughan, Philip the Good, 1970): the Order bound the nobility of the scattered lands to the duke, and that sworn loyalty is what the resistance to conversion, the game’s defection, renders. Its statutes also invoked the defence of the faith, and its knights took crusading vows at the Feast of the Pheasant (Lille, 17 February 1454), never fulfilled. The extra armour stands for the nobility the Order headed, equipped in Milanese and Low Countries plate; Coustilliers benefit as part of the lance, not as members. Armour rather than HP keeps it distinct from the Franks’ mounted HP bonus. It replaces Flemish Revolution, which turned the duke’s own subjects into the militias that historically rebelled against him. Hauberk shared and renamed (level 1) would render only the plate and break the ceiling, and a ‘Great Bombards’ tech for the ducal artillery park would repeat the gunpowder passive, so the new tech is preferred. Imperial Age at the Castle, the slot of Flemish Revolution; the chronological order of RULES 6.4 binds only two Castle techs (RULES 6.16.19(a)), so the later common coinage (1433–34) can be a Castle Age tech at the Town Center.

Hussars appear in Hungary in the later 15th century and in western Europe later still, while the Burgundian window ends in 1477. Light Cavalry remains, so no substitute is needed; the Franks also lack the Hussar.

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, the projector of Greek fire, a state secret never to be given to another nation (De Administrando Imperio 13); its game effect, an explosive charge for fire ships, has no medieval Western equivalent. The fire-ship line itself stays as the engine’s convention for close-range incendiary warships.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

The towns of Flanders and Brabant had sworn crossbow guilds (the Saint George guilds among the schuttersgilden) that supplied contingents to urban and ducal armies, and Charles the Bold’s lances included crossbowmen; their absence was the most anti-historical gap of the tree (RULES 6.16.3: crossbow evidence). Ring Archer Armor is not added, a design choice for differentiation rather than a gap in evidence (the ordinance archers did wear brigandines or jacks): the archer discount does not come with the English design’s full archery upgrades (the recommended default of the differentiation question, level-1 review, section 7).

The dukes besieged with great artillery: Dinant (August 1466) was breached after about a week’s bombardment, and in the Ghent war of 1452–53 the ducal guns took the castles of Schendelbeke, Poeke (where Jacques de Lalaing was killed by a cannon shot, July 1453) and Gavere; the eleven-month siege of Neuss (1474–75) failed despite the great artillery park (Vaughan 1970, 1973; Smith and DeVries 2005).

Philip the Good kept a fleet based at Sluis and sent crusading galleys to the Black Sea (Waleran de Wavrin, 1444–45). Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, from these ducal ships and galleys to Charles the Bold’s fleet against Warwick (1470), under Hendrik van Borselen, lord of Veere; it keeps every generic tier, with the Galleon as the skeleton’s flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2). The Cannon Galleon and its Elite tier stay, as in the game, since gun-armed Burgundian warships are documented inside the window: a Burgundian inventory of 1445, the years of the crusading galleys, lists five guns, two other mounted pieces and twelve handguns aboard a galley (Kelly DeVries, ‘A 1445 Reference to Shipboard Artillery’, Technology and Culture 31, 1990, 818–829, known here from the summary in John Lienhard, The Engines of Our Ingenuity, no. 573; the article itself was not read for this design). The line abstracts light pieces aboard oared galleys and ships; the great ducal guns stay with the gunpowder passive, the Bombard Cannon and Siege Engineers.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Arambai. The Yuan shi describes the army of Mian at Ngasaunggyan (1277): cavalry in front, then elephants that wore armour and carried war towers, with large bamboo tubes on both sides holding dozens of short spears that the riders took to strike with (juan 210). Marco Polo, who was not there, gives each elephant a wooden tower with twelve to sixteen fighting men (see contested). The Persians’ War Elephant, the game’s heavy close-combat elephant with a howdah, is the existing model nearest to this description: it is shared with the Persians, trained at the Castle with its Elite upgrade there, and keeps its game name, since no specific Burmese term for it has been verified. The Elephant Archer is not used: it is a regional unit in the game, which does not count as a unique unit (RULES 6.1, 6.16.10), and no source shows elephant-borne archers. No Scenario Editor unit fits better (RULES section 5). The Arambai it replaces is the javelin of the Meitei horsemen of Manipur, whose cavalry served Burmese kings mainly from the 1750s.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Arambai. The Yuan shi describes the army of Mian at Ngasaunggyan (1277): cavalry in front, then elephants that wore armour and carried war towers, with large bamboo tubes on both sides holding dozens of short spears that the riders took to strike with (juan 210). Marco Polo, who was not there, gives each elephant a wooden tower with twelve to sixteen fighting men (see contested). The Persians’ War Elephant, the game’s heavy close-combat elephant with a howdah, is the existing model nearest to this description: it is shared with the Persians, trained at the Castle with its Elite upgrade there, and keeps its game name, since no specific Burmese term for it has been verified. The Elephant Archer is not used: it is a regional unit in the game, which does not count as a unique unit (RULES 6.1, 6.16.10), and no source shows elephant-borne archers. No Scenario Editor unit fits better (RULES section 5). The Arambai it replaces is the javelin of the Meitei horsemen of Manipur, whose cavalry served Burmese kings mainly from the 1750s.

New in the codex (level 1). Burmese kings raised their armies from crown servicemen bound to hereditary units (infantry, cavalry, elephant and boat groups, and later gunners), who held land in return for service and farmed it between campaigns: Pagan’s crown bondsmen (kyundaw) appear in its inscriptions (Aung-Thwin 1985), and the Toungoo kings extended the system and the levies of their vassals (Lieberman 1984). Cheaper food for soldiers renders an army that fed itself from its service lands. At the Town Center because the system was the state’s organisation of manpower (RULES 6.2). A structural trait promoted to fill the slot: no in-window state reform was found, and the system’s mature, datable form (Thalun’s revenue inquest of 1638) lies after the window (RULES 6.3; see contested).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Manipur Cavalry (Cavalry +4 attack vs. Ranged Soldiers). Late element, RULES section 2, and the civ’s only one. The Toungoo kings built their empire with firearms and foreign gunners: Portuguese musketeers and gunners served Tabinshwehti at the siege of Martaban (1541), Diogo Soares de Melo commanded in his service, and Bayinnaung kept Portuguese gunners in his armies (Lieberman; Couto); Portuguese also served Burma’s rivals, notably Arakan, whose forces with Toungoo’s destroyed Pegu in 1599. Bayingyi, from Persian farangi (‘Franks’), is the Burmese name of the Portuguese gunner communities. The window runs to the fall of the First Toungoo Empire (1599), with this tech as its one late element (RULES section 2, 6.16.17). Manipur Cavalry, which it replaces, belongs to the Meitei horse of the 18th–19th centuries.
Little evidence of Burmese mounted archers; the Manipuri horsemen who later served the kings threw javelins (arambai).
As for the Cavalry Archer.
As for the Cavalry Archer.

No stone-throwing engine is attested in Burmese sieges, which were won by blockade, assault and, from the 15th–16th centuries, guns; the counterweight trebuchet reached China only in 1273, and there is no evidence that it reached Burma, although Yuan armies fought there in 1277–87 and 1300–01. The Bombard Cannon and the rams keep the civ able to destroy buildings (RULES 6.11). The Bombard Cannon is kept as the game’s abstraction of the firearms of Ming origin that Ava used in the 15th century, inside the window (Sun Laichen 2003; see the Hand Cannoneer), since this design has found no Burmese gun heavier than a hand gun before 1500; the Toungoo artillery of the 16th century confirms the arm after 1500 but is not its basis, since resting the arm on it would make a second late element beside Bayingyi (RULES section 2).

The Burmese navy is classed as the boat tier (RULES 6.16.1), by its vessels: the war fleets of Pagan and Ava, the core of the window, were river war boats, long, shallow-draft and oared, which carried the armies on the Irrawaddy and fought on it, manned in later centuries by the crown’s boat-service groups (Lieberman 1984; Charney 1997); the 18th–19th-century descriptions show them built on hulls hollowed from a single trunk and widened, a construction projected back here (see contested). The seagoing shipping of the Mon ports came under Toungoo only from 1538–39, at the edge of the window; the tier follows the river fleets of the core (RULES 6.16.19(d)), and the Toungoo use of Mon and Portuguese seagoing vessels is flagged (see contested). The high-seas sailing warships (Galleon, Carrack) are removed, while the Galley, Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines keep their Castle Age tiers (War Galley, Fire Ship, Demolition Ship and War Hulk; the Burmese already lacked the Fast Fire Ship and Heavy Demolition Ship) as a generic abstraction of river fleets for water maps. The Scenario Editor’s Canoe (RULES section 5), which the Aztec, Maya, Mapuche, Tupi, Malian and Avar designs use as the Galley’s look, was considered and not adopted: only its look would be used, a dugout war canoe, the Galley keeping its stats as in those designs, while the Irrawaddy war boats were long oared vessels carrying a fighting crew, nearer in scale and role to the Galley, and their dugout construction is itself projected back from later sources.
As for the Galleon.

No gun-armed war boats are documented for Pagan or Ava, whose river fleets were oared war boats (see the Transport Ships bonus); a case resting on the Toungoo river fleets of the 16th century, with their Portuguese gunners, would make a second late element beside Bayingyi (RULES section 2).
As for the Cannon Galleon.
No printing in the window: Burmese texts were copied on palm leaf and in folded paper books (parabaik), and printing reached Burma only in the 19th century.

Ava used firearms of Ming origin, hand guns among them, in the 15th century, inside the window (Sun Laichen 2003), and Toungoo armies used them on a large scale with Portuguese musketeers (Martaban, 1541). The civ had Bombard Cannon but no hand-held gun, against its own game history text.
Bows were in regular use in Burmese armies, and the weak archer armour was a balance choice without historical reason. The Arbalester stays out (see contested).
As for the Leather Archer Armor.

Kept from the game (level 1). The Praecepta Militaria of Nikephoros II Phokas (c. 965) and the Taktika of Nikephoros Ouranos (c. 1000) describe the kataphraktoi: horse and rider armoured in felt and iron, armed with iron maces, sabres and lances, formed in a blunt wedge to break the enemy centre (McGeer, 1995); Leo the Deacon shows Nikephoros II placing his ironclad horsemen in the van before Tarsus (965). A small, short-lived elite (c. 950–1050), with horse archers inside the formation. The model is shared with the Koreans' Gaema Musa (owner's decision).

Kept from the game (level 1). The Praecepta Militaria of Nikephoros II Phokas (c. 965) and the Taktika of Nikephoros Ouranos (c. 1000) describe the kataphraktoi: horse and rider armoured in felt and iron, armed with iron maces, sabres and lances, formed in a blunt wedge to break the enemy centre (McGeer, 1995); Leo the Deacon shows Nikephoros II placing his ironclad horsemen in the van before Tarsus (965). A small, short-lived elite (c. 950–1050), with horse archers inside the formation. The model is shared with the Koreans' Gaema Musa (owner's decision).

New in the codex (level 1). The themes (themata) were the late Roman field armies, withdrawn into Anatolia after the Arab conquests (630s–640s) and quartered in districts that took their names: the Anatolikon from the army of the magister militum per Orientem, the Armeniakon from that per Armeniam, the Thrakesion from that per Thracias and the Opsikion from the praesental Obsequium; their strategoi gradually took over civil authority. By the 9th–10th century many thematic soldiers held lands registered for military service (stratiotika ktemata), which supported them, their equipment and their horses, so the state paid only modest periodic roga; 10th-century novels (Constantine VII, Nikephoros II) forbade the alienation of these lands (Haldon, 1999; Lemerle, 1979). In the 10th–11th centuries thematic service was increasingly commuted into cash.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Greek Fire (Fire Ships +1 range; Dromons and Bombard Towers increased blast radius), formerly at the Castle. Theophanes says that Kallinikos, an architect who had fled from Heliopolis in Syria, devised (kataskeuasas) the sea fire c. 672; projected from siphons, it burned the Arab and Rus' fleets (717–718, 941), and Anna Komnene describes its last secure naval use, against the Pisans (1099). Constantine VII told his son never to give it to any other nation (De Administrando Imperio 13). It moves to the Dock because it was a naval weapon. The game's Bombard Tower clause, which tied a petroleum incendiary to gunpowder, is left out, because the Byzantines lose the Bombard Tower (see the tree).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Logistica (Cataphracts and Varangian Guards deal trample damage). Logistica uses the 19th-century military sense of logistics (Jomini) and has nothing to do with trample damage. The effect is the shock of the kataphraktoi wedge, whose front ranks carried iron maces (siderorabdia), described in the treatise of Nikephoros II Phokas (c. 965), known by its editors' conventional Latin title Praecepta Militaria (its Greek title is Stratēgikē ekthesis kai syntaxis Nikēphorou despotou; McGeer, 1995). The Varangian half rests not on the treatise, which predates the Guard, but on the guard itself, which stays in the tree under its own name as a regional unit that does not count as a unique unit (RULES section 4 and 6.16.10): it grew from the c. 6,000 Rus' warriors whom Vladimir of Kiev sent to Basil II in 988/989 (Stepanos Taronetsi), took in Scandinavians such as Harald Hardrada (1034–1043) and, after 1066, many Englishmen (Orderic Vitalis), and fought on foot at Dyrrhachium (1081), where Anna Komnene calls its men the axe-bearing barbarians (Alexiad; Blöndal, 1978).

Camel riders are attested only on the desert frontiers of the late Roman East: the alae dromedariorum of the Notitia Dignitatum (c. 400) and, in the 6th century, a levy of camels and camel riders (dromedarioi) at Nessana in the Negev, apportioned among local institutions, among them churches and the church of the kastron (P. Ness. 35), with an account of military camels (P. Ness. 37). Their editor read them as a camel corps of the local garrison (C. J. Kraemer, Excavations at Nessana III, 1958); C. Whately (“Camels, Soldiers, and Pilgrims in Sixth Century Nessana”, Scripta Classica Israelica 35, 2016, 121–135) argues, against the earlier reading of the two terms as two kinds of camel, that dromedarios means a camel rider, and re-examines how far the papyri show a military camel unit and whether the kastron was a purely military space. Either way they were local troops of the desert limes, not an arm of the field armies, and they ended with the loss of Syria, Palestine and Egypt (636–642), three decades before the core of the design (c. 670–1100). With this evidence the camels still stay out. The tree follows the period the design represents (RULES 6.16.19(d)): the camel riders served only at the opening edge of the window, as local troops, and ended before its core, the same core period that breaks the tie between the two heavy engines (see Trebuchet). A camel line for the whole empire would also misrepresent its armies.
Removed with the Camel Rider (see above).

The counterweight engine joined the Byzantine arsenal only in the last third of the window, by 1165 on P. E. Chevedden's reading or at the end of the 12th century on M. S. Fulton's (see the civ-level contested list), beside the traction engine. Its removal is a game-role choice, as in the Chinese design, not a finding that the engine never reached Byzantium: both engines arrive in the Imperial Age (the Trebuchet at the Castle, the Traction Trebuchet at the Siege Workshop) with almost the same role, so the tree keeps one. RULES 6.16.19(d) alone would not remove the counterweight engine: it served for some two and a half to three centuries (from 1165 or the late 12th century to 1453), not only at the edge of the window, and the same reading keeps the Arbalester (see the crossbow entry of the contested list). The removal is the one-slot game-role choice, and the core (c. 670–1100) only breaks the tie between the two engines that share the slot: the tree keeps the traction engine, Byzantium's heavy engine from the late 6th century to 1453 and the only one of its core. Restoring the counterweight engine as a Komnenian siege tech with a second, exclusive effect is an N2 idea.

Byzantium never had a siege artillery train: according to Doukas, the founder Orban first offered his services to Constantine XI, who could not pay him, and then cast Mehmed II's great guns. The Traction Trebuchet, rams, Siege Onager and Siege Engineers keep the civ's siege.

Gunpowder appears only at the very end of the window: in 1453 the defenders had a few small guns and handguns on the walls, partly brought and manned by the Genoese and Venetian contingents (Giustiniani's c. 700 men), and the recoil of the larger pieces shook the walls (Doukas; Leonard of Chios; Barbaro). Gunpowder destroyed Byzantium rather than defined it, and the tree follows the period a civ represents (RULES 6.16.19(d), as for the Georgians' firearms), so the handgun goes; the Arbalester covers ranged infantry (see the crossbow entry of the contested list).
Removed with the Hand Cannoneer (see above); the Keep and Guard Tower remain, and Greek Fire's effect leaves out its Bombard Tower clause.
Removed with the Hand Cannoneer (see above); the Keep and Guard Tower remain, and Greek Fire's effect leaves out its Bombard Tower clause.
No printing in the window: the first book printed entirely in Greek, Constantine Laskaris' Erotemata, appeared in Milan in 1476, after the fall of Constantinople.

The logothete of the herds ran imperial stud farms (mētata) in Asia and Phrygia, and the imperial stable (under the komes tou staulou) kept remounts at Malagina in Bithynia, the first assembly camp of eastern expeditions (Three Treatises on Imperial Military Expeditions, ed. Haldon, 1990). Denying horse breeding to a heavy cavalry civ contradicts the sources.

Hospitals (xenones) with salaried doctors, such as the Pantokrator (1136) (Miller, 1997), and the paid rescuers (deputatoi) of the Strategikon (II.9), who carried wounded men off the field for a nomisma each; its absence clashed with the healing team bonus.

Byzantium kept Roman siegecraft alive: the siege treatise of the so-called Heron of Byzantium (10th century) and the siege chapter of Leo VI's Taktika; formal sieges took Chandax in Crete (960–961), Mopsuestia and Tarsus (965).
Bolt-shooting engines stayed in service: Leo VI's Taktika (c. 905) has torsion or tension bolt-throwers carried in the infantry baggage (ed. Dennis, 2010).

The Mangonel line is the light stone-thrower (RULES 6.16.5), here the light engines that Byzantine armies and garrisons used throughout the window, and the Siege Onager is its generic top tier. The empire whose engineering Krum's engines copied (812, through an engineer from Byzantine service) gets it on the same grounds as the Bulgarians, who keep it; the heavy engine is the Traction Trebuchet (see that entry).

The rope-pulled heavy stone-thrower was Byzantium's heavy engine from the late 6th century to the end of the window, and its only one in the core (c. 670–1100): the helepoleis of the late 6th- and 7th-century sources, which G. T. Dennis reads as heavy traction stone-throwers (“Byzantine Heavy Artillery: The Helepolis”, Greek, Roman and Byzantine Studies 39, 1998), and the stone-throwing engines of the siege warfare of the 10th-century reconquests (Haldon, 1999). The first clear description of the engine in the Mediterranean world is of the Avar-Slav siege of Thessalonica, dated 586 or 597 (Miracles of St Demetrius I). Theophylact Simocatta (II.16) says that a Roman captive, the soldier Busas, taught the Avars to build a helepolis at Appiaria (587), but what that engine was (ram, tower or stone-thrower) and how reliable the story is are debated, so the design does not rest on it. Whether the Byzantines knew the engine before the Avar sieges of the late 6th century or learned it from the Avars is debated (Dennis 1998; S. McCotter, Byzantines, Avars and the Introduction of the Trebuchet, 2003; see the Avars' contested list). Under the traction test (RULES 6.16.5) it replaces the counterweight Trebuchet as the long-range siege weapon (RULES 6.11), trained at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age, as for the Avars.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Woad Raider. The kern, from Irish ceithern, a band of light foot (one soldier was a ceithernach), Englished as kern: the light foot of Gaelic armies, documented as a distinct type, often hired, from the 13th to the 16th century and rooted in the early war-band (Simms 1987; Nicholls 1972; eDIL s.v. ceithern), unarmoured, raiding and skirmishing with darts, spears and axes (Gerald of Wales). The Woad Raider’s fast, lightly protected infantry fits them; only the name changes (see the renames). No medieval source describes Gaelic warriors painting themselves: the motif is classical (Caesar on the Britons, De Bello Gallico V.14; Claudian and Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae XIX.23.7, on the Picts) and modern (the film Braveheart).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Woad Raider. The Woad Raider’s fast, lightly protected infantry fits them; only the name changes (see the renames). Renamed from Elite Woad Raider. Same as the Woad Raider rename.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Furor Celtica (Siege Weapons +40% HP). The schiltron, the dense formation of Scottish spearmen in the wars of independence: at Falkirk (1298) Wallace’s schiltrons held off the English cavalry until archers and crossbowmen shot gaps in them; at Bannockburn (1314) Bruce used them to attack, and on the second day his schiltrons advanced on Edward II’s cavalry and pinned it on cramped ground by the Bannock Burn (on the carse or on the dry field of Balquhiderock; the exact site is debated), while the Scottish horse under Robert Keith scattered the English archers (Barbour; Vita Edwardi Secundi; Barrow). Scottish armies went on fighting in schiltrons, and were broken in them by the English archers at Dupplin Moor (1332) and Halidon Hill (1333) and beaten again at Neville’s Cross (1346). Robert I’s parliament at Scone (December 1318) fixed the arms of the host by wealth: every man with £10 in goods was to have an aketon, basinet, gloves of plate, sword and spear, and every man with goods worth one cow a good spear or a good bow with 24 arrows (Records of the Parliaments of Scotland). Why a tech when the Anglo-Saxons’ shield wall is a passive: the schiltron has a datable moment of adoption, Bruce’s use of it as an attacking formation at Bannockburn (1314), an adopted technique (RULES 6.2), and the Gaels have no other datable moment fit for the Castle slot, so the formation is promoted to a tech (RULES 6.3); the Anglo-Saxons’ Castle slot goes to their own datable reform, the Fyrd, and the shield wall, used for six centuries, stays a passive. The war had a Gaelic side: Bruce was Earl of Carrick, still largely Gaelic-speaking c. 1300, and in Barbour’s account Angus Óg of Islay stood with the men of Carrick, Argyll and the Isles in the king’s own division at Bannockburn. The effect renders the mutual protection of the massed spears; the Spearman-line’s own weakness to archers keeps the lesson of Falkirk. An existing tech fits, so no new (level-2) tech is needed (RULES 6.5). It replaces Furor Celtica, a classical stereotype of Gaulish fury (Polybius; ‘furor Teutonicus’ in Lucan) in faulty Latin, applied to siege engines.

New in the codex (level 1). Buannacht (anglicised ‘bonaght’): Gaelic lords kept their hired soldiers, galloglass above all and later bands of kern too, by billeting them on their subjects, who owed them food and quarters; Anglo-Irish lords adopted the practice, which the Dublin government condemned as ‘coign and livery’ (Nicholls 1972; Simms 1987). Cheaper food renders soldiers fed by the land rather than paid from the lord’s purse; it leaves the gold cost alone, so the Galloglass (Varangian Guard model, which earns gold in combat) does not become a gold-free unit that earns gold. An exaction of lordship rather than a community institution (RULES 6.3): Gaelic Ireland was ruled through its lordships, and the Town Center tech follows them although the kingdom of Scotland is in scope. An existing tech fits, so no new (level-2) tech is needed (RULES 6.5); a new tech aimed at the hired soldiers alone (‘Kerns and Galloglasses cost -20%’) would be a level-2 item for a narrower reading of the same exaction and is not used.

Scottish siege engineering was limited and mostly unsuccessful (the stone-thrower, belfry and sow that failed at Carlisle in 1315, Lanercost Chronicle; the Fleming John Crab’s engines in the defence of Berwick, 1319, Barbour; James I’s failed siege of Roxburgh with guns, 1436), and Gaelic Ireland had none to speak of; the elite siege upgrades rested on the invented ‘siege civilization’ identity. The lower siege units stay as the engine’s minimum abstraction, resting on the Scottish kingdom (see the civ-level contested list). The Trebuchet rests on the stone-throwers the Scots built at Carlisle (1315) and for the defence of Berwick (1319), whose type is not recorded; in the age of Edward I’s great counterweight engines (the Warwolf at Stirling, 1304) the design reads them as counterweight trebuchets, an inference (RULES 6.16.5).
Same reason: castles were taken by surprise and escalade, then slighted (see the anti-building bonus); the Capped Ram is kept.

Gaelic cavalry was light: the Irish rode without saddle or spurs (Gerald of Wales, Topographia Hibernica III). Heavy cavalry existed only among the Anglo-Norman-descended nobility of Scotland, which the Knight and Cavalier cover now that the kingdom is in scope (RULES section 4).

The Hussar is a 15th-century Hungarian and Serbian type, removed as in the Anglo-Saxons’ and Burgundians’ designs. Light Cavalry stays for the Gaelic horsemen, the lords’ mounted following in raids and pursuit, who rode without saddle or spurs (Gerald of Wales; Simms 1987). The top tier is not renamed ‘Hobelar’: the hobelar was a troop type of the English lordship of Ireland, not a Gaelic one (see contested).

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. No mounted crossbowmen are recorded in Gaelic Ireland or Scotland, and the crossbow itself was marginal (Pictish sculpture shows crossbow hunters, as on the Drosten stone at St Vigeans); the foot Crossbowman stays as the generic Castle Age tier (RULES 6.16.3).
Same reason as the Mounted Crossbowman.

The one solid siege tradition of the civ, resting on the Scottish kingdom, which the design includes (RULES section 4): James II of Scotland used artillery against the Douglases (Threave, 1455), received Mons Meg (made at Mons in 1449 for Philip the Good of Burgundy) between 1454 and 1457 (the sources differ), and was killed at the siege of Roxburgh (3 August 1460) when one of his guns burst.

The name evokes Insular manuscript art (the Book of Kells, c. 800, the Book of Durrow and the Cathach), the best-known Gaelic achievement of the Middle Ages; the effect (faster recovery of faith) is generic. Atonement, Redemption and Block Printing stay out: the first two would add power without a Gaelic basis, and the Gaelic world printed nothing before John Carswell’s Gaelic Book of Common Order (1567).

The great monastic federations (familiae) of Iona and Armagh, ruled by abbots who were often of royal kin; the effect is generic. Added with Illumination for a civ whose monasticism shaped its history (see the team bonus).
Substitute for the removed lumberjack bonus (RULES 6.11), so that the wood economy is not crippled; Ireland kept large oak woods until the 16th–17th-century plantations.

Added at the Barracks as the Galloglass (see the renames): the galloglass (gallóglaigh, ‘foreign warriors’) were heavy infantry from the Hebrides and the West Highlands, of mixed Norse-Gaelic descent, in mail and iron helmet with a long-hafted axe, the steady core of Gaelic armies until the 16th century (Simms 1987; Duffy 2007). The model is axe-armed shock infantry strong against cavalry. A renamed regional unit at the Barracks, like the Anglo-Saxons’ and Danes’ Housecarl, not a unique unit (RULES 6.16.10), so the civ has one unique unit, the Kern; that the cheap kern trains at the Castle and the costly galloglass at the Barracks is a game convention. The infantry Teutonic Knight model, now unused by the Germans’ design, would give a slow heavy unit but a plate-armoured swordsman, and the Scenario Editor’s Norse Warrior and Heavy Swordsman (RULES section 5) are sword-armed too; the axe-armed Varangian Guard fits the galloglass’s weapon better, so the design keeps the renamed regional unit (the recommended default, level-1 review, section 7) and leaves a dedicated unit to the N2 idea.

Renamed from Varangian Guard. The galloglass (Irish gallóglaigh, ‘foreign warriors’). The first recorded contingent is the 160 warriors who came with the daughter of Dubgall mac Ruaidrí at her marriage to Áed Ó Conchobair in 1259 (Annals of Connacht); the compound term appears in the annals only from the end of the 13th century. The model’s gold generation has no Gaelic basis (at most the spoils of the creach); see the N2 idea.
Same as the Varangian Guard (Elite Galloglass).
Renamed from Elite Varangian Guard. Same as the Varangian Guard rename.

Kept from the game (level 1). The repeating crossbow (lian nu) is attested from a 4th-century BC Chu tomb at Qinjiazui (Hubei) to the Wubei zhi (1621). The Sanguozhi credits Zhuge Liang with improving it, and Pei Songzhi's commentary describes his yuanrong, which shot ten iron bolts at once; hence the later name zhuge nu. It was light and short-ranged, used above all to defend walls and houses, sometimes with poisoned bolts (Needham and Yates 1994). Kept at the level-1 review's default, since the repeating crossbow's fame tips the borderline case (see relevance). A “Shenbi Crossbowman” on the Genoese Crossbowman model (strong against cavalry, as the Song heavy crossbow was against the Jin horse), after the “divine-arm bow” of 1068, remains the N1 alternative; sharing the model would be allowed (RULES section 5, reusing a unit's art: the unit as it is, with only a new name, is N1). Until then the heavy crossbow is carried by the Archer-line bonus and the N2 idea.

Kept from the game (level 1). Fire-throwing warships are real: the Wujing Zongyao (1044) describes the double-acting piston pump for “fierce fire oil” (menghuo you), and the Wuyue fleet used such oil against its rival in 919 (Needham). A longer-reaching, harder-hitting fire ship in place of the Fast Fire Ship is a fair abstraction of Chinese incendiary naval warfare, from Tangdao and Caishi (1161), where Song fleets burned and bombed the Jin invasion fleets, to Lake Poyang (1363), where Zhu Yuanzhang burned Chen Youliang's fleet with fire ships. Navy tier: a fleet of ships (RULES 6.16.1), resting on the Song standing river and coastal fleets (tower ships, haihu and paddle-wheel chechuan) and the early Ming fleets; the Galleon stays as the skeleton's flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2).

Kept from the game (level 1). Walls were a constant of Chinese defence, but the tech is anchored on one datable moment: the Sui long walls, raised with mass levies against the Türks between 585 and 608 (Sui shu). Later works carry the same tradition: Song walled cities and Yu Jie's mountain fortresses in Sichuan, such as Diaoyucheng, which held the Mongols from 1243 to 1279 and before which Möngke died in 1259; Nanjing's brick-faced city wall (1366–1393); and, after the Tumu disaster (1449), Yu Zijun's rammed-earth line across the Ordos (1474) (Waldron 1990). The Bombard Tower clause fits the Ming. Walls as a whole are a structural trait; the tech stays paid rather than becoming a passive because the effect is large (RULES 6.2, step 4), and no separate walls passive is added, for the power budget.

Kept from the game (level 1). Gunpowder rockets are a Chinese invention. The Huolongjing (attributed to Jiao Yu and Liu Ji; preface 1412) describes rocket arrows and launchers, although its text grew after the preface (see contested), and the Wubei zhi (1621) shows the later Ming multiple launchers. In Korea, which took its gunpowder from China, rocket arrows (singijeon, standardised in 1448) were fired up to a hundred at a time from Munjong's hwacha of 1451; the first hwacha (1409) shot iron-fletched arrows from gun tubes. Bed crossbows (chuangzi nu), the Scorpions, were front-line Song weapons: a bolt from one killed the Liao commander Xiao Talin at Chanyuan in 1004. Tower ships (louchuan), documented from the Han to the Ming, carried the river fleets; they are the river-navy element that RULES 4 brings from the Three Kingdoms, and as siege warships they also fill the anti-building role of the Cannon Galleon, which is held back as a power choice, not a historical one: gun-armed early Ming warships are documented (a bowl-mouth gun of 1372 is inscribed for the Navy Left Guard, and Andrade reads shipboard guns at Lake Poyang in 1363), so RULES 6.16.1 would allow it (Needham 1986, 1994). Wu's Sitting Tiger (Traction Trebuchets and Lou Chuan trebuchet weapons fire additional projectiles), whose name matches the crouching-tiger pao of the Wujing Zongyao, stays with the out-of-scope Wu for the power budget (the level-1 review's default).

New in the codex (level 1). Military-agricultural colonies run through the history of imperial China: Cao Cao's of 196, revived on the Tang frontiers, and made the backbone of the early Ming garrison system (weisuo), in which soldiers farmed state land, about seven farming for three on guard on the frontier and eight for two in the interior (Ming shi, Shihuo zhi; Brook 2010). The Hongwu emperor is credited with the boast that he fed a million soldiers without costing the people a grain of rice. At the Town Center because the colonies were a state institution of land and revenue (RULES 6.2).

The counterweight trebuchet reached China in 1273, when the Muslim engineers Ismail and Ala al-Din, sent to Kublai by the Ilkhan Abaqa, built the engines that broke Fancheng and Xiangyang (huihui pao, “Muslim trebuchet”; Yuan shi). The Song border prefectures copied it the same year (Song shi, Bing zhi), and it served for about a century, to the founding of the Ming: at Suzhou in 1367 Xu Da's army still set up “Xiangyang trebuchets” beside its guns (Ming shi). Its removal is a game-role choice, not a historical finding: both engines arrive in the Imperial Age with almost the same role, the native traction pao served China for the whole window (alone until 1273, beside the counterweight engine afterwards), and the Bombard Cannon carries early Ming siegecraft (RULES 6.11). Removed in N1 (the level-1 review's default): keeping it beside the pao would cost power, since it outranges and outhits it (range 16 against 14); restoring it as Xiangyang Pao, with a second, exclusive effect, is an N2 idea.

China invented the metal-barrelled gun: the Xanadu gun, inscribed 1298, is the oldest securely dated, and the Heilongjiang hand gun is dated by its context to c. 1288. Under the Hongwu emperor the Ming shi allots ten firearms to every company of a hundred men, and the Yongle emperor (r. 1402–1424) founded a firearms division, the Shenjiying, which the Ming shi says was set up to drill with the method of the “divine-engine” guns (shenji qiangpao) obtained in the conquest of Jiaozhi (Đại Việt, 1407) (Ming shi, Bing zhi; Andrade 2016; see contested). Its absence was the most serious error of the current tree.

Early Ming foundries cast iron cannon: three cast-iron “general” guns dated 1377 survive in Shanxi, the oldest cast-iron cannon found in China (Hu Zhenqi 1982), and such pieces armed city walls and passes (Needham 1986; Andrade 2016). It also removes the incoherence of a Bombard Tower without a Bombard Cannon.

Chinese siegecraft was among the most advanced of its time: the Wujing Zongyao (1044) catalogues siege engines, assault towers and rams; Chen Gui's Shoucheng lu records the counter-siege craft of De'an (1132); and the early Ming took Suzhou (1366–1367) from wooden towers and three-storey platforms that overlooked the city, armed with crossbows and guns (Ming shi, biography of Zhang Shicheng).

Song cities were organised in merchant and craft guilds (hang), and the state issued the first government paper money (jiaozi, 1024); a lower market fee is a fair abstraction of the Song commercial economy (Elvin 1973). Its absence was incoherent.

Added and renamed Champa Rice (see the rename) for the Song agricultural expansion, which the game's farm team bonus stood for although it fails RULES 6.2 (see the team bonus). Twenty of the 56 current civs lack Crop Rotation; with it the Chinese farm economy is stronger in the Imperial Age than the current civ's (+175 food per new farm, against the 10% extra farm food of the lost team bonus). Power budget: against the current civ the design gains the Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Traction Trebuchet, Siege Engineers, Guilds, Champa Rice, Tuntian and the Archer-line bonus, and loses the fire-lancer speed bonus, the counterweight Trebuchet and the farm team bonus; the Cannon Galleon, Elite Cannon Galleon, Carvel Hull and a walls passive stay out as power choices. No further trim (the level-1 review's default; N1 avoids absurdities but does not promise balance, RULES 6.14).

Renamed from Crop Rotation. In 1012 the Song court had 30,000 hu of Champa rice fetched from Fujian and given out as seed in the Jiangnan, Huainan and Liangzhe circuits, to be sown on the people's higher, drier fields (Song shi, Shihuo zhi): an earlier-ripening, drought-tolerant rice that extended paddy to higher ground and, in places, allowed two crops a year, while agricultural treatises spread the new methods (Chen Fu, Nongshu, 1149; Wang Zhen, Nongshu, 1313) (Elvin 1973; Bray 1984; see contested). Same effect (more food from each farm), as with Crop Rotation → Milpa.

The man-powered traction trebuchet (pao) was China's siege artillery from the Warring States until 1273 and stayed in use beside the counterweight engine afterwards: the Wujing Zongyao (1044) illustrates heavy engines with up to seven poles worked by large teams of pullers, and Chen Gui's Shoucheng lu, drawn from his defence of De'an (1132), sets the defenders' pao behind the walls against the besiegers' engines (Needham and Yates 1994). Moved from the out-of-scope Three Kingdoms (RULES 4); it replaces the counterweight Trebuchet. The light “whirlwind” pao of the same manual, the Song-era counterpart of the Ming Rocket Cart, is left out only by a design convention of this region (one Castle-Age blast weapon per civ: the Chinese Rocket Cart, the Jurchen Bomb Thrower, the Khitans' Whirlwind Pao), not for want of evidence. The convention mirrors the game, where none of the four civs that train the Rocket Cart (Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans) has the Mangonel line; so the Khitans field that line as the Whirlwind Pao, a name from the Song manuals, while the Chinese, who keep the Rocket Cart, lack it (the Koreans' design, on the owner's sketch, keeps both). The Chinese stay without the Mangonel line (the level-1 review's default).

Song fleets threw bombs from ship-borne traction trebuchets: at Caishi (1161) the paddle-wheel warships of the Song fleet, hidden behind Jinshan island, launched thunderclap bombs of lime and gunpowder at the Jin invasion fleet and destroyed it (Needham 1986, Science and Civilisation in China 5.7), and the Yuan fleets built in Chinese yards carried the same kind of bombs against Japan (see the Mongols' design). Added beside the Cannon Galleon, which stands for the guns of the early Ming navy; the siege warship is then shared with the Mongols and stays a regional unit (RULES 6.1). Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships.
Only this civ has this unit in the codex, so it counts as a unique unit (RULES 6.1).

Kept from the game (level 1). The horse archer was the core of every Cuman army; Qïpčaq is the people's own name in Muslim and Turkic sources (the Codex Cumanicus records their language). The volley of several arrows abstracts massed fire.

New in the codex (level 2). The Cumans had no state: their hordes, each under its own khan, decided war and peace in councils of khans and elders. In 1103, as the Rus' princes marched into the steppe, the Polovtsy took counsel: Urusoba urged them to ask Rus' for peace, and the younger khans overruled him (Primary Chronicle); after Igor's defeat in 1185 Konchak and Gzak debated whether to strike at the Kiev lands or at the Seim, and then went their separate ways (Hypatian Chronicle). For a people without a state the Town Center tech stands for a community institution (RULES 6.3); the faster work of the Town Centers, the camps of the hordes (see the extra Town Center bonus), abstracts the joint action the councils made possible, a weak link said openly.

Kept from the game (level 1). Cumans served their neighbours as auxiliaries, in raids and pitched battle alike, and settled among them: Oleg Sviatoslavich brought the Polovtsy against his Rus' rivals, beating Vsevolod on the Sozhitsa in 1078 and taking Chernigov in 1094 (Primary Chronicle); Togortak (Tugorkan) and Maniak (perhaps Boniak) fought at Levounion for Alexios I (1091; Anna Komnene); the Kipchak families David IV settled in Georgia (c. 1118–1120) fought at Didgori (1121); Cuman allies brought the Asen brothers back across the Danube in 1186 (Choniates), won Kaloyan's victory at Adrianople (1205) and ravaged Thrace in 1205–1206 (Villehardouin); Köten's people entered Hungary in 1239, and the Hungarian Cumans fought at the Marchfeld (1278). The Mongol conquest (1237–1241) turned this service into the diaspora that carried Cuman history to c. 1400. Mercenary and auxiliary service was a long tradition rather than a datable moment, which RULES 6.2 would make team-bonus material (the team slot holds the marriage alliances), so Cuman Mercenaries keeps the Imperial Age Castle slot as a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19(b)); its effect already reaches the whole team.

The Cumans had no siege train of their own and besieged mostly by blockade, so the top siege tiers are cut; the Onager and the Capped Ram remain as the generic minimum the civ needs to destroy buildings (RULES 6.11).
As Siege Onager; the Capped Ram remains.

The counterweight trebuchet is not attested among the Cumans: they had no siege train of their own and besieged rarely, mostly by blockade (Torchesk, 1093), and Konchak's engines of 1184/1185 were great crossbows and a Muslim specialist's “living fire” (Hypatian Chronicle; see the Heavy Scorpion). Removed under the codex rule for engines that never reached a civ (RULES 6.16.5); the Mangonel-line stays as the generic stone-thrower. No heavy stone-throwers are attested for the Cumans either, so the traction test gives no Traction Trebuchet, and the civ has no long-range siege weapon, which the same rule allows when none is attested. The engines that Cumans of the diaspora met in Hungarian, Bulgarian or Mamluk service, such as the great engines the Mamluks hauled to Acre in 1291 (Abu'l-Fida), belonged to their host states, which have their own designs; the tree follows the steppe core (RULES 6.16.19(d)).
The Rus' chronicles list camels among the booty taken in Polovtsian camps (for example in 1103), as pack animals, not cavalry.
The Cumans fought almost entirely on horseback; the Two-Handed Swordsman remains for allied or subject foot.

The Cumans had no war fleet, so the basic navy only, under the codex navy rule (RULES 6.16.1): the Galley-line to War Galley, the Fire Galley and Fire Ship, the Hulk-line as the game's generic melee warship, the demolition ships and the Dock techs, with no Galleon, Carrack, Fast Fire Ship or siege warship.
As Galleon.
As Galleon: no ocean-going ships.
The Cumans had no war fleet and no ship-borne artillery, so no siege warship and no substitute, under the codex navy rule (RULES 6.16.1).
A horse-archer people without the last archery upgrade contradicted its identity; Byzantine, Rus' and Hungarian sources describe Cuman archery, feigned flight and ambush.

In 1184/1185 Konchak advanced on Rus' with crossbows so stiff that fifty men could barely draw them, and with a Muslim specialist who shot “living fire” and was captured when Konchak fled from the Khorol (1 March 1185; Hypatian Chronicle). A heavy bolt-thrower fits this record better than early rams; the engineer was a foreigner and the record is isolated (civ-level contested list).

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: the Cumans had no siege train of their own and besieged mostly by blockade (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

Kept from the game (level 1). The Jomsvikings of Jómsvíkinga saga (c. 1200), a warrior brotherhood at Jomsborg, usually identified with Wolin (Adam of Bremen's Iumne), where Harald Bluetooth died in exile. The battle of Hjǫrungavágr (c. 986), which the sagas make their defeat, is attested in near-contemporary skaldic verse, and the sagas make Thorkell the Tall, whose ‘immense raiding army’ came to England in 1009 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle), one of their chiefs. The torches render the burning of settlements and ships.

New in the codex (level 1). The Danevirke, the rampart across the neck of Jutland, was rebuilt in successive phases from c. 500 to the 12th century: a first stage c. 500 or earlier (radiocarbon), dendro-dated phases in 737 and 968, Godfred's work of 808 (Royal Frankish Annals) and the brick wall of Valdemar the Great (reigned 1157–1182). It held the border through wars: Otto II broke through it in 974, and the Danes regained the border region after 983. The semicircular rampart of Hedeby was joined to it by a connecting wall in the 10th century, hence the Town Centers. Regeneration renders this continuous royal upkeep, which suits a rampart rebuilt and repaired over six centuries better than a flat walls effect such as the Chinese Great Wall (Walls, Watch Tower-line and Bombard Towers +30% HP), which would also come close to the Anglo-Saxons' walls bonus.

New in the codex (level 2). From about 1429 Erik of Pomerania, king of the Kalmar Union, levied a toll on every ship passing the Sound at Helsingør, where he built the castle of Krogen to enforce it; the Sound Dues remained a main revenue of the Danish crown until they were abolished in 1857. A state revenue, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2).

Dropped with the invented ‘Siege’ identity of the game's Danes (Northmen's Fury, the siege discount), whose top tier it was; the Mangonel and Onager stay as the light stone-thrower (RULES 6.16.5). The Trebuchet stays as a flagged inference (see contested): Danish kings used throwing engines from the 1130s, and the design reads those of the counterweight era (13th–15th centuries) as counterweight engines.

No ship-borne catapults are known in Danish fleets; the Longship (strong vs buildings) keeps the anti-building naval role. The fire-ship line, Fast Fire Ship included, is kept: Abbo of Saint-Germain describes the Danes sending burning ships against the bridge of Paris (885).

Danish archers used the European draw and the missile troops of the later kingdom were crossbowmen, so the tech is removed: the Thumb Ring goes only where the thumb draw is attested for a civ's own archers or for an archery tradition its armies demonstrably used (the steppe, Islamic and East Asian traditions; RULES 6.16.4). The Anglo-Saxons' design, among others, removes it on the same ground.

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. No Danish mounted crossbowmen are recorded as a troop type: the crossbow served the castles and fleets of the later kingdom, and its mounted service was that of armoured lords (see the Cavalier), so the line, which the game's Danes had without any stated basis, is removed; the Swedes' and Norwegians' designs drop it on the same test.
As for the Mounted Crossbowman.
A 15th-century spanning device for the mounted crossbow line, which the Danes no longer have.
Built as the Trelleborg ring fort (see the bonus and the rename).

Renamed from Krepost. The Danish royal ring fortresses of c. 980, named after the excavated fort at Trelleborg near Slagelse; the function (a small fortress that houses and trains troops) is the same.

Valdemarian Denmark fought with armoured knights (Lyndanisse 1219, Bornhöved 1227): in the 12th–13th centuries the naval levy was largely commuted into a tax, and military service shifted to tax-exempt lords serving as armoured horsemen (the herremænd).

Crossbows were common in the castles and fleets of 13th–15th-century Denmark, which gives the top tier the crossbow evidence RULES 6.16.3 asks for; the Danish crossbow is rendered on foot, by the Crossbowman and Arbalester (see the Mounted Crossbowman).
The Danevirke and Valdemar's brick wall make the Danes one of the great wall-building peoples of the North.
The Danevirke and Valdemar's brick wall make the Danes one of the great wall-building peoples of the North.
Stone and brick building of the medieval kingdom: Lund Cathedral (high altar consecrated 1145), Valdemar's brick wall and churches, the royal castle of Vordingborg.

Guns reached Scandinavia in the 14th century (the Loshult gun, found in Scania, is one of the oldest surviving in Europe), and the Kalmar-era kings fought with hired German infantry: King Hans's army at Hemmingstedt (1500) was built around the mercenary Great Guard, a Landsknecht band of the kind that by 1500 included handgunners (their number in the Guard is not recorded in the sources used for this design), which was routed in the marsh with the loss of its guns and baggage. The tree follows the period the design represents (RULES 6.16.19(d)), and the Kalmar Union, which the Danish crown led to 1523, is part of it, so the guns of the late Kalmar kings enter (Hemmingstedt, 1500); the Swedes take the Hand Cannoneer on their own evidence (Brunkeberg, 1471), and the Norwegians, whose window ends in 1469, have no guns.

Danish royal forces carried guns by the end of the 15th century: King Hans's flagship Gribshunden carried guns when she sank in 1495 (see the Cannon Galleon), and Hans lost his field guns in the marsh at Hemmingstedt (February 1500). A cannon shot from Christian II's army mortally wounded the Swedish regent Sten Sture the Younger at Bogesund (January 1520), a confirmation after 1500 rather than the basis.

Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, from the Viking-age warships of Hedeby and Skuldelev to the royal fleet of the Union kings. The game's gap of the Danes, no demolition ships, is kept, the Longship covering the anti-building role, and the Galleon is a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2). King Hans's flagship Gribshunden, sunk off Ronneby in 1495, was a large carvel-built warship of the new type, the kind of ship the Carrack stands for.
Gribshunden carried guns (1495), an early case of shipboard artillery in northern waters.

Renamed from Varangian Guard. The húskarlar, household troops of the Danish kings, from Cnut's guard in England (1016–1035) to the law of the retainers that Sven Aggesen attributes to Cnut (Lex Castrensis, 1180s); whether the heregeld paid them is debated (see contested). The axe-armed heavy infantry model is the same one the Anglo-Saxons' design renames Housecarl, so that one model serves one Anglo-Danish institution; the Varangian Guard itself stays Byzantine (RULES section 4). The Goths' dropped Huskarl, which bears the Old Norse name, is not used: the Varangian Guard renders the housecarls better in role, being strong against cavalry, as the Dane axe was against horsemen at Hastings (the Bayeux Tapestry shows an English axeman striking a horse; Wace, Roman de Rou), whereas the Huskarl is weak against cavalry; its axe, which the game's Gothikon has it throw, fits the Dane axe too, and one model shared with the Anglo-Saxons' design keeps one institution under one look. The Norse Warrior (Scenario Editor, RULES section 5) was weighed as the look of the Housecarl and not used: its base stats make it a light swordsman rather than an armoured guard (to be checked in game), a look alone would not remove the Varangian Guard's gold mechanic (see the N2 idea), and it would split the one model the Anglo-Saxons' design shares.
Renamed from Elite Varangian Guard. Same as the Varangian Guard rename.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Urumi Swordsman. The Velaikkarar were elite regiments named in Chola inscriptions from Rajaraja I onwards, bound, in Nilakanta Sastri's reading, by oath to the king's person. They were also a force in Sri Lanka: a Velaikkara corps in the service of the Sinhalese king Vijayabahu I mutinied c. 1084 rather than sail against the Chola king (Culavamsa, ch. 60), and in the early 12th century a Velaikkara mercenary corps in Sinhalese service undertook to guard the Temple of the Tooth Relic at Polonnaruwa (Tamil slab inscription). Their weapons are not known in detail, so the unit takes the nearest available infantry model, the game's Ghulam spearman (its pass-through thrust is game invention; see contested), a model no other design uses, since the Hindustanis' Ghulam is a horse archer on the Kipchak model; spears, swords, bows and shields are what the Tamil hero stones (nadukal) show, and Marco Polo saw the men of Ma'bar go to war with lance and shield. It replaces the martial-arts Urumi Swordsman: the urumi, the flexible whip-sword, belongs to the Keralan martial art kalarippayattu (Zarrilli 1998), and we know of no source that puts it on a medieval battlefield; renaming that unit would have hung its whip-sword art and invented blast attack on a real corps (RULES 6.10). Decision: the civ keeps a land unique unit beside the Kalam, on this model, rather than the Kalam alone or the Urumi Swordsman kept under its own name as a stretched martial-arts unit. Scenario Editor infantry (RULES section 5) were checked as well: the Heavy Swordsman (75 HP, 7 attack, no armour) and the Eastern Swordsman (60 HP, 9 attack, 0/1 armour) are sword infantry that might suit the bare-bodied sword-and-shield men of the hero stones better than the Ghulam's armoured spearman, but their look could not be checked here, and the spear fits Marco Polo's lance and shield; they stay candidates for the N2 remodel (see ideas), their stats and look to be checked in game.

Decision: the civ keeps a land unique unit beside the Kalam, on this model, rather than the Kalam alone or the Urumi Swordsman kept under its own name as a stretched martial-arts unit.
