Renamed from Elite Ghulam. Follows the unique unit (Ghulam model → Velaikkarar), for the Tamils only. The name Elite Ghulam also belongs to a different unit of this codex, the Hindustanis' renamed Elite Kipchak (Kipchak model); the site keys units by model.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Thirisadai. Rajendra I's Tanjore inscription (1030–31) says he sent ‘many kalam’ (ships) across the rolling sea and caught the king of Kadaram; kalam, the word of the inscription, is preferred to marakkalam, the common Tamil word for a ship. Its fighting role rests on Rajaraja I's earliest title, from c. 988, kāntaḷūr cālai kalam aṟutta, which Nilakanta Sastri read as the destruction of the Chera ships in the roadstead of Kandalur Salai; the design follows that reading, which is contested (see below), and otherwise the anti-ship role is an abstraction of the fleet. ‘Thirisadai’ is not attested in any inscription or text: it came from the ‘Chola Navy’ article of the English Wikipedia, whose invented ship classes were exposed as a hoax in 2022 and removed.

New in the codex (level 2). Two inscriptions of Parantaka I at Uttaramerur (919 and 921) set out how the assembly (sabha) of this brahmin village chose its committees (variyam) for the year, for the tanks, the gardens, gold and the village's annual business, by lot (kudavolai, ‘pot-tickets’) among the qualified brahmin landholders of its thirty wards, barring those who had failed to render accounts and their kin (Nilakanta Sastri; Karashima 2014). Such assemblies (sabha, ur, nadu) ran the irrigation works, temple endowments and local dues of the Chola countryside; villagers working faster render that local management as an abstraction. Decision: the village assemblies take the Town Center slot rather than Rajaraja I's land survey (c. 1001, whose officer bore the title ulagalanda, ‘who measured the world’) or Kulottunga I's abolition of tolls (an N2 idea at the Market, see ideas).

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Medical Corps (Elephant Units regenerate 30 HP per minute). In 1025 Rajendra I's fleet crossed the Bay of Bengal and sacked a string of ports listed in his Tanjore inscription, from Srivijaya to Kadaram (Kedah), and ‘caught Sangrama-vijayottungavarman, the king of Kadaram, together with the elephants of his army’; his later records style him ‘who took the East, the Ganges and Kadaram’ (purvadesamum gangaiyum kadaramum konda), and Virarajendra intervened at Kadaram again c. 1068, restoring a king who had asked for his help (Nilakanta Sastri; Spencer 1983; Kulke et al. 2009). Effect 1 is an abstraction of the fleet's reach across the Bay of Bengal, effect 2 of the landing parties that sacked the port towns. Medical Corps, which it replaces, moves to the Bengalis as Hastyayurveda, for the royal elephant herds of the land the Indian tradition held to breed the best elephants, and is not shared with this civ, whose elephant arm the Elite Battle Elephant carries.

Kept from the game (level 1). Crucible steel of high carbon content was made in South India and Sri Lanka and exported to the Islamic world, where it became the ‘Damascus’ blade (Srinivasan and Ranganathan 2004). ‘Wootz’ is an 18th-century English corruption of the Kannada and Telugu ukku, ‘steel’; classical Tamil has the cognate eḵku, ‘steel’ and ‘spear’ (Tirukkural 759; Burrow and Emeneau). Decision: the tech keeps the name ‘Wootz Steel’, the standard term of the scholarship, rather than ‘Ekku’ (Tamil eḵku), a word that few readers would recognise. The word ukku and many production sites belong to the Deccan as much as to the Tamil country, so a future Deccan civ would have an equal claim to the tech and could share it. Ignoring armour is an exaggerated abstraction of blade quality.

The window ends in 1323; firearms reached South India only from the later 14th and 15th centuries, with the Bahmanis (1366 according to Firishta, contested), an Indo-Islamic sultanate (see the Hindustanis' N3 idea of a civ for the regional sultanates), and Vijayanagara, which belongs to a future Deccan civ (see ideas).
Same basis. The Mangonel-line, the Siege and Armored Elephants and the Petard keep the civ able to break fortifications; elephants and assault were the attested ways of taking forts.
Same basis: no gunpowder fortifications in the Tamil country before 1323.
Same basis: no gunpowder fortifications in the Tamil country before 1323.

Same basis. The Galley and Fire Ship lines and the Kalam keep the anti-ship role at sea and the single-use Heavy Demolition Ship the anti-building role; no substitute siege warship is added (RULES 6.16.1). Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships. It rests on planked, sea-going ships that crossed open water under royal command and carried armies into battle: the ‘many kalam’ that Rajendra I sent across the Bay of Bengal, whose forces sacked the ports of Srivijaya and Kadaram in 1025 (Tanjore inscription, 1030–31; see the Kalam), and the fleets that carried Pallava, Chola and Pandya armies to Sri Lanka (Culavamsa) and Chola armies to the Maldives (Rajaraja I's inscriptions; see the Transport Ship bonus). A fight at sea is recorded only on Nilakanta Sastri's contested reading of Rajaraja I's destruction of the Chera ships at Kandalur Salai (c. 988; see the Kalam). Whether these ships were royal or requisitioned merchantmen (see contested), they made a war fleet of the Tamil kings, raised and sent by the crown, unlike the merchant shipping of the Gurjaras' ports, so the tier holds on either reading. The Galleon stays as a flagged abstraction of the game's skeleton (RULES 6.16.2), and the Carrack as a generic tier of that fleet.
Same basis.

No crossbows are attested in Pallava, Chola or Pandya armies. The Arbalester needs crossbow evidence, so the crossbow tier goes and the Crossbowman stays as the generic Castle Age bow upgrade until the N2 bow/crossbow split (RULES 6.16.3).

Only where the thumb draw is attested (RULES 6.16.4), and no thumb draw or thumb rings are attested for Pallava, Chola or Pandya archers. Other designs drop the tech on the same ground (among them the Ethiopians, Malians and Gurjaras), and the Bengalis do not get it; the thumb draw belongs to the steppe tradition of the Turkish horse archers, for whom the Hindustanis keep it. The Archer-line and the Elephant Archers keep the civ's archery.

No trebuchets are attested in Pallava, Chola or Pandya warfare: Tamil literature (the Silappatikaram on the walls of Madurai) lists defensive engines such as stone-throwers and mechanical bows, closer to the Mangonel and Scorpion lines, and forts were taken with elephants and by assault. Removed as an engine that never reached the civ (RULES 6.16.5). The traction test of the same rule fails as well, so no Traction Trebuchet is given: the Silappatikaram, usually dated before the window (proposals run from the 2nd to the 6th century), lists only engines mounted on a city's walls for its defence, and no heavy stone-throwing engine is recorded at a Pallava, Chola or Pandya siege in the sources used here. The Mangonel-line stays as the generic stone-thrower, and with the Siege and Armored Elephants, the Petard and Kadaram's infantry it keeps the civ able to break buildings. The civ has no long-range anti-building weapon, which RULES 6.16.5 accepts when none is attested. Decision (power budget): the kit stands as designed, four economic slots (pearls, tanks, temples and Uttaramerur) and the Elite Battle Elephant against the loss of all gunpowder, the Trebuchet, the Arbalester, Thumb Ring, Siphons, Incendiaries, Block Printing, the +200 wood per Age and the Skirmisher and Elephant Archer attack speed, with Kadaram's attack against buildings given to the landing parties' infantry rather than to the warships; no compensation is added (RULES 6.16.13).

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ. The Scenario Editor's Flamethrower (RULES section 5; codex/tools/scenario-units.md), a short-range flame-spraying siege engine, is not used either: no siphon or other flame-projecting engine is attested in Pallava, Chola or Pandya warfare.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.
No printing in the window (to 1323): Tamil texts were copied on palm leaf, and the first book in Tamil type, the Thambiran Vanakkam, was printed by Jesuits in 1578.

The Tamil country is one of the great stone-building traditions: the Pallava monoliths and Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram (7th–8th centuries), the granite vimana of the Rajarajeshvara at Thanjavur, about 66 m high (c. 1010), and Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Its absence was the most ironic gap of the old tree.

An abstraction of faster building: no treadwheel cranes are attested in India, and the tech stands for the scale of Chola building in granite. How the Thanjavur vimana was raised is not recorded; a local tradition speaks of a long earthen ramp, which no inscription mentions.
Same basis as Architecture: the Chola temples were built of granite quarried and hauled from far afield.

Tamil kings fought from elephant-back and kept large elephant corps: the Chola crown prince Rajaditya fell on his elephant at Takkolam (949), and Chola records remember him as ‘the lord who died on the elephant’; Rajadhiraja I was killed on his elephant at Koppam (1054); the 12th-century war poem Kalingattupparani celebrates the elephants of Kulottunga I's Kalinga campaign; and Amir Khusrau counts elephants among the spoils that Malik Kafur took from the Pandya Ma'bar in 1311 (Nilakanta Sastri; Amir Khusrau).
Tank and canal irrigation allowed more than one paddy crop a year in the Kaveri delta (Karashima 2014); the absence of the field tech sat ill with the new farm bonus.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no trebuchet is attested in Pallava, Chola or Pandya warfare; the nearest attested engines are the stone-throwers on the walls of Madurai in the Silappatikaram, defensive pieces (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Shotel Warrior. From Amda Seyon (1314–1344) onward the core of the royal army were the chewa, standing regiments raised and maintained by the king (Glorious Victories of Amda Seyon; Taddesse Tamrat, 1972), and al-Umari (cited by Taddesse Tamrat) names the spear as the Ethiopians' main weapon, with swords rare. The Inca Kamayuk, an infantryman with a long spear strong against cavalry and infantry, is the nearest existing unit: the highland spearmen had to stand against the cavalry of Ifat and Adal. The model is shared with the Inca Awqa Kamayuq, the Berbers' Murabit and the Mapuche Colihue Lancer.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Shotel Warrior. From Amda Seyon (1314–1344) onward the core of the royal army were the chewa, standing regiments raised and maintained by the king (Glorious Victories of Amda Seyon; Taddesse Tamrat, 1972), and al-Umari (cited by Taddesse Tamrat) names the spear as the Ethiopians' main weapon, with swords rare. The Inca Kamayuk, an infantryman with a long spear strong against cavalry and infantry, is the nearest existing unit: the highland spearmen had to stand against the cavalry of Ifat and Adal. The model is shared with the Inca Awqa Kamayuq, the Berbers' Murabit and the Mapuche Colihue Lancer.
Renamed from Elite Kamayuk. Follows the unique unit (Kamayuk → Chewa Spearman) for the Ethiopians only.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Royal Heirs (Shotel Warriors and Camel Riders receive -3 damage from Mounted Units). Gult was the right to collect tribute, largely in kind, from the peasants of a district, granted by the king to soldiers, nobles and churches; it fed the regiments without cash wages (Taddesse Tamrat, 1972; Crummey, 2000). A royal grant of land revenue belongs at the Town Center. Royal Heirs named a real institution (the princes held on Amba Geshen to prevent succession wars) but its effect had nothing to do with it.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Torsion Engines (Siege Workshop Units' blast radius increased). From Amda Seyon (1314–1344) onward the core of the army were the chewa, standing regiments raised and maintained by the king and later settled on land (Glorious Victories; Taddesse Tamrat, 1972). al-Umari (cited by Taddesse Tamrat) names the spear as the Ethiopians' main weapon, with the bow beside it, so the tech covers spearmen, the Chewa Spearmen among them, and archers. No existing Ethiopian tech fits (Torsion Engines evoked Greco-Roman torsion artillery, never attested in Ethiopia), so this is a new tech (level 2).
There were no Ethiopian siege guns before 1543: the highland kingdom took places by blockade and assault, and it was Adal that used a cannon (from 1531, according to Arab Faqih).

The top tier of the stone-thrower line is dropped (the tech tree audit rates it unfounded); the Mangonel and Onager stay as a generic abstraction of assault and blockade, since mountain warfare turned on ambas and blockades (RULES 6.16.5).

No torsion or traction artillery is attested in Ethiopia, where the highland kingdom took places by blockade and assault, so the counterweight engine never reached the civ and is removed (RULES 6.16.5); the Mangonel and Onager stay as the generic stone-thrower, and the Siege Ram as the late anti-building engine. The civ has no long-range anti-building weapon, as RULES 6.16.5 allows where none is attested.

The navy is a fleet of ships (RULES 6.16.1), resting on late Aksum: for Kaleb's expedition to Himyar (c. 525) the king had ten ships of his own built, beside sixty merchant ships from the Roman Red Sea ports (Aila, Clysma, Iotabe, Berenike), the Farasan islands and India, gathered at Gabaza, the harbour below Adulis (Martyrium Arethae, ed. Detoraki and Beaucamp, 2007; Bowersock, 2013), and Abyssinian raiders still struck Jeddah in 702, after which the Umayyads occupied the Dahlak islands (Insoll, 2001, after Tedeschi and Munro-Hay; see contested). So the generic tiers stay (galleys, the Galleon as a flagged abstraction under RULES 6.16.2, Carrack, Shipwright), without the Fast Fire Ship and Carvel Hull, as in the game. After Aksum the kingdom had no navy of its own, and the coast was held only loosely through the Bahr Negash until the Ottomans took Massawa (1557). No gunpowder warships, so the Cannon Galleon goes.
Camels belonged to the lowlands (Afar, Somali, Adal), not to the Christian highland army, which rode horses and mules.
As Camel Rider.
No horse archery is attested in the Christian army, whose horsemen fought with spears (tech tree audit).
As Cavalry Archer.

No crossbow is attested in Ethiopia, so the crossbow tier goes (RULES 6.16.3); the Crossbowman stays as the generic Castle Age bow upgrade until the N2 bow/crossbow split, and the archers rest on the +18% fire rate, Bracer and Chewa (RULES 6.11). The tech tree audit rates the Ethiopian Arbalester unfounded; no blanket compensation makes up for the power it takes from this archer civ (RULES 6.16.13).

No thumb draw or thumb rings are attested for Ethiopian archery (RULES 6.16.4); the thumb draw belongs to the steppe and Asian traditions (names theme), and other designs drop the tech on the same ground (among them the Malians, Malay, Maya, Inca and Muisca).

Late element, RULES section 2, and the civ's only one (the unit is Imperial Age only). The great firearms episode of Ethiopian history is the war of 1529–1543: Adal received Arab and Ottoman musketeers from Zabid (1542), Cristóvão da Gama landed with c. 400 Portuguese musketeers (1541; Castanhoso, 1564), and after Wayna Daga (1543) the Ethiopians took up the musket. Before 1541 the kingdom had only a handful of guns, so Ethiopian musketeers proper come after 1500, but the war of 1541–1543 gives the unit clear fame. The game's tree had it the other way round (Bombard Cannon without Hand Cannoneer).

Added and renamed Baql, with the look of the Scenario Editor's Donkey (see the bonus and the rename): it stands beside the Lumber and Mining Camps instead of replacing them, as in the Tatars' design, where it is the Araba. The Ethiopians are one of the Mule Cart's four holders (RULES 6.16.7).

Renamed from Mule Cart, with the look of the Donkey. Mules were the pack animals of the highlands, and transport there was by pack mule and porter, with almost no wheeled vehicles (Pankhurst, 1961; see the bonus), so a cart is foreign to the civ (RULES 6.16.15). The look is the Scenario Editor's Donkey (The Forgotten), existing game content (RULES section 5), which stands in for the mule it closely resembles and fits the highland pack train better than the Caucasian cart, as the Ox Wagon fits the Tatars' Araba. Only the look is used, so the unit keeps the Mule Cart's function, and the Donkey's art, loads and scale on a drop-site unit must be checked in game. It is a level-1 look change for an existing holder, not an extension of the Mule Cart (RULES 6.16.7). The name is the Ge'ez baql, ‘mule’ (Amharic baqlo), which Dillmann's lexicon records with citations from the Ge'ez Bible (Dillmann, 1865): the written language of the whole window names the pack animal itself, so it is the period term RULES 6.16.15 asks for, with ‘pack mule’ as its English gloss.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no torsion or traction artillery is attested in Ethiopia, where places were taken by blockade and assault (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

Kept from the game (level 1). The francisca, the Frankish throwing axe: Procopius describes it (Wars VI.25, the Frankish invasion of Italy in 539), Gregory of Tours shows axes in Frankish hands (Histories II.27, the ewer of Soissons), Isidore of Seville explains the name (Etymologiae XVIII.6.9), and axes are found in graves such as Childeric I’s at Tournai (481/482).

Kept from the game (level 1). The francisca, the Frankish throwing axe: Procopius describes it (Wars VI.25, the Frankish invasion of Italy in 539), Gregory of Tours shows axes in Frankish hands (Histories II.27, the ewer of Soissons), Isidore of Seville explains the name (Etymologiae XVIII.6.9), and axes are found in graves such as Childeric I’s at Tournai (481/482).

Changed by the codex (level 2); replaces Ordonnance Companies (Castle unique tech, Mounted Crossbowmen cost -40% gold). The Ordinance of Orléans (2 November 1439) reserved to the king the raising of troops and the taille that paid them, which was thereafter levied every year without the Estates’ consent; on that basis Charles VII’s ordinance of 1445 created fifteen companies of 100 ‘lances’ (a man-at-arms, a coutilier, a page and two mounted archers, some with bows and some with crossbows, plus a valet), keeping the best of the écorcheurs in pay and dismissing the rest: the first permanent royal army of France and one of the first standing armies in Europe (Contamine 1972; cf. Mallett 1974). At the Town Center because the reform rested on the crown’s monopoly of armed force and of the tax that paid for it, a state matter (RULES 6.2); the effect renders the army that tax paid for, its gold discount a force paid by the crown, and the Knight-line renders the men-at-arms (gendarmes) at the head of each lance, the heavy cavalry at the core of the companies; the mounted archers of the lances, who usually dismounted to shoot, stay with the foot Archer line. The taille paid the companies’ wages at the musters (montres), monthly at first and quarterly from 1450, and the man-at-arms answered out of them for the men and horses of his lance; a lance found ill kept was ‘broken’ (cassée) (Contamine 1972). The sources tie the discount to a force paid by a permanent tax, not to a size: the magnitude is set by the minimum of balance where history leaves the choice (RULES 6.14). The owner asked for less than the Polish -60% (19 October 2026), and the design sets half of it, -30%: the game’s -60% belongs to the Poles, whose Knight-line stops at the Cavalier, while the Franks keep the Paladin and the mounted HP passive. At -30% (52.5 gold) a Frankish Paladin (192 HP and 14 attack; the Franks’ tree has no Bloodlines) buys a little less HP × attack per gold than the game’s Polish Cavalier at -60% (140 HP with Bloodlines, 12 attack, 30 gold), the yardstick the game sets for this discount: about 51 against 56. At -40% (45 gold) it would already buy more, about 60, and at -60% (30 gold) about 90, some 1.6 times the Polish figure. Taken one at a time, its HP and attack per gold stay well below the Polish Cavalier’s at -30% (about 3.7 HP and 0.27 attack against 4.7 and 0.40) and still below them at -40% (4.3 and 0.31); the product is the measure used here, as a unit’s worth in a fight grows with both. The francs-archers of 1448, one archer per parish exempted from the taille, are not given a tech of their own: an uneven militia, mocked in the ‘Franc-archer de Bagnolet’ and disbanded after Guinegate (1479), they fail the relevance test beside the companies.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Chivalry (Stables work +40% faster), in the Castle slot. Jean Bureau and his brother Gaspard, who ran Charles VII’s artillery from the 1440s, built up the royal siege train: in the reconquest of Normandy (1449–50) its guns forced the surrender of town after town, among them Harfleur, Caen and Cherbourg, so that the duchy fell in about a year, and at Castillon (17 July 1453) Jean Bureau’s entrenched artillery park broke Talbot’s attack and ended the English hold on Guyenne (Contamine 1972). Faster Siege Workshop units render the speed with which the train moved from siege to siege. A datable military reform, so at the Castle (RULES 6.2), in the Imperial Age after the Ordonnance Companies (1445), which also puts the civ’s techs in chronological order; the analysis proposed the tech.

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, the projector of Greek fire, a state secret never to be given to another nation (De Administrando Imperio 13); its game effect, an explosive charge for fire ships, has no medieval Western equivalent. The fire-ship line itself stays as the engine’s convention for close-range incendiary warships. Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, from the royal galleys built at the Clos des Galées of Rouen (founded under Philip IV in the 1290s) and the fleets of the Hundred Years War (Arnemuiden, 1338; Sluys, 1340) to the fleet of Charles VIII, whose ship guns bombarded the Aragonese (Neapolitan) landing force at Rapallo while Swiss and French infantry attacked it (1494; Guicciardini, Storia d’Italia I), the basis of the Cannon Galleon. The Galleon stays as the skeleton’s flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2).

France has some of the earliest stone halls and keeps (Doué-la-Fontaine, a hall turned into a keep c. 950; Langeais; Loches), and Philip Augustus (1180–1223) carried the great tower across the royal domain with round towers built to a common design, the ‘tours philippiennes’: the Grosse Tour of the Louvre (c. 1190–1202), Gisors and, after the conquest of 1204, Rouen and Falaise (Mesqui 1991–93; Baldwin 1986). In the game the Franks were the only civ of their region without the Keep.

France fielded crossbowmen in numbers: the Master of Crossbowmen (maître des arbalétriers) commanded the king’s foot and engineers from Louis IX’s reign until the office was abolished in 1534, towns kept crossbow companies, and Genoese crossbowmen were hired in thousands in the 14th century (Contamine 1980). French missile troops were numerous despite the English image of Crécy (RULES 6.16.3: crossbow evidence).

Late medieval crossbowmen and archers wore brigandines or padded jacks and fought behind large pavises. Added although it brings the tree closer to the English one: the item rests on this period evidence, and no trim for differentiation was applied to it (the recommended default of the region’s differentiation question, level-1 review, section 7). Bracer is not added, because Arbalester and Ring Archer Armor already bring the archers of this cavalry civ close to the archer civs’, and Bracer would also strengthen its cheap castles.

Étienne Boileau’s Livre des métiers (c. 1268) recorded the statutes of about a hundred Paris crafts, and the Champagne fairs of the counts of Champagne (Troyes, Provins, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube) were the great market of 12th–13th-century Europe, before they declined after the county passed to the Crown.

Kept from the game (level 1). The monaspa (roughly “host of servants”) was the royal guard that David IV formed in his military reform of c. 1118, well armed (modern overviews give it lance and bow) and serving the king directly. Growing stronger near other heavy cavalry abstracts a cohesive elite. The model is shared with the Castilians' Freire (owner's decision) and the Poles' Kopijnik.

New in the codex (level 1). The Kipchak horse archers whom David IV settled in Georgia c. 1118–1120, after his marriage to Gurandukht, daughter of the khan Atrak (Otrok in the Rus' chronicles); his historian speaks of 40,000 warriors (Life of David; Golden, 1984; Rayfield, 2012). Kipchak contingents fought at Didgori (Ibn al-Athir), and many modern historians consider them decisive. The same unit as the Cumans' Kipchak, since the Qivchaqni of the Georgian sources belonged to the same Cuman-Kipchak confederation (see the Cumans' contested note); trained at the Castle with its Elite upgrade there, as for the Cumans. The model also serves, each use on its own history, the Hindustanis' Ghulam and the Arabs' Mamluk, and the Bulgarians' Cuman Alliance gives free Elite Kipchaks to their team; RULES 6.7 and 6.16.12 accept this reuse. It benefits from Thumb Ring and, from the Imperial Age, from the aznauri population bonus.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Svan Towers (Fortifications +2 attack; Watch Tower-line deals pass through damage), dropped for relevance: the Svan tower-houses were family defences in one province and did not shape the kingdom's history. David IV's military reform of c. 1118–1121 rested on the Kipchaks: after marrying Gurandukht, daughter of the khan Atrak, he settled Kipchak families on royal land in a kingdom emptied by the Seljuk “Great Turkish troubles” of the 1080s, each family owing a soldier, which gave the crown a standing army independent of the great lords (Life of David; Golden, 1984). At Didgori (12 August 1121), according to Ibn al-Athir, a Kipchak detachment feigned to desert and fell on the Muslim leaders before the royal army broke Ilghazi's coalition (Walter the Chancellor and Matthew of Edessa also mention a small Frankish contingent), which opened the way to Tbilisi (1122). The tech lets the settled Kipchaks be raised outside the Castle. It also stands for Didgori, which has no tech of its own: the battle was the outcome of the same reform (RULES 6.3), and no source describes a lance charge there that a charge effect could render. Svan Towers is not kept as a fame exception: the slot goes to the reform that reversed the Seljuk conquest.

New in the codex (level 2). In 1103 David IV called the church council of Ruisi and Urbnisi, which deposed unworthy bishops, many of them creatures of the great families, and set the church in order; he joined the see of Chqondidi to the office of chancellor (mtsignobartukhutsesi), so that the archbishop-chancellor (the Chqondideli), first his tutor Giorgi, became the first of the king's ministers and headed the royal administration for the rest of the golden age (Life of David; Suny, 1994; Rayfield, 2012). Faster Town Centers abstract the stronger central government; this effect is preferred to “All gold income +10% faster” (the royal fiscal administration) and to the Tamils' Uttaramerur effect (David's restoration of the realm), since the reform built a government rather than a treasury or a work force.

New in the codex (level 2). David IV founded the monastery and academy of Gelati in 1106, and his historian calls it a second Jerusalem and another Athens (Life of David). Tradition links it with the philosophers Ioane Petritsi and Arsen Iqaltoeli (on Petritsi, L. Gigineishvili, The Platonic Theology of Ioane Petritsi, 2007). It became the intellectual centre of the golden age and the burial place of David IV. It is a distinct datable moment from the military and church reforms (RULES 6.3), so it keeps a third tech slot, level 2 like the other two, since no existing tech fits these moments.

Firearms are not attested in Georgian armies of the core period (1089–1213), and no evidence of their use is known before the kingdom split (c. 1490). Any guns of its last decades would be marginal, so the tree follows the period the civ represents, as for the Byzantines' guns of 1453 (RULES 6.16.19(d)).
No naval artillery and no significant war fleet in the period, despite the Abkhazian Black Sea coast; the civ has the basic navy (RULES 6.16.1), with no substitute siege warship.
No significant war fleet of its own (see Cannon Galleon): the basic navy only (RULES 6.16.1: Galley and War Galley, Fire Galley and Fire Ship, Hulk and War Hulk, demolition ships and the Dock techs).
As Galleon.
No printing in the window: the first book in Georgian type, a Georgian–Italian dictionary, was printed in Rome in 1629.

The Kipchaks whom David IV settled in Georgia (c. 1118–1120; Golden, 1984) were steppe horse archers: a steppe archery tradition the kingdom's armies demonstrably used (RULES 6.16.4). Modern overviews also arm the royal guard (monaspa) with the bow, but its composition is debated (see the civ-level contested list), and the basis does not rest on it. The civ had Heavy Cavalry Archer and Parthian Tactics without Thumb Ring.
A strong monastic culture: the academy of Gelati (1106), Iviron on Mount Athos (c. 980), Petritsoni (1083) and the Monastery of the Cross in Jerusalem.
As for Illumination: the full monastery tree for one of the great Orthodox monastic cultures.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Huskarl. Heavy horsemen armed with lance and sword and without bows, the striking arm of the Ostrogothic army (Procopius, Wars V.27); the Visigothic levies also had archers and slingers (Ervig's law, Liber Iudiciorum IX.2.9). The Leitis model (strong vs infantry and cavalry, weak vs archery units, its lance ignoring armour) follows Procopius: Belisarius explained his victories by the Goths' lack of mounted archers (V.27), and at Taginae (552) the Gothic lance charge was shot down by Narses' 8,000 foot archers (VIII.31–32). Neither the Coustillier nor the Cataphract is used: the Coustillier is ‘strong vs archery units’, against this evidence, and the Cataphract stands for Byzantine heavy cavalry; the 6th-century Roman horse that beat the Goths were armoured lancer-archers (Wars I.1), the opposite of the bowless Gothic horse. Of the Scenario Editor cavalry (RULES section 5), the Sogdian Cataphract's very high pierce armour contradicts the Goths' weakness to archers and the Imperial Centurion renders a Roman officer, so the Leitis stays as the closest role. The Huskarl is dropped: húskarl is an Old Norse word for the household troops of 10th–11th-century Scandinavian kings, three to five centuries after the Gothic kingdoms.

Renamed from Elite Leitis. Follows the unique unit (Leitis → Gothic Lancer), for the Goths only; the Lithuanians' design drops the Leitis.

New in the codex (level 1). Leovigild made the Visigothic kingdom a peninsular state by war: John of Biclaro records a campaign almost every year from 570, against the Byzantine south and rebel Córdoba (570–572), Cantabria (574), the revolt of his son Hermenegild (579–584), the Basques (581) and the Suevic kingdom, which he annexed (585). Isidore says he enlarged the realm by war and was the first Gothic king to sit on a throne in royal dress (Historia Gothorum 49–51), and he was the first to strike gold coins in his own name (Collins 2004). Faster training renders the royal host called out year after year, and the charge the Visigothic horse, which trusted most in the swift charge (Historia Gothorum 70); the Militia-line charge is a game abstraction with no Gothic evidence. Royal and military, so at the Castle (RULES 6.2). It keeps the Imperial Age of Comitatenses (RULES 6.16.11), so, with the Liber Iudiciorum also in the Imperial Age, the Goths have no unique tech in the Castle Age.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Perfusion. The Visigothic law code (Recceswinth, 654; revised by Ervig, 681) was one law for Goths and Romans, and its military title (IX.2) is the fullest record of an early medieval levy. Its older laws (antiquae, of uncertain date) muster the host in a decimal frame of thiufadi (commanders of a thousand), quingentenarii, centenarii and decani and punish officers who let men off and men who desert; Wamba's law (673) obliged free men, clergy and magnates to answer the call against invasion or revolt, and Ervig's (681) required them to bring a tenth of their slaves armed, some in mail, most with shields, swords, lances or bows, some with slings (IX.2.8–9). The effect renders this compulsory levy rather than a paid army. The laws also show how hard it was to raise armies: Ervig had the Twelfth Council of Toledo (681) restore the legal standing of those punished under Wamba's law (King 1972; Collins 2004). Royal legislation, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2). Perfusion, a medical term, had no Gothic referent; the Swedes' design reuses its effect for Engelbrekt's Rising.
Gunpowder reached Europe c. 1320, six centuries after the last Gothic kingdom fell (553/711).
As for the Hand Cannoneer.
Belisarius explained his victories by the Goths' lack of mounted archers: their horsemen used only spears and swords and their bowmen fought on foot (Procopius, Wars V.27).
As for the Cavalry Archer.
Hungarian and Serbian light cavalry of the 15th century, eight centuries after the Gothic kingdoms; Light Cavalry stays.

The counterweight trebuchet appears in the 12th century, five centuries after the Gothic kingdoms, and the Goths were notoriously poor besiegers (Fritigern ‘at peace with walls’, Ammianus 31.6.4), so it is removed as an engine that never reached them (RULES 6.16.5). No heavy stone-thrower of their own is attested in the sources used for this design (Julian of Toledo's account of Wamba's siege of Nîmes, 673, has not been checked for engines), so the Goths have no heavy stone-thrower on land, which RULES 6.16.5 allows; the Siege Ram, rendering their rams, is the substitute (RULES 6.11), and the kept Siege Tower renders their towers. The Mangonel and Scorpion lines stay only as generic abstractions: at Vitiges' siege of Rome (537) the torsion engines stood on the walls, on Belisarius' side (Procopius, Wars V.21). They stay as such, like the Champion and Halberdier and the Plate Mail Armor this design adds, until the late-antiquity ceiling planned for N3 (see the ideas).

The fire siphon was a Byzantine invention of c. 672 and a state secret (De Administrando Imperio 13), after the Ostrogoths and never shared with the Visigoths. Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, resting on the thousand dromons that Theodoric ordered for the kingdom's grain transport and defence (Cassiodorus, Variae V.16–17) and on the Visigothic fleet that, Isidore says, took the Goths to war at sea under Sisebut (612–621; Historia Gothorum 70), represented by keeping the regional Dromon (Wamba's naval victory over an Arab fleet rests only on the late Chronicle of Alfonso III); the Galleon, Carrack, Fast Fire Ship, demolition ships, Petard and Heated Shot stay as abstractions of the game's skeleton (RULES 6.16.1–2). No Dromon bonus is added: the Gothic fleets were short-lived, and Totila's was destroyed at Sena Gallica (551; Procopius, Wars VIII.23).
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

Theodoric restored the walls of Rome and other cities (Anonymus Valesianus 67; Cassiodorus, Variae), Leovigild founded walled Reccopolis (578), and Toledo, Septimania and the Pyrenean passes had Visigothic fortifications; a wall-less ‘nomad’ tree is the barbarian stereotype.
Comes with the Stone Wall.
Late Roman city walls, which the Goths kept and repaired, were studded with towers.
Late Roman city walls, which the Goths kept and repaired, were studded with towers.
The Aurelian walls of Rome and the walls of Ravenna and Toledo were held and repaired by Gothic kings.
The Aurelian walls of Rome and the walls of Ravenna and Toledo were held and repaired by Gothic kings.

Gothic warriors were not unarmoured peasants: the elite wore mail and Roman-type segmented helmets, and Ervig's law expects mail among the levy; the top armour tier is a generic abstraction. Plate Barding Armor, which the game's Goths lack, is not added: no horse armour is attested for the Gothic cavalry, whose vulnerability to archers (Procopius, Wars V.27, VIII.32) the design keeps.

The Goths kept their Homoian (‘Arian’) church as a mark of identity, the Ostrogoths to the end and the Visigoths until Reccared's conversion at the Third Council of Toledo (589); units dying rather than changing sides renders that confessional loyalty.
Substitute for the removed Trebuchet as the late anti-building engine (RULES 6.11): the Goths' siege engines were rams and towers, as at Vitiges' siege of Rome (537; Procopius, Wars V.21–22).

Restored: the game withholds this generic tech from its Goths only in exchange for a stronger civ bonus (Infantry +1/+2/+3 attack vs. buildings), which this design drops (see dropped). The Goths' weakness was storming walls, not burning what they overran: after 376 they laid Thrace waste with fire and slaughter (Ammianus 31.6), Alaric's army ravaged Greece in 395–396 (Zosimus 5.5–6), and when Rome fell in 410 the houses by the Salarian Gate, among them the house of Sallust, were burned (Procopius, Wars 3.2.24). The weakness against walls stays in the dropped bonus; the generic tech returns.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no Gothic siege engine is attested, and the Goths were poor besiegers (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

Kept from the game (level 1). Pratihara cavalry is well attested (the Akhbar, 851), and an indigenous record, the Pehowa inscription of Bhoja's reign (882), shows horse dealers trading at the fair of Prithudaka inside the empire. The name comes from the Chatsu inscription of the Guhilas, which records horses called śrīvaṃśa, able to cross ‘seas of sand’, given to Mihira Bhoja by his Guhila feudatory Harsha (Hooja 2006). A fast light horseman is a fair image of a cavalry raised on desert-bred horses. As in the game it is trained at the Stable; with the Chakram Thrower dropped, the Castle trains it too, so that the Castle keeps a unique unit (as the game's Huns can train the Tarkan at both, with Marauders). Decision: the Stable-and-Castle arrangement stands; no other Castle unit is restored.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Kshatriyas (Military Units cost -25% food). Under Mihira Bhoja (836–885) the Pratihara empire reached its widest extent as a hierarchy of samantas, subordinate rulers who served the overlord with contingents they raised and fed themselves: his records run from the Daulatpura plate (843) in Rajasthan to the Pehowa inscription (882) in Haryana, and feudatories such as the Guhilas of Chatsu, the Chahamanas of Shakambhari and the Tomaras served him and his son Mahendrapala I (Puri 1957; Chattopadhyaya 1994; Hooja 2006). The later Rajput states rested on lineage lands held in return for service. Hence an army that costs its king less food. Same effect, renamed: ‘Kshatriyas’ turned the varna that Rajput lineages claimed into a technology, and its effect had no link to the concept. Decision: the name Samantas, an office-holder's title of the inscriptions, replaces it.

Kept from the game (level 1). ‘Pratihara’ means door-keeper, and the dynasty traced its descent to Lakshmana, door-keeper of Rama. The Gwalior prashasti of Mihira Bhoja credits Nagabhata I with crushing the armies of a powerful mleccha ruler (the Arab governors of Sind, c. 730s); the Akhbar (851) calls the Gurjara king the greatest enemy of the Muslims in India; and al-Mas'udi, who visited India c. 915–16 (Muruj al-Dhahab, written 943–47), says that the king of Kannauj kept one of his four armies facing the Muslim ruler of Multan. After the Rashtrakuta Indra III sacked Kannauj (c. 916) the Pratiharas ceased to be the main bulwark, and from the 11th century the threat came through the Ghaznavid Punjab. The effect, armour for the camels and elephant archers of the western armies, is a game abstraction attached to an apt name: no source describes a dedicated camel-and-elephant frontier corps. It stays in the Imperial Age: with a single Castle tech RULES 6.4 sets no order, and +4 melee armour in the Castle Age would strengthen a civ that now also gains the Knight and Cavalier. Decision: the game's effect is kept, which keeps the tech identical in play and level 1; a defensive effect such as ‘Watch Tower-line +2 range’ (the game's Korean Eupseong), which the analysis proposes, would make it a new tech (level 2) and is not used.

The Rajput kingdoms fought essentially without guns: at Khanwa (1527) Babur's matchlocks and field guns faced Rana Sanga's cavalry (Baburnama). Guns reached the region in the 15th century through the sultanates of Malwa and Gujarat (Iqtidar Alam Khan 1981), which lie outside this civ, as does the Gujarati fleet that fought at Diu (1509) (see contested and ideas); whether Rajput garrisons used guns before 1527 is not established in the sources used here.

Same basis; Rumi Khan's siege guns at Chittor (1535) served Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, after the window. The Trebuchet stays as attested in Rajput hands: during the siege of Ranthambore (1299–1301) a stone from a maghribi in the Chauhan fort, the engine whose Arabic name denotes the counterweight trebuchet, killed the Delhi general Nusrat Khan (Barani; see contested). With the Mangonel-line, the Siege and Armored Elephants and the Petard it keeps the civ able to break buildings (RULES 6.11).

Same basis: gun-armed ships belong to the Gujarati fleet of Malik Ayaz, not to the Rajput kingdoms. The Galley and Fire Ship lines keep the anti-ship role at sea and the single-use Heavy Demolition Ship the anti-building role; no substitute siege warship is added (RULES 6.16.1).

Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): no war fleet of its own, so the basic navy only. The Pratihara and Rajput kingdoms were land powers; the Gujarat ports of the team bonus served the ships of merchants, the nakhudas and nauvittakas (Chakravarti 2000), and the Gujarati war fleet of Chaul and Diu (1508–09) belongs to the Gujarat Sultanate, outside this civ (see contested). So the civ keeps the Galley-line to War Galley, the Fire Galley and Fire Ship, the Hulk and War Hulk, the demolition ships and the generic Dock techs, with no Galleon, Carrack or siege warship.
See Galleon.

Only where the thumb draw is attested (RULES 6.16.4), and no thumb draw or thumb rings are attested for Pratihara or Rajput archers: in India the thumb ring (zihgir) is above all Mughal, and the thumb draw belongs to the steppe tradition of the Turkish horse archers, for whom the Hindustanis keep the tech. Other designs drop the tech on the same ground (among them the Ethiopians, Malians and Tamils), and the Bengalis do not get it; the Archer-line and the Elephant Archers keep the civ's archery.

Rajput armies fought above all as shock cavalry with lance and sword: at the first battle of Tarain (1191) Prithviraj Chauhan's army broke the Ghurid wings and wounded Muhammad of Ghur (Minhaj), and at Khanwa (1527) Rana Sanga's horsemen charged Babur's line (Baburnama). The contrast at Tarain (1192) was between this cavalry and the Turkish horse archers, so the Cavalry Archer stays out.
Same basis; no Paladin, so the Knight and Cavalier mark the Rajput shock cavalry. The Hindustanis get only the Knight, as a power-budget trim.

Pratihara and Rajput armies fielded war elephants: the Hudud al-Alam (982) gives the rai of Kannauj 800 of them (via Hooja 2006), the Chatsu inscription praises the elephant force of the Guhila Harsha, and Minhaj puts elephants in Prithviraj Chauhan's army at Tarain (1191–92). Without the Elite upgrade: a design choice that keeps the cavalry at the centre of the civ, not a historical judgement on the size or quality of these elephant corps.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Ghulam (Infantry): unique Infantry that thrusts its spear through multiple targets. The ghulams or bandagan of the Ghaznavids, the Ghurids and the Sultanate were Turkish slave soldiers bought young and trained above all as mounted archers and officers: Sabuktigin, founder of Ghaznavid power, and the sultans Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban had all been military slaves (Bosworth 1963; Jackson 1999; Kumar 2007). The system is older than the Mongol invasions (Aibak bought Iltutmish in the 1190s, according to Minhaj), and Delhi's bandagan also included other Turks and Indian-born slaves; but from the 1220s the Mongol conquest of the Kipchak steppe filled the slave markets that supplied both Delhi's Shamsi bandagan and Cairo's Bahri mamluks (Jackson 1999), and Minhaj gives Iltutmish and Balban an Ilbari origin. So the Cuman Kipchak, a horse archer firing several arrows, is the nearest existing model, as for the Arabs' Mamluk (a deliberate parallel: one institution, largely the same supply after the 1220s). The old spear-thrusting infantry inverted their role. The name also belongs to a different game unit, the infantry Ghulam (its own model), which passes to the Tamils' Velaikkarar; a codex unit may take the name of a different game unit (RULES 6.16.15), and the site keys units by model. Decision: the model is shared with the Cumans' and Georgians' Kipchak and the Arabs' Mamluk until the N2 armoured horse archer (see ideas). The alternatives were weighed and set aside: a heavy cavalry model such as the Persians' Savar would show the armour but lose the bow that defined the ghulam, and so would the Scenario Editor's Sogdian Cataphract, a melee horseman (RULES section 5); the Scenario Editor's Khan, a horse archer with some armour, would show the ghulam better, but as it is (level 1) its hero stats (160 HP and 12 attack at range 4, codex/tools/scenario-units-stats.md) would outclass every trainable horse archer, and with adapted stats it is level 2, so it is left to the N2 remodel.

Renamed from Elite Kipchak. Follows the unique unit (Kipchak → Ghulam), for the Hindustanis only, as the Arabs' design renames it Elite Mamluk.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Grand Trunk Road (All gold income +10% faster; Market trading fee reduced to 10%). Iltutmish (1211–36) gave the Sultanate a standard coinage, the silver tanka with the billon jital, struck at Delhi and the provincial mints; the successor sultanates of Bengal, Gujarat and the Deccan kept the tanka, and Sher Shah's silver rupiya (1540s) took over its role (Wright 1936; Jackson 1999). Same effect, new name: ‘Grand Trunk Road’ is a 19th-century British name for a road that Sher Shah Suri rebuilt in the 1540s. The tech was called ‘Sultans’ until 2022; the design names it after the coin, the institution it renders, rather than reviving that name.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Shatagni (Hand Cannoneers +2 range). After the Mongol siege of Delhi (1303) Alauddin Khalji raised a large standing cavalry on fixed cash pay (Barani gives 234 tankas a year for a trooper with one horse) and, to stop men passing muster with a borrowed or worn-out horse or with a substitute, had every horse branded (dagh) and a descriptive roll (huliya) kept of every trooper (Barani; Jackson 1999). The horses so checked were largely war-horses imported from Central Asia, Afghanistan and the Gulf, larger and stronger than Indian-bred mounts, and Delhi's hold on that trade was a pillar of its power over its Indian rivals (Digby 1971). Sturdier mounted archers, the bulk of the cavalry and the Ghulam among them, render sound, inspected horses; the same effect stands for the Ottoman timar in the Turks' design, another institution that kept Turkish horse archers mounted. The datable reform takes the Castle slot, while the structural elephant stables are a passive (RULES 6.2). It stays in the Castle Age, its game age; the design's power budget (no Cavalier, no Elite Battle Elephant, no gunpowder) does not call for moving it to the Imperial Age. Shatagni, which it replaces, gave an ancient Sanskrit word for a spiked missile weapon (śataghnī) to 16th-century hand-gunners: the firearm reading was popularised by Oppert (1880) on the strength of the Śukranīti, which Lallanji Gopal (1962) showed to be a 19th-century text. The paired term ‘dagh-o-chehra’ belongs to Akbar's revival of the system in the 1570s. Decision: Dagh keeps the Sipahi effect, identical in play and level 1, rather than becoming a new level-2 tech with ‘Mounted Units +15% HP’ (the Franks' ‘Mounted Units +20% HP’ at a lower magnitude, which would also cover the lancers' horses): reuse is accepted (RULES 6.16.12), and since the Arabs' design no longer pairs the effect with its Kipchak-model Mamluk, the reason to diversify it has gone.

No hand-guns are documented in Delhi's armies: Babur's account of Panipat (1526) mentions no guns on Ibrahim Lodi's side, and the matchlocks of that day were Babur's. Iqtidar Alam Khan argues for 13th-century knowledge of gunpowder from the Mongols, as pyrotechnics rather than firearms (2004), and for cannon in north India from the 1440s (1981) (see contested); guns weigh in north Indian battle only from Babur, and they belong to the Mughals, after the time frame. The Hand Cannoneer is not kept for gameplay either (for example in the Imperial Age), since it would represent no Sultanate weapon.

Same basis: no artillery of Delhi's own is documented before Babur's guns at Panipat. The Trebuchet, attested in the maghribi engines of Alauddin's sieges (see ideas), the Mangonel-line, the Siege and Armored Elephants and the Petard keep the civ able to break buildings (RULES 6.11).

No gun-armed ships for a land power of the Ganges plain. The Galley and Fire Ship lines keep the anti-ship role at sea and the single-use Demolition Ship the anti-building role; no substitute siege warship is added (RULES 6.16.1).
Same basis.

Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): no war fleet of its own, so the basic navy only. The Sultanate and its Ghaznavid and Ghurid forerunners were land powers (see Cannon Galleon), so the civ keeps the Galley-line to War Galley, the Fire Galley and Fire Ship, the Hulk and War Hulk, the demolition ships and the generic Dock techs, with no Galleon, Carrack or siege warship.
See Galleon.
No printing in the window: the first press in India was set up by the Jesuits at Goa in 1556.

Besides the horse archers, the Sultanate fielded armoured horsemen fighting with lance, sword and mace: Fakhr-i Mudabbir's manual of war, dedicated to Iltutmish, sets out their arms (a normative text), and Jackson (1999) shows such cavalry in the Sultanate's field armies. The army that repelled the Chagatai invasions of 1297–1306 (Jaran-Manjur 1298, Kili 1299, the siege of Delhi survived in 1303, Amroha 1305, the Ravi 1306) combined both arms (Barani; Jackson 1999). No Cavalier: a power-budget trim, a design choice rather than a historical ranking, since Delhi's imported war-horses made its heavy cavalry no lighter than that of the Rajput kingdoms.

Harassment from all sides was the stock tactic of the Turkish horse archers, as of the steppe peoples who already have the tech: Minhaj describes the Ghurid mounted divisions wearing down the Rajput army at Tarain (1192); the feigned retreat appears in later chronicles such as Firishta.

The Arbalester, the crossbow tier, needs crossbow evidence (RULES 6.16.3). Fakhr-i Mudabbir's manual of war, written for Iltutmish (1211–36), describes the crossbow (charkh) among the Sultanate's weapons; battle accounts say little about it, so how common it was is unclear (see contested). The same manual is the basis of the Persians' Arbalester. Decision (power budget): no further trim; the Arbalester stays, since the crossbow evidence decides (RULES 6.16.3), and Dagh stays in the Castle Age (see Dagh).

One of the great building cultures of the age: the Qutb Minar (begun c. 1199, finished under Iltutmish), the Alai Darwaza (1311) and the walled cities of Siri (c. 1303), Tughlaqabad (1321–25) and Firuz Shah's Firozabad (1350s).

An abstraction of faster building: no treadwheel cranes are attested in India, and the tech stands for the scale of the Sultanate's building programmes in stone, from the Quwwat al-Islam mosque to Firuz Shah Tughluq's new towns and canals.
The massive bastioned walls and towers of Siri and Tughlaqabad, and the hill-forts the sultans took and garrisoned (Ranthambore 1301, Chittor 1303).
The massive bastioned walls and towers of Siri and Tughlaqabad, and the hill-forts the sultans took and garrisoned (Ranthambore 1301, Chittor 1303).

War elephants were, with the horse, the second pillar of Sultanate power (Digby 1971; see the cost passive). No Elite upgrade: a design choice, not a historical judgement, since the sultan's elephant stables were large (Babur reckoned nearly 1,000 elephants with Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat). The cost passive renders the Hindustani elephant arm as a numerous, cheaper support for a horse-archer civ, and the Elite tier is left to the elephant countries that filled Delhi's stables by capture and tribute (Bengal, Orissa, the Deccan and the Pandya Ma'bar), of which the Bengalis and the Tamils have it.

Kept from the game (level 1). The armoured Avar nobility: the Strategikon (XI.2) says that the Avars wear mail and that the horses of their illustrious men are covered in front with iron or felt; these leaders headed the raids and sacks of Balkan and Italian towns. Tarkhan, a title of the Göktürks, Khazars and Bulgars (of disputed Turkic or East Iranian origin), is counted among the Avar titles known from the written sources (Pohl 2018); its function among the Avars is unknown, but it fits them far better than Attila's Huns, in whose world it is not attested.
