Kept from the game (level 1). Large-scale raiding was the khaganate's lever on its neighbours: after taking Sirmium (582) the khagan sacked Singidunum, Viminacium and Anchialus (583–584); Avar hosts repeatedly struck Moesia and Thrace (583–587, 592–599), invaded Friuli c. 610, taking Cividale (Paul the Deacon IV.37), and ravaged Thrace again around 619–623, with both the armoured elite and the general host. Training the elite horse at ordinary Stables stands for that scale. Raiding was a long tradition, a structural trait that RULES 6.2 would make a passive, so Marauders keeps the Castle slot as a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19(b)). Decision: the khaganate's one clearly datable military moment, the adoption of siege engines in the 580s or 590s, stays with the trebuchet passive that RULES section 4 sets, rather than becoming an Imperial Age Castle tech (a ‘Petroboloi’ carrying the engine effect) with Marauders' effect turned into a passive.

New in the codex (level 2). Byzantine gold was the khaganate's main revenue. After defeating the future Tiberius II the Avars obtained 80,000 solidi a year (574, attested by 578; Menander); Sirmium surrendered in 582 after a three-year blockade, and the treaty restored the 80,000-solidi tribute with its arrears (Menander); it rose to 100,000 in 584/585, to 120,000 around 598–600 and to 200,000 by 623/624 (Howard-Johnston 2021). The gold shows in the Byzantine solidi of Early Avar graves, and when payments stopped after 626 the khaganate entered a crisis (Pohl 2018); a numismatic study finds them resumed on a smaller scale in the 680s (Zapolska 2017). Tribute was a structural economic base, formalised by the treaty of 574 and renewed by later treaties, so it is promoted to the Town Center tech under RULES 6.3. The name follows the project's Byzantines; the payers called themselves Romans (Rhomaioi), as the site notes.
The counterweight trebuchet appears only in the late 12th century, four centuries after the khaganate; replaced by the Traction Trebuchet.

A Byzantine warship, the type of the imperial fleet that destroyed the khagan's dugouts in the Golden Horn in 626 (Chronicon Paschale); the Avars never had one, and their navy is the boat tier (see Galleon).

Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): the boat tier. It rests on the Slav dugouts (monoxyla) of the khagan's assault on the Golden Horn in 626, manned by the khaganate's Slav levies (Chronicon Paschale; see the Slav-levy passive), and on the khaganate's river boats; the ships that Lombard shipwrights, sent by King Agilulf, built for the khagan, who then took an island in Thrace (Paul the Deacon IV.20), are a single episode and do not make a fleet of ships. The boat tier keeps the generic Galley line, on the canoe model of the Slav dugouts (see the renames), and the Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines as the game gives the Huns, as an abstraction for water maps, and removes the high-seas sailing warships: the Galleon here, the Huns already lacking the Carrack and the Fast Fire Ship.
Hungarian and Serbian light cavalry of the 15th century, six to seven centuries after the khaganate (RULES 6.10); Light Cavalry stays for the Avar light horse, as in the Goths' design.

The rope-pulled engine of the Avar sieges of Thessalonica (586 or 597; c. 617/618) and Constantinople (626); it replaces the counterweight Trebuchet as the Avars' heavy siege weapon (RULES 6.11), as it does for the out-of-scope Three Kingdoms, under the traction test (RULES 6.16.5), and carries the cost bonus. Trained at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age.

The Strategikon (XI.2) describes most Avar riders as doubly armed, the lance slung on the shoulder and the bow in the hand; the regional lancer unit (RULES 6.1) stands for the lance-armed riders of the host.
Upgrade of the Steppe Lancer: the warriors of the host wore mail (Strategikon XI.2); the leaders on armoured horses belong to the Tarkan.

Renamed from Galley, with the look of the Canoe. The boat tier rests on dugouts (see the Galleon): before Constantinople in 626 the khagan launched Slav dugouts (monoxyla, ‘single-trunk’ boats), manned by the Slav levies, on the Golden Horn, where the imperial fleet destroyed them (Chronicon Paschale; Theodore Synkellos). The Scenario Editor Canoe (RULES section 5; codex/tools/scenario-units.md), a light boat that shoots arrows like the Galley, gives the Galley the look of a dugout, which fits the boat tier far better than a Mediterranean galley, the type of the fleet that sank the monoxyla; the Galley keeps its stats, and the Canoe's look (its crew included), scale, attack and role must be checked in game. Same rename as in the Aztec, Malian, Mapuche, Maya and Tupi designs. The sources' word, monoxylon, is the Byzantines' Greek, and no Slav or Avar word for the boats is recorded in the window, so the generic English name of those renames goes with the look.
Renamed from War Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Upgrade tier of the renamed Galley, with the same Canoe look (see Galley).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Kamayuk. Inca armies were provincial levies, each with its own arms (slings, star-headed maces, clubs, lances and, from the Antisuyu, bows); long spears belonged to that arsenal: Xerez (1534), describing the arms and order of Atahualpa's armies (1532–33), puts in the rearguard pikemen with lances thirty palms long (some 6 m), who wore on the left arm a sleeve padded with cotton on which they worked the lance (Xerez; Hemming 1970; D'Altroy 2014). The unit keeps its stats but not its truncated name: kamayuq means ‘specialist’ or ‘person in charge’ (as in khipukamayuq), while Guaman Poma calls the age grade of all adult warrior-tributaries auca camayoc (awqa kamayuq, ‘warrior’). The model is shared with the Berbers' Murabit, the Ethiopians' Chewa Spearman and the Mapuche Colihue Lancer.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Kamayuk. Inca armies were provincial levies, each with its own arms (slings, star-headed maces, clubs, lances and, from the Antisuyu, bows); long spears belonged to that arsenal: Xerez (1534), describing the arms and order of Atahualpa's armies (1532–33), puts in the rearguard pikemen with lances thirty palms long (some 6 m), who wore on the left arm a sleeve padded with cotton on which they worked the lance (Xerez; Hemming 1970; D'Altroy 2014). The unit keeps its stats but not its truncated name: kamayuq means ‘specialist’ or ‘person in charge’ (as in khipukamayuq), while Guaman Poma calls the age grade of all adult warrior-tributaries auca camayoc (awqa kamayuq, ‘warrior’). The model is shared with the Berbers' Murabit, the Ethiopians' Chewa Spearman and the Mapuche Colihue Lancer.
Renamed from Elite Kamayuk. Elite tier of the renamed unit.

Kept from the game (level 1). The sling (warak'a) was the main Andean missile weapon, preferred to the bow in the highlands: Xerez (1534), describing the order of Atahualpa's armies, puts the slingers in the van, and conquest accounts stress that sling stones could badly hurt men and horses (Hemming 1970). Removing the minimum range abstracts a weapon that could be used at any distance. A kept existing tech for a long weapon tradition, held as a tech rather than a passive by the effect-size tie-break (RULES 6.2.4); its Castle Age follows the current game, since neither Castle tech marks a datable moment. Decision: it stays a tech, as does Fabric Shields, as a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19 b) rather than becoming a passive bonus: it is the game's own Inca tech, its strong effect suits the brake of a tech, and the civ's datable moments, the roads and the resettlements, hold the Town Center.

Kept from the game (level 1). The name is the game's, and the effect renders the Andean soldier's shield together with padded cotton. Andean shields were of wood or cane, sometimes faced with hide or cloth (analysis, rated plausible). Xerez (1534), describing the arms and order of Atahualpa's armies, gives the slingers of the van shields of narrow, very strong slats and doublets quilted with cotton, and the pikemen of the rearguard a cotton-padded sleeve on the left arm; the state stored cloth and arms in the qullqa and issued them for war (Murra 1980). This tech carries Xerez's cotton evidence alone: no Blacksmith tier is renamed after it, since the slingers' doublets fit the generic Padded Archer Armor, whose name already means quilted armour, and the pikemen's sleeve is a lance rest, not body armour (see Tin Bronze). A kept existing tech for an equipment tradition, held as a tech by the effect-size tie-break (RULES 6.2.4), a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19 b); its Imperial Age follows the current game. In-game text: ‘Kamayuks, Slingers and Champi Warriors +1 melee/+1 pierce armor’; only the unit name changes.

New in the codex (level 2). The Qhapaq Ñan, a network of some 30,000–40,000 km of roads with stairways, suspension bridges and waystations (tampu) about a day's walk apart, moved armies, mit'a labourers and llama caravans across the empire (Hyslop 1984; Cieza de León). Built mainly under Pachacuti and Thupa Inca, and incorporating older Wari and Chimú roads (Hyslop 1984), it is the state infrastructure of the empire (RULES 6.2: state). Faster infantry and villagers render the roads; the relay runners (chaski) are an N2 idea (see ideas). Villager speed is not also given as a passive bonus, so the roads are not counted twice.

New in the codex (level 2). The Inca moved whole communities from their homelands to other provinces as mitmaqkuna (‘those moved out’): loyal colonists to garrison the frontiers and watch newly conquered peoples, restive groups away from their homes, and farmers and craftsmen to work for the state, as in the Cochabamba valley, where Huayna Capac settled thousands of workers to grow maize for the state storehouses (Wachtel 1982; D'Altroy 2014). The chroniclers credit Pachacuti and above all Thupa Inca with the policy, together with the decimal census (Cieza; Sarmiento; the census is an N2 idea). Settlements that raise spearmen and skirmishers render the garrison colonies of the frontiers. A distinct institution, so a second Town Center tech (RULES 6.2, 6.3); Imperial Age, after the roads, since the largest colonisation projects, such as Cochabamba, belong to Huayna Capac's reign.
Removed with the Siege Workshop: there were no rams and no wheeled vehicles in the Andes.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Battering Ram).
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Battering Ram).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: no torsion or traction artillery existed in the Americas.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Mangonel).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: no bolt-throwers existed in the Americas.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Scorpion).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: a wheeled assault tower.
Counterweight artillery never existed in the Americas.
No siege engines are left to improve.

The crossbow was unknown in the Americas, which have neither crossbow tier (RULES 6.16.3); Inca missile troops were slingers, with bowmen from the eastern lowlands (Antisuyu). Archers and Slingers cover the role. In the current game the Bulgarians also lack crossbows (so do the current Spanish; the Castilian and Bulgarian designs restore the Crossbowman).
Removed with the Crossbowman (see there).
No thumb rings or thumb draw are attested in the Americas, so the tech goes (RULES 6.16.4).

Removed under the codex convention for the American civs (RULES 6.16.6, the owner's decision on their power budget): a playability line, not a historical one, since the kept Pikeman bears as European a name; the American spear line stops at the Pikeman, as the game already does for the Aztecs and Muisca. The Inca have the region's strongest case for the tier: Xerez (1534), describing the arms of Atahualpa's armies, gives axes with a metal blade a palm wide, ‘como alabarda’ (like a halberd), beside pikemen with lances thirty palms long. The pikes are the Awqa Kamayuq, Spearman and Pikeman remain, and the Andes knew no cavalry before 1532.

Ocean-going sailing warships were unknown. Andean seafaring used balsa rafts with cotton sails, such as the raft that Bartolomé Ruiz intercepted off Ecuador c. 1526, which probably belonged to coastal merchants rather than to the Inca state, and reed boats; no Inca war fleet is documented, and Thupa Inca's raft voyage into the Pacific, told by Sarmiento, is contested. Basic navy (RULES 6.16.1), since the Inca had no war fleet of their own: the galleys, fire ships, the Hulk line, the demolition ships and the generic Dock techs stay as an abstraction for water maps, without the Galleon, Carrack, Fast Fire Ship or a siege warship; the demolition ships are generic post-1500 items kept as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.2). The Scenario Editor Canoe, a dugout, does not render sailing rafts, so the Galley keeps its look (the balsa raft is an N3 idea).
High-castled sailing warships were unknown (see Galleon).
A sailing ship carrying a catapult: both a European ship type and a siege engine.
Removed under the basic navy (see Galleon); the Fire Ship stays.
There was no printing, nor writing in the usual sense: records were kept on knotted cords (khipu). With no equivalent for the function the tech is removed (18 of the game's 56 civs already lack it).

The Inca economy ran on mit'a labour, storehouses and redistribution, with local barter (qhatu) but, apart from the debated coastal merchants of Chincha (see contested), no professional merchant class like the pochteca (Murra 1980); the current game gave Guilds to the Inca but not to the Aztecs, who had the pochteca.

The Inca were master builders in fitted stone (Sacsayhuamán, the Qurikancha, Ollantaytambo), yet the civ had Masonry and Keep but not Architecture. The Keep fits them, since the region keeps it only where stone towers are documented: Sacsayhuamán had three towers, Muyuq Marka, Sallaq Marka and Paucar Marka, which Garcilaso describes. Treadmill Crane, which the Inca hold in the game, is renamed Mit'a, after the rotating labour service that raised these buildings (see the renames).

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no siege engine of any kind existed in the pre-contact Americas (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice. The Siege Workshop stays in the tree for this engine alone. For its other units the design’s reading stands: Andean armies built no siege engines: forts (pukara) were taken by assault, blockade and fire, and the frontier forts of Pambamarca were held for years of war against the Cayambe. The Champi line, Arson, Sappers and Petards replace them (owner's decision, RULES 6.16.5; RULES 6.11 and section 10). Before the heavy-engine floor every Castle had to be taken by units standing in its arrow fire; the Traction Trebuchet now does it from range, as a game convention, until an N2/N3 assault unit exists, with no compensating bonus (RULES 6.16.13). The Petard, a 16th-century gunpowder charge, stays unrenamed as a flagged generic abstraction of assault parties with fire, outside the one-late-element limit (RULES 6.16.2). Incendiary sling stones, recorded at Manco Inca's siege of Cusco (1536), are left to the ideas as an N2 burning effect.

Renamed from Horse Collar. There were no draft animals. Stone-walled, often irrigated terraces (andenes, the term used in Andean scholarship) turned the mountain slopes into fields, as at Pisac, Moray and the Colca valley (Donkin 1979). A rename beyond the agreed list, applied under RULES 6.16.6. Crop Rotation keeps its generic name as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.6), since no Andean equivalent with a period term was found.
Renamed from Heavy Plow. Agreed rename. The chakitaqlla, a foot plough with a footrest, was the Andean tillage tool; Guaman Poma draws it in his agricultural calendar.

Renamed from Hand Cart. Agreed rename. There were no carts; llama caravans carried about 25–30 kg per animal across the Andes. Wheelbarrow keeps its generic name as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.6): there were no wheeled vehicles, and loads went on porters' backs and on llamas. The generic Caravan (Trade Units) keeps its name, so two caravan techs appear. Decision: kept so, since renaming Caravan as well would add a name without an equivalent. The Trade Cart also keeps its generic name and wheeled look, as a flagged abstraction of porters and llama trains (RULES 6.16.6). A llama look for it would be possible in level 1 (the herdable Llama, or the Alpaca of the Scenario Editor, RULES section 5, whose look and behaviour as a trade unit would have to be checked in game), but the Inca had no trade between markets for the unit to render, since exchange ran on redistribution and local barter (see Guilds), and the llama name is already this tech's; so the llama trade unit stays with the N3 idea of llamas as pack animals.

Renamed from Banking. Agreed rename. Knotted-cord records kept by specialists (khipukamayuq) registered census, tribute and storehouse accounts (Urton 2003). The rename keeps Banking's effect (tributes to other players are free) for the shared ground of state accounting; it does not imply that khipu moved goods between polities. Coinage, which Khipu requires, keeps its generic name as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.6): the Inca had no money, and exchange ran on labour service, storehouses and local barter (Murra 1980).

Renamed from Treadmill Crane. There were no cranes or treadwheels: the stones of Inca masonry were hauled with ropes and levers and raised on earthen ramps, such as the ramp by which blocks from the Kachiqhata quarries were dragged up to the Temple of the Sun at Ollantaytambo (Protzen 1993), by labourers who came by the mit'a (‘turn’), the rotating labour service that tributary households owed to the state (Murra 1980; D'Altroy 2014). Cieza (part II, chapter 51) says that the provinces sent twenty thousand men for the works of the fortress of Cusco (Sacsayhuamán), who worked there for a limited time and were then relieved by others. Same effect as Treadmill Crane (Villagers construct buildings +20% faster): organised labour in turns is the Inca equivalent of faster building, as the Aztecs' Coatequitl renders the Mexica labour draft for public works. A rename beyond the agreed list, applied under RULES 6.16.6 and 6.16.15: mit'a is a period term (the chroniclers' mita), and building by rotating labour is the same function inside the window. The mit'a also covered work on the state's fields and herds, weaving and military service (see the Villagers bonus); the rename gives the building turns their name and adds no element of its own.

Renamed from Iron Casting. There was no iron. After the Inca conquest tin bronze spread at the expense of the older arsenical bronze in regions such as the Upper Mantaro Valley, while plain copper remained common (Owen 2001), and Lechtman describes tin bronze as the alloy the Inca state spread through its provinces (Lechtman 2007); bronze served for tools and for the star-shaped heads of champi maces. Same effect as Iron Casting; a rename beyond the agreed list, applied under RULES 6.16.6. The other Blacksmith tiers keep their generic names as a flagged generic equipment level (RULES 6.16.6): Forging and Blast Furnace, since Andean metallurgy worked gold, silver, copper and bronze, never iron, and the huayrachina furnace does not fit Blast Furnace (see contested); Bodkin Arrow, although there were no iron arrowheads; and Scale Mail, Chain Mail and Plate Mail Armor and Ring Archer Armor, since there was no metal body armour, only the metal discs some warriors wore on the chest and back, which marked rank as much as they protected. No infantry armour tier is renamed after cotton (RULES 6.16.15): the only infantry cotton item in Xerez is the pikemen's padded sleeve, a lance rest rather than body armour, and the quilted doublets he gives the slingers fit the generic Padded Archer Armor, whose name already means quilted armour; that evidence is carried by Fabric Shields. Chemistry stays for its +1 ranged attack as a flagged abstraction, although the Inca had no gunpowder.

Kept from the game (level 1). Genoese crossbowmen formed the core of Genoa's own forces and fleets and served France (Crécy, 1346), Castile, Byzantium and the Italian states (Epstein, 1996). Behind their pavises they stood up well to cavalry, so 'strong vs. cavalry' is an abstraction. The model is shared with the Portuguese Besteiro do Conto.

Kept from the game (level 1). Genoese crossbowmen formed the core of Genoa's own forces and fleets and served France (Crécy, 1346), Castile, Byzantium and the Italian states (Epstein, 1996). Behind their pavises they stood up well to cavalry, so 'strong vs. cavalry' is an abstraction. The model is shared with the Portuguese Besteiro do Conto.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Silk Road. The commenda (colleganza in Venice), in which a sedentary investor financed a travelling merchant's voyage for a share of the profit, appears in series in the cartulary of the Genoese notary Giovanni Scriba (1154–1164) and financed Italian long-distance trade from Caffa and Tana to Alexandria and Acre (Lopez, 1971; Epstein, 1996). 'Silk Road' is a term coined by Richthofen in 1877, and Italian trade with Asia went mostly through the Levant and the Black Sea.

New in the codex (level 1). From the late 11th century the cities of the Regnum Italiae became communes: sworn associations of citizens led by elected consuls (attested from the 1080s–1130s at Pisa, Genoa, Milan and elsewhere) and, from the late 12th century, by a foreign podestà, which governed, taxed, legislated and defended themselves. Citizens owed watch on the walls and service in the militia; the communes of the Lombard League defeated Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano (1176), and at the Peace of Constance (25 June 1183) he recognised their consuls and regalian rights, including the right to fortify their cities and to keep their league (Wickham, 2015; Jones, 1997). A Town Center that defends itself without sheltering villagers abstracts the city held by its own sworn citizens. The commune keeps the Town Center rather than a fiscal institution (the funded public debt of Venice, 1262, and Florence, 1345; the Catasto, 1427; the Casa di San Giorgio, 1407) or the podestà (level-1 review decision).

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Pirotechnia. Italian states hired their heavy cavalry by contract (condotta): companies of lances, each a man-at-arms with a mounted squire and a page, under captains such as John Hawkwood, Francesco Sforza and Bartolomeo Colleoni, whom Venice made captain-general in 1455, a post he held until his death in 1475. In the 15th century Venice and Milan kept many companies on long contracts, quasi-permanent forces that could take the field as soon as a campaign was decided (Mallett, 1974; Mallett and Hale, 1984; for the 14th-century companies, Caferro, 2006). Their men-at-arms wore Milanese plate from workshops such as the Missaglia's, which with the South German centres made the best armour of 15th-century Europe. Faster Knight-line training abstracts the readiness of these contracted lances. Pirotechnia, which it replaces, is Biringuccio's treatise of 1540 on metallurgy and cannon-founding, outside the window and unrelated to hand cannoneers. The tech is the civ's expression of its heavy cavalry (level-1 review decision): Chivalry (Stables work +40% faster) would also speed the Stradiots and Light Cavalry; the Paladin and the Siege Ram stay out of the tree, as in the game, as counterweights to the stronger economy, although the lances in Milanese plate and the communal sieges (Crema, 1159–1160) could justify them, and Italian siegecraft of the 15th century relied on bombards, which the civ has; the mounted crossbowmen of the 15th-century armies (balestrieri a cavallo) keep the regional Mounted Crossbowman (see the civ-level contested list).

New in the codex (level 2). The Arsenal of Venice, traditionally founded in 1104, was the commune's own shipyard. Enlarged as the Arsenale Nuovo (c. 1303–1325) and later the Novissimo (from 1473), it built the state's war galleys and the great galleys of the merchant convoys (mude), kept hulls in reserve and stored their oars, rigging and arms, so that fleets could be fitted out at speed (Lane, 1934 and 1973). Dante took its winter work, the pitch boiling to caulk damaged hulls, as the image of the fifth pit of Malebolge (Inferno XXI, 7–15), and in the late 1430s the Castilian traveller Pero Tafur watched ten galleys come out fully armed between three and nine o'clock, towed past the windows from which their stores were handed out (Tafur, tr. Letts, 1926, ch. XX: the passage belongs to his description of Venice, which follows his return from the East in May 1438, though it is often dated 1436). The galley fleets of the republics decided their wars: Genoa broke Pisa at Meloria (1284) and beat Venice at Curzola (1298), and the two fought the war of Chioggia (1378–1381). Faster training of galleys and fire ships abstracts the series production and rapid fitting-out of the state yard; cheaper Docks, the second half of the tech as the level-1 review proposed it (section 7, Italians Q7), abstract a yard that kept its hulls, timber and fittings in stock. From the Castle Age the discount does little for the fishing economy, whose bonus the design drops for relevance (see Market technologies free).

The Thumb Ring is given where the thumb draw is attested for a civ's own archers or for an archery tradition its armies demonstrably used (the steppe, Islamic and East Asian traditions); civs whose archers used the European draw, or whose missile troops were crossbowmen, do not get it. The Italian states do not: their archers used the European draw and their missile troops the crossbow (see the Genoese Crossbowman) (RULES 6.16.4).

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ. The Italians keep the fleet-of-ships tier (RULES 6.16.1): the war galleys of Venice, Genoa and Pisa and the round ships of their merchant fleets (Lane, 1973; Epstein, 1996), with the Galleon as the skeleton's flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2). The Cannon Galleon rests on gun-armed warships inside the window (RULES 6.16.1): in the fighting in the lagoon of Chioggia (1379–1380), Venetians and Genoese mounted bombards on galleys, cogs and the boats called ganzaroli, which Lombardo, from the contemporary chronicles, reads as the first massive use of shipborne artillery (Lombardo, 2021; see contested). These were bombards aboard oared galleys and round ships, not the broadside guns of the game's unit, so the line is an abstraction, as for the Castilians and the Vietnamese.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

Communal infantry with polearms was decisive in medieval Italy: the Milanese foot held around the carroccio against Barbarossa's knights at Legnano (1176), and Italian polearms (roncone, partisan) were widespread; in the game 43 of the 56 civs have it, but not the Italians.

Italy's military engineering (Taccola, Francesco di Giorgio Martini) was exported across Europe: the Bolognese Aristotele Fioravanti built the Dormition Cathedral in Moscow and served Ivan III as master of artillery after 1475. Its absence contradicted the civ's own University bonus.

Renamed from Hussar. The stradioti, Albanian and Greek light horsemen in Venetian service in the Morea (Nauplia, Modon, Coron), were brought into Italy in the 1470s against the Ottoman raids into Friuli; they harried the French at Fornovo (1495, just after the window) and were then hired across Europe (Pappas). 'Hussar' is a 15th-century Hungarian name; the function, light raiding cavalry, is identical. The rename meets RULES 6.16.15: the same function inside the window, a period term (stradioti, the Venetian name of these horsemen), and a generic name foreign to the civ.

Kept from the game (level 1). ‘Samurai’ (from saburau, ‘to serve’) first meant armed retainers, then a social status. A foot swordsman with a long sword (uchigatana, nodachi) fits the 14th–16th centuries, when warriors fought more and more on foot; ‘strong vs. unique units’ is pure game design.

Kept from the game (level 1). ‘Samurai’ (from saburau, ‘to serve’) first meant armed retainers, then a social status. A foot swordsman with a long sword (uchigatana, nodachi) fits the 14th–16th centuries, when warriors fought more and more on foot; ‘strong vs. unique units’ is pure game design.

New in the codex (level 1). Owner’s decision, in place of the Cavalry Archer attack bonus (see dropped). After the first Mongol invasion (1274), the Kamakura bakufu ordered the housemen (gokenin) and landholders of Kyūshū, in the 3rd month of 1276, to build a stone wall along the shore of Hakata Bay, the landing place of 1274: each provided a stretch in proportion to his land, and each province held its own sector (the men of Hyūga and Ōsumi at Imazu, those of Higo at Ikinomatsubara). The wall ran for about 20 km and stood some 2 m high, and the guard duty against foreign attack (ikoku keigo banyaku) kept Kyūshū warriors on it and repairing it until the end of the Kamakura shogunate. In 1281 the Eastern Route Army found it manned and could not land at Hakata: it seized the island of Shikanoshima instead, where the Japanese counter-attacked by land and by boat, and the invasion stayed offshore until the typhoon (Conlan 2001; the Mōko shūrai ekotoba shows the Higo warrior Kikuchi Takefusa and his men seated on the wall). Genkō Bōrui is the modern name (see contested); the item name is in plain romanization (RULES 6.16.15). At the Castle because a defence line is a military work (RULES 6.2; defence lines go to the Castle, RULES 6.16.19(c)); Castle Age, the age of the Great Wall it copies, and before Tanegashima (1543), as the chronological order of the two Castle techs requires (RULES 6.4). Level 1: the existing effect, identical in play.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Kataparuto (Trebuchets attack and pack/unpack faster). Late element, RULES section 2, and the civ’s only one (with the Hand Cannoneer already in the tree, also Imperial Age only). Portuguese traders landed on Tanegashima in 1543 (Teppōki, 1606) or 1542 (António Galvão, 1563); the island’s lord bought two matchlocks and had the swordsmith Yaita Kinbei copy them, and within a generation the gun was made in numbers (the Teppōki tells of Sakai and Negoro); Oda Nobunaga’s arquebusiers at Nagashino (1575) are its famous use. Owner’s decision: it replaces Kataparuto, the modern katakana loanword for English ‘catapult’, whose effect has nothing to apply to once the counterweight Trebuchet goes. A new tech, so level 2: no existing tech has this effect. Imperial Age, after Genko Borui (1276), in the chronological order of the two Castle techs (RULES 6.4).

New in the codex (level 1). In late 1185 the retired emperor Go-Shirakawa authorised Minamoto no Yoritomo’s men to levy commissariat rice (hyōrōmai) of five shō per tan on the estates and public lands of the home provinces and the west and to manage the land (Gyokuyō, Bunji 1.11.28); the Azuma kagami (c. 1300) presents the same grant as the appointment of constables (shugo) and land stewards (jitō). The jitō, drawn from Yoritomo’s housemen, kept order on the land and took a share of its revenue, so the warriors were fed from the estates they policed (Mass 1974). The rice levy itself was withdrawn in 1186, and the Muromachi half-tax edicts (hanzei, 1352 and 1368) later gave the shugo half of estate revenues to supply their troops. Cheaper food for soldiers renders an army provisioned from the land. At the Town Center because the shugo–jitō network was the governing institution of the first shogunate (RULES 6.2). The item name is in plain romanization (Shugo-Jitō in Hepburn; RULES 6.16.15). The owner’s sketch named no Town Center tech.

Owner’s decision. No Japanese use of the counterweight trebuchet is known; Japanese sieges were won by blockade, fire and assault, and from the late 16th century by European-type cannon. Kataparuto, which improved it, gives its slot to Tanegashima.

Owner’s decision. Japan keeps the fleet-of-ships tier (RULES 6.16.1): its planked ships ranged from the embassy ships to Tang China and the fleets of the Genpei War, which fought the sea battle of Dan-no-ura (1185), to the ships of the tally trade and the atakebune of the 16th-century clan navies, with the Galleon kept as the skeleton’s flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2). The Cannon Galleons go and no substitute siege warship is given, because Japanese fleets carried little artillery, their great weakness against the Korean panokseon in the Imjin War (1592–98); Kuki Yoshitaka’s gun-armed ships for Oda Nobunaga (1578) were an exception.
As for the Cannon Galleon.

Owner’s decision. The rice–barley (or wheat) cycle of medieval western Japan, extended near Amagasaki by a third crop of buckwheat (Song Hui-gyeong, 1420); its absence contradicted one of the period’s main agricultural advances.

Owner’s decision. Japan keeps some of the oldest wooden buildings in the world (Hōryū-ji, late 7th century) and raised the colossal Great Buddha Hall of Tōdai-ji (8th century); its absence contradicted this.

Owner’s decision, resting on a documented transfer of the engines themselves: in 618 Goguryeo presented to the court of Suiko trophies taken from the Sui, among them crossbows and stone-throwers (抛石), as a diplomatic gift (Nihon Shoki, Suiko 26). The level-1 review counts this documented transfer as meeting the traction test (RULES 6.16.5), although the source does not say how large the engines were and no Japanese building or use is securely recorded afterwards (see contested). It replaces the counterweight Trebuchet as the long-range siege weapon (RULES 6.11).
Renamed from Thumb Ring. Japanese archers draw the string with the thumb, like steppe archers, but protect it with a glove (yugake) rather than a ring; same function, identical effect (RULES 6.10).

Kept from the game (level 1). Song accounts of Shunchang (1140) call the guard of Wuzhu (Wanyan Zongbi) the “iron pagoda” (tie futu): 3,000 men all in heavy armour, with iron helmets and neck guards, advancing in files of three linked by thongs; at Yancheng the Song sources speak instead of guaizi ma (Song shi, biographies of Liu Qi and Yue Fei; Yue Ke, Jin Tuo cuibian). Jin heavy cavalry is well attested; the name is Song, not Jurchen, and the unit abstracts that cavalry.

Kept from the game (level 1). Song accounts of Shunchang (1140) call the guard of Wuzhu (Wanyan Zongbi) the “iron pagoda” (tie futu): 3,000 men all in heavy armour, with iron helmets and neck guards, advancing in files of three linked by thongs; at Yancheng the Song sources speak instead of guaizi ma (Song shi, biographies of Liu Qi and Yue Fei; Yue Ke, Jin Tuo cuibian). Jin heavy cavalry is well attested; the name is Song, not Jurchen, and the unit abstracts that cavalry.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Grenadier. The Jin used gunpowder bombs in their last wars: iron-cased bombs at the siege of Qizhou (1221, described by Zhao Yurong) and the “heaven-shaking thunder” (zhentianlei), used from boats at Hezhong in 1231–32 and, at Kaifeng in 1232, lowered on iron chains onto Mongol sappers or launched by trebuchets; the Jin shi says its blast pierced iron armour (Jin shi 111 and the biography of Chizhan Hexi; Andrade 2016). “Grenadier” is a 17th-century European word; the plain English name follows the game's own Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart.

New in the codex (level 1). In 1114 Aguda organised his people into mouke of 300 households and meng'an of ten mouke, units that were at once social, fiscal and military. The Jin shi (44, Bing zhi) says that in the early years every able-bodied man was a soldier, left in peacetime to hunt, fish and shoot as his work, and that when troops were levied the weapons and provisions of foot and horse were all supplied by the households themselves; after the conquest the households were settled across north China on allotted land as military colonies (Tao 1976). Cheaper food for all military units renders troops fed by their own households, as for the Byzantine themes. At the Town Center because the meng'an mouke was the Jurchens' state and social order, not only an army (RULES 6.2).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Fortified Bastions (Fortifications and Town Centers regenerate 500 HP per minute). The Jin dug and raised the longest border works of their time, the jiehao (“boundary trenches”): lines of ditch and rampart with forts across Inner Mongolia and Manchuria, built mainly in the second half of the 12th century against the Tatars and Mongols and kept up by frontier garrisons (Jin shi; Franke 1994). Regeneration abstracts that constant upkeep. “Bastion” named the angled bastion of 16th-century Italian fortification; the other proposed name, mamian (projecting wall towers), is a single architectural feature (RULES 6.9).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Thunderclap Bombs (Rocket Carts, Grenadiers and Lou Chuans detonate when defeated; projectiles produce additional explosions). At Qizhou (1221) the Jin besiegers threw iron-cased bombs from trebuchets (Zhao Yurong, Xinsi Qi Qi lu). In the twelfth month of Zhengda 8 (December 1231 or January 1232), when Hezhong fell to the Mongols, the Jin commander Wanyan Eke, known as “Banzi” Eke (the other imperial-clan Eke at Hezhong, “Caohuo” Eke, was captured and killed), broke out down the Yellow River by boat with some three thousand men of the beaten garrison, and when Mongol warships barred the river his men set off zhentianlei one after another from the boats and hacked through the blocking ships, reaching Tongguan (Jin shi 111, biography of Wanyan Eke; Andrade 2016). At Kaifeng in 1232 the defenders used the zhentianlei (“heaven-shaking thunder”), an iron pot of gunpowder launched by trebuchet or lowered on chains onto the Mongol sappers, whose roar the Jin shi says was heard a hundred li away and whose blast pierced iron armour; with the flying fire lances, these were the only two weapons the northern troops feared (Jin shi, biography of Chizhan Hexi; Needham 1986; Andrade 2016). The tech takes the Jin name, in plain pinyin (RULES 6.16.15), since “thunderclap” (pili) named the older, soft-cased Song bomb; the English “Heaven-Shaking Thunder” was the alternative (the level-1 review's default keeps Zhentianlei).
The counterweight trebuchet reached China in 1273, four decades after the fall of the Jin (1234).

The oldest securely dated metal-barrelled gun is the Xanadu gun of 1298 (the Heilongjiang gun is dated by context to c. 1288); a possibly earlier Tangut bronze piece from Wuwei is of disputed date. The Jin fought with fire lances and bombs, not cannon.

Multiple-rocket carts are Ming (and the Korean hwacha of 1451); whether the Jin “flying fire” of 1232 was a true rocket is disputed. The Bomb Thrower stays as the civ's blast weapon, so no Mangonel-line substitute is added (the Khitans, who have no other, get the light pao). One Castle-Age blast weapon per civ is a convention of this region that mirrors the game, where none of the four civs that train the Rocket Cart (Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans) has the Mangonel line; the light pao is left out by it and for power, not for want of evidence (the level-1 review's default).
Upgrade of the removed Rocket Cart.

No Jin tower ships (louchuan) or ship-borne stone-throwers are recorded, so the siege warship is removed, with no substitute: special warships appear only where the type is documented (RULES 6.16.1). The zhentianlei used at Hezhong in 1231–32 came from river boats in a breakout (see Zhentianlei), not from a fleet's siege ships. The Jin did have war fleets of their own, raised for Wanyan Liang's invasion of 1161: the Song destroyed the sea fleet off Tangdao and beat back the attempt to cross the Yangtze at Caishi (Jin shi; Song shi). Navy tier: a fleet of ships, resting on these fleets, so the Galleon and Carrack stay as generic tiers, the Galleon as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.1 and 6.16.2). The Fast Fire Ship, which the game's Jurchens lack, is not added: the tier would allow it, but no Jin fire-ship type is documented (the Jin fleets suffered Song fire weapons in 1161; see Siphons), so the game's omission stands and the fire-ship line ends at the Fire Ship.

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13). China had its own liquid-fire projector, the pump for “fierce fire oil” (menghuo you) of the Wujing Zongyao (1044), but no ship-borne liquid fire is documented for the Jin fleets, which suffered Song fire weapons in 1161 (see Lou Chuan).
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

Song reports collected by Xu Mengxin describe early Jin units whose front ranks, in heavy armour, fought with lances and clubs while the rear ranks, lightly armoured, shot bows (Sanchao beimeng huibian), and the Jin shi's annals of Aguda have him shoot at a flock of birds and hit three times running before an astonished Liao envoy (Tao 1976). The Jurchens shared the thumb-draw archery of northeast Asia; the Manchu thumb ring (banzhi) is only a later echo. Parthian Tactics is not added (the level-1 review's default): the Jin's mounted archers were the lightly armoured ranks, and with the +25% attack speed of the Mounted Units bonus it would give Jurchen Cavalry Archers the full Mongol package.

After the conquest the Jin army relied heavily on drafted Han infantry, the qianjun (“signed-up troops”), and on Khitan and Bohai contingents; Wanyan Liang's mass levies for the invasion of 1161 provoked revolts, the Khitan rising among them (Tao 1976; Franke 1994). An all-cavalry army is true only of c. 1114–1130.

The Jin used man-powered traction trebuchets in mass at Taiyuan and Kaifeng (1125–1127) and in the defence of Kaifeng in 1232, where they threw iron bombs; it replaces the counterweight Trebuchet as heavy siege artillery (RULES 6.11), as for the out-of-scope Three Kingdoms.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Liao Dao. The Pishi army (pishi jun) was the Liao imperial guard. Abaoji picked over a thousand strong warriors from the tribes for his trusted guard (fuxin bu), which the Liao shi identifies with the Pishi army, and Taizong enlarged it with picked troops from across the realm into the core of the emperor's cavalry (Liao shi, Bingwei zhi and Baiguan zhi; Wittfogel and Feng 1949). The Liao shi uses pishi only as the name of the guard units (Southern, Northern, Left, Right and Yellow Pishi); its usual gloss as “vajra” (jingang, “diamond”) goes back to the Qing scholar Li E (Liao shi shiyi). The model is the Tiger Cavalry of the out-of-scope Wei, Cao Cao's guard (hubao qi): an elite guard cavalry whose growth with victories abstracts veteran status, and a model no in-scope civ shares. The Keshik is already shared by the Mongols' and Tatars' designs, and the Hei Guang Cavalry is a regional unit that would not count as a unique unit (RULES 6.16.10), so the Tiger Cavalry stays (the level-1 review's default). The Scenario Editor's Khan and Sogdian Cataphract (RULES section 5) were also weighed and not used: the Khan is a mounted archer only, a role the Heavy Cavalry Archer bonus already carries for the Liao armoured horse archer, and the Sogdian Cataphract is by name and origin a Central Asian heavy horseman, a worse fit for the Liao guard than the Chinese-style Tiger Cavalry; either would also need its in-game look and stats checked first. The Liao Dao (“Liao blade”) named no documented unit, and infantry was secondary in Liao armies.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Liao Dao. The Pishi army (pishi jun) was the Liao imperial guard. Abaoji picked over a thousand strong warriors from the tribes for his trusted guard (fuxin bu), which the Liao shi identifies with the Pishi army, and Taizong enlarged it with picked troops from across the realm into the core of the emperor's cavalry (Liao shi, Bingwei zhi and Baiguan zhi; Wittfogel and Feng 1949). The Liao shi uses pishi only as the name of the guard units (Southern, Northern, Left, Right and Yellow Pishi); its usual gloss as “vajra” (jingang, “diamond”) goes back to the Qing scholar Li E (Liao shi shiyi). The model is the Tiger Cavalry of the out-of-scope Wei, Cao Cao's guard (hubao qi): an elite guard cavalry whose growth with victories abstracts veteran status, and a model no in-scope civ shares. The Keshik is already shared by the Mongols' and Tatars' designs, and the Hei Guang Cavalry is a regional unit that would not count as a unique unit (RULES 6.16.10), so the Tiger Cavalry stays (the level-1 review's default). The Scenario Editor's Khan and Sogdian Cataphract (RULES section 5) were also weighed and not used: the Khan is a mounted archer only, a role the Heavy Cavalry Archer bonus already carries for the Liao armoured horse archer, and the Sogdian Cataphract is by name and origin a Central Asian heavy horseman, a worse fit for the Liao guard than the Chinese-style Tiger Cavalry; either would also need its in-game look and stats checked first. The Liao Dao (“Liao blade”) named no documented unit, and infantry was secondary in Liao armies.
Renamed from Elite Tiger Cavalry. Follows the unique unit (Tiger Cavalry → Pishi Guard).

New in the codex (level 2). When Taizong had gained the Sixteen Prefectures (936–938) and, briefly, Kaifeng (947), the Liao divided its officials into north and south: “the Khitan were governed by the national system, and the Han were treated by the Han system” (Liao shi 45, Baiguan zhi). The northern officials ran the palace camps (ordo), the tribes and the dependent states; the southern ones ran the Han prefectures and counties (zhou, xian), their land tax and their troops, “governing each according to its custom” (see contested). Abaoji had already given his Han subjects officials and advisers of their own, such as Han Yanhui, but the system took shape under Taizong (Wittfogel and Feng 1949; Twitchett and Tietze 1994). Through it a Khitan minority ruled a mostly settled empire: Wittfogel and Feng estimate the Liao population at some 750,000 Khitans beside 2.4 million Han, 450,000 Bohai and 200,000 others (a modern estimate; the Liao shi gives only partial figures). Extra population space at each Town Center stands for the settled Han and Bohai subjects, registered in the prefectural seats, whom the southern officials governed under their own law; governing them let a pastoral state sustain far more people than its herds alone could. The Chinese bonus uses the same mechanic for the grid of county and prefectural seats; here it renders a different institution, the separate government of a settled majority. Population space rather than a gathering or trade effect, because what the system added to the Liao was governed people, not a resource; Farms beside Pastures as a second effect is the more specific rendering, left to N2 (see ideas). At the Town Center because the system was the frame of the Liao state (RULES 6.2). A new tech (level 2), because no existing tech expresses it; the level-1 review made it the Town Center tech and moved the Chanyuan Treaty to the Market (review section 9).

New in the codex (level 1). In January 1005, after a Liao invasion had stalled before Chanyuan, where the Liao commander Xiao Talin was killed by a bed-crossbow bolt, the Song agreed to pay 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year, raised in 1042 to 200,000 taels and 300,000 bolts, and the two courts treated each other as equals; border markets (quechang) were opened at Xiongzhou, Bazhou and other border towns (Song shi, Shihuo zhi; Twitchett and Tietze 1994). The yearly silver becomes extra gold income and the border markets the lower market fee. At the Market (RULES 6.2: trade), because what the covenant brought the Liao was silver, silk and border trade; the Town Center slot goes to the Dual Administration, the Liao's weightiest state trait (level-1 review, section 9).

Kept from the game (level 1). The tech is anchored on the founding of the ordo system. Abaoji (r. 907–926) set up the first ordo, the Suan ordo (Hongyi palace), as his own palace camp, built on his trusted guard, and every later emperor set up his own at his accession, until the Liao shi counts twelve palace camps and one residence (shi'er gong yi fu) (Liao shi 31, Yingwei zhi). The ordo (wolüduo) was thus each emperor's own camp-household, with attached households, herds and guard cavalry that outlived him: at his death it served his tomb while its able-bodied men still went to war. By regulation the regular soldier's three horses, forager and camp guard kept him mounted and supplied (Liao shi 34; Wittfogel and Feng 1949). Regeneration in combat is an abstraction of remounts and camp support. Imperial Age, the game's age (RULES 6.16.11), for the system at its full extent.
The counterweight trebuchet reached China in 1273, a century and a half after the fall of the Liao (1125).
Multiple-rocket carts are Ming and Joseon (15th century); there is no evidence of Liao rockets.
Upgrade of the removed Rocket Cart.
The fire lance appears in a mid-10th-century Dunhuang painting, but its first recorded use in battle is Song (De'an, 1132), after the fall of the Liao, and no Liao gunpowder weapon is documented.
Upgrade of the removed Fire Lancer.
No gun-armed ships: the Liao had neither a war fleet of note nor gunpowder artillery, so the gun ship was doubly anachronistic (the game's Khitans already lack the Galleon).

No war fleet: the Liao had none of note, so the civ keeps the basic navy only (RULES 6.16.1): the Galley-line to War Galley, Fire Galley and Fire Ship, Hulk and War Hulk, demolition ships and the generic Dock techs.
As Carrack.

Liao camels drew carts and carried baggage (tomb murals of camel-drawn carts), but no Khitan camel cavalry is recorded (see contested); the Mongols' and Tatars' designs remove theirs for the same reason. The Halberdier replaces it as the anti-cavalry unit (RULES 6.11), since the Pishi Guard is strong against ranged soldiers and weak against the Spearman-line and so is no substitute. Keeping the camels as a declared abstraction was the alternative; the level-1 review's default removes them.
Upgrade of the removed Camel Rider.
Missing despite the Liao horse herds; now free (see bonuses).

The Liao printed the Buddhist canon (carving begun c. 1031; fragments found in the Yingxian pagoda in 1974), and Shen Kuo notes that Liao law punished with death the export of books to the Song (Mengxi bitan).

Liao timber architecture survives: the Guanyin Pavilion of the Dule Temple (984) and the Yingxian wooden pagoda (1056), about 67 m high, the tallest surviving premodern timber pagoda (Steinhardt 1997).
The Liao had five walled capitals (Shangjing, Dongjing, Nanjing at Beijing, Zhongjing, Xijing) and many walled prefectural towns.
The Liao had five walled capitals (Shangjing, Dongjing, Nanjing at Beijing, Zhongjing, Xijing) and many walled prefectural towns.

Added as the light traction pao and renamed Whirlwind Pao (see the rename): it replaces the removed Rocket Cart as the civ's Castle-Age blast weapon (RULES 6.11), since the Khitans have no Bomb Thrower or other substitute. One such weapon per civ is a design convention of this region, not a historical finding: the Chinese keep the Rocket Cart, the Jurchens the Bomb Thrower, the Khitans this pao. The convention mirrors the game, where none of the four civs that train the Rocket Cart (Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans) has the Mangonel line; so the Khitans field that line as the Whirlwind Pao, a name from the Song manuals, while the Chinese, who keep the Rocket Cart, lack it (the Koreans' design, on the owner's sketch, keeps both). Only the Mangonel tier is added: the Onager tier, the generic upgrade of the stone-thrower line, is left out by the same convention and for power.

Renamed from Mangonel. Same unit, East Asian name. The Wujing Zongyao (1044) describes the “whirlwind” pao (xuanfeng pao), a light single-pole traction trebuchet on a pivoting post that could turn in any direction and threw light stones at troops (Needham and Yates 1994), and the Song shi (486) has the Tangut poxi corps mount whirlwind pao on camel saddles. The name is thus Song and Tangut: no Liao source names a pao type, so for the Khitans it is a regional name for the light traction engine that every army of the region used. The function, a light anti-personnel stone-thrower with area damage, has this historical equivalent (RULES 6.10); in many medieval sources “mangonel” itself meant the traction trebuchet, but the game's Mangonel shows a torsion engine, which neither China nor the steppe used. The Traction Trebuchet stands for the heavy multi-pole pao, so the two units do not overlap.

The anti-cavalry substitute for the removed camels (RULES 6.11), as in the Mongols' design. Liao foot soldiers came mainly from the militias of the Han and Bohai prefectures and of the capitals (Liao shi, Bingwei zhi); the Halberdier stands for their spear and polearm infantry.

The man-powered traction pao was the heavy stone-thrower of every army in the region until the counterweight engine arrived in 1273 (Needham and Yates 1994), and the Liao besieged walled towns from the Bohai capital (926) to Yingzhou (1004). It replaces the counterweight Trebuchet (RULES 6.11).

Kept from the game (level 1). The reliefs of the Bayon and Banteay Chhmar (Jayavarman VII, 1181–c. 1218) show heavy double-bow crossbows mounted on elephants and on wheeled carts; in some scenes the crews seem to wear the Cham headdress. Their frequency is unknown, and ‘can destroy trees’ is a game invention.

Kept from the game (level 1). The reliefs of the Bayon and Banteay Chhmar (Jayavarman VII, 1181–c. 1218) show heavy double-bow crossbows mounted on elephants and on wheeled carts; in some scenes the crews seem to wear the Cham headdress. Their frequency is unknown, and ‘can destroy trees’ is a game invention.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Tusk Swords (Battle Elephants +3 attack). By royal edict Jayavarman VII founded hospitals (ārogyaśālā) across the empire: the Ta Prohm stela (1186) counts 102 of them, supplied from the royal stores, and the hospital edict inscribed in their chapels, as at Say Fong near Vientiane, says that the king suffered from his subjects’ illnesses more than from his own. At the Town Center because the hospitals were a state foundation (RULES 6.2), each with a Buddhist chapel. Tusk Swords, which it replaces, has no support in the Angkorian reliefs: blades on tusks are attested mainly in India and later.

Kept from the game (level 1). An adopted technique of Jayavarman VII’s reign (RULES 6.2). The double-bow engines appear in the reliefs of his temples, the Bayon and Banteay Chhmar, mounted on elephants and on wheeled carts and in some scenes worked by men in Cham headdress, and not in the army procession of Angkor Wat (c. 1113–50), the earlier depiction of the Khmer army on the march. They resemble the multiple-bow bed crossbows of Song China and were probably taken up in the Cham wars of 1177–1203 (see contested). The tech stands for the adoption of the engine, on carts (the Scorpions) as on elephants; the Ballista Elephant stands for the elephant platform that set the Khmer use apart. Unlike the Burmese Howdah, dropped as an old equipment feature of the elephant, this is a weapon whose adoption the reliefs date to one reign. The name matches the double bow; the effect misreads it (see below). With the Ballista Elephant and Arogyashala, three of the nine slots come from Jayavarman VII’s reign, the best-documented reign of Angkor and the one of its greatest war; giving the Castle a datable moment of another reign instead, such as the oath of allegiance that Suryavarman I’s officials swore in 1011, inscribed on a gopura of the Royal Palace (a new, level-2 tech), was considered and not adopted.

No evidence of Khmer mounted archers; cavalry was marginal (small horses and riders with lances in the reliefs). The only mention of mounted archery in the Khmer–Cham wars is on the Cham side: in 1171 a man from Fujian advised the Cham king to adopt it against the Khmer elephants, and Champa bought horses (Song shi, ch. 489).
As for the Cavalry Archer.
As for the Cavalry Archer.

The Knight line is the game’s heavy shock cavalry, while Khmer cavalry was light and marginal: small horses and riders with lances in the reliefs, and soldiers without armour in Zhou Daguan (see contested). The Light Cavalry and Hussar stand for these horsemen, and the shock role falls to the Battle Elephant, as in the Malay design. Keeping the Knight and Cavalier as a game abstraction against Zhou Daguan, to strengthen the civ, was considered and not adopted (RULES 6.16.13).
As for the Knight.

There is no evidence of firearms at Angkor, or in the Siamese attacks on it, before 1431, although Ming-derived guns spread in Đại Việt and the northern mainland from c. 1390 (Sun Laichen 2003); Cambodian firearms belong to the post-Angkorian kingdom of Longvek (16th century), with adventurers such as Diogo Veloso and Blas Ruiz in the 1590s.

No gunpowder in the Angkorian period. The Khmer keep the fleet-of-ships tier (RULES 6.16.1): the reliefs of the Bayon and Banteay Chhmar show the naval battles against the Cham on the Tonle Sap (c. 1177–81) fought from long oared war galleys crowded with paddlers and spearmen, although the reliefs do not show how the war galleys were built. Zhou Daguan (1296–97) describes large boats built of hardwood planks, split with axes and fastened with iron nails, beside small dugouts chiselled from a single trunk, softened by fire and spread; his nailed-plank boats show that the Khmer built planked hulls, and the tier rests on that inference. The Galleon stays as the skeleton’s flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2), but no gun-armed warship is documented, so the Cannon Galleons go.
As for the Cannon Galleon.

Zhou Daguan says the Khmer had no stone-throwers (paoshi), and none has been identified in the reliefs, which show the double-bow engines in detail (see contested); the counterweight trebuchet reached China only in 1273. The Siege Ram and the Battle Elephants keep the civ able to destroy buildings (RULES 6.11). With no Bombard Cannon either, the Khmer have no long-range siege weapon (no Trebuchet, Traction Trebuchet or Bombard Cannon) and rely on the Siege Ram as the RULES 6.11 substitute, as RULES 6.16.5 allows where no engine is attested; no traction engine is given because Zhou Daguan denies them.
As for the Trebuchet: Zhou Daguan denies stone-throwers of any kind, so no traction engine replaces them; the Scorpions and the Ballista Elephant remain against massed troops.
As for the Mangonel.
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
Given by the Dharmashala bonus: the rest houses of the royal roads (Preah Khan stela, 1191).

Renamed from Caravanserai. The rest houses that Jayavarman VII set along the royal roads. The Preah Khan stela calls them vahnigṛha (‘houses with fire’), and dharmaśālā is the modern scholarly label for the rest-house reading (see contested). Same building and effect; the function, a staged network that served travellers, has this historical equivalent (RULES 6.10).

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: Zhou Daguan says the Khmer had no stone-throwers, and none appears in the reliefs (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

Kept from the game (level 1). The geobukseon is mentioned in 1413 in the Annals of King Taejong and was used by Yi Sun-sin from 1592 (Sacheon, Dangpo, Hansan), armed with cheonja and jija cannons. There were very few, probably three to five; the panokseon was the backbone of the fleet. It originated inside the window, so its later fame raises no late-element issue (RULES section 2).

Kept from the game (level 1). The geobukseon is mentioned in 1413 in the Annals of King Taejong and was used by Yi Sun-sin from 1592 (Sacheon, Dangpo, Hansan), armed with cheonja and jija cannons. There were very few, probably three to five; the panokseon was the backbone of the fleet. It originated inside the window, so its later fame raises no late-element issue (RULES section 2).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces War Wagon. Owner’s decision. Goguryeo tomb murals show riders and horses in full lamellar armour: the battle scenes of Samsil-chong (the Three Chambers Tomb) at Ji’an, the Gaemachong (‘Armoured Horse Tomb’) near Pyongyang, named after its mural, and Anak Tomb No. 3 (357, occupant debated). Armoured horse and rider were Goguryeo’s elite arm in its age of expansion under Gwanggaeto and Jangsu (391–491), when the Gwanggaeto stele (414) boasts of over 10,000 suits of armour captured in 407. Goguryeo still fielded a heavily armoured army in 645, when the Tang took 10,000 suits of armour after the battle of Jupilsan (Zizhi tongjian 198), and its barded cavalry probably fought the Sui and Tang, though barding is not recorded then. ‘Gaema musa’ (‘armoured-horse warrior’) is a modern label built on the old word gaema (鎧馬, ‘armoured horse’). Goryeo later raised a large cavalry corps (sin’gigun) in Yun Gwan’s Byeolmuban of 1104 against the Jurchen horsemen; whether it was barded is not recorded. The Cataphract, a heavily armoured lancer on a barded horse, is the existing model. The Scenario Editor’s Sogdian Cataphract (RULES section 5), a Central Asian horseman with high pierce armour but no melee armour (110 HP, 0/5 armour; codex/tools/scenario-units-stats.md), was considered; neither it nor any other Scenario Editor unit renders the Goguryeo armoured lancer better than the Cataphract. The War Wagon it replaces had no known Korean prototype: the hwacha were rocket or gun carts, already represented by the Rocket Cart (renamed Hwacha here).

Renamed from Elite Cataphract. Follows the unique unit (Cataphract → Gaema Musa), for the Koreans only; the Byzantines keep the Cataphract.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Eupseong (Watch Tower-line +2 range). Owner’s decision: the name keeps its meaning, town walls (邑城). Against the wakō raids of late Goryeo and early Joseon, the state walled the county towns of the southern coasts; the court of King Sejong issued standards for them in 1438 (Chukseong sindo), and walls of the programme survive at Haemi and Nagan. The owner’s ‘walls, gates and towers +30% HP’ is the Great Wall effect, used word for word so that the tech stays level 1. Walling towns was also a military work; it sits at the Town Center because the court ran and standardised it as a programme for the county seats, the units of local government (RULES 6.2), and fortified towns go to the Town Center (RULES 6.16.19(c)). Moving it to the Castle as the Castle-Age tech (1438, before Singijeon in 1448) and giving the Town Center a state institution (the Goryeo civil examinations of 958, the Gwajeon land law of 1391 or the Gyeongguk daejeon code of 1485) was considered and not adopted. The game’s effect (+2 tower range) had no relation to the name and is dropped. The tech is not renamed Sanseong, since the mountain-fortress tradition grounds the stone and tower bonuses.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Shinkichon (Rocket Carts and Turtle Ships +1 range, fire additional projectiles). Singijeon (神機箭) were rocket arrows derived from Goryeo’s juhwa, renamed and standardised in 1448 and fired in volleys of up to 100 from Munjong’s hwacha (1451); their specifications are in the Gukjo oryeui seorye (1474). The romanisation is corrected (Revised Romanization), and the Turtle Ship part is removed because the ships fired large arrows from cannon, not singijeon. The Rocket Cart it improves takes its Korean name (see the renames).
The counterweight trebuchet reached China only in 1273 (Xiangyang), and the Korean sources record traction engines only; Korea then turned to guns (Choe Mu-seon’s Office of Firearms, 1377).
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

Owner’s decision. Silla’s heavy crossbows were famous: the Samguk Sagi (year 669) says the Tang emperor summoned the artisan Gu Jinchon, whose crossbows were said to reach 1,000 paces; those he made in China reached only 30, then 60 paces, he blamed the timber, and he was suspected of hiding his secret. The civ had the Scorpion without its upgrade. The same Silla crossbow tradition is the evidence on which the Arbalester, kept from the game, stays (RULES 6.16.3).
Owner’s decision. The fully armoured horses (gaema) of the Goguryeo murals; it also serves the Gaema Musa.

Owner’s decision, read as the light traction stone-thrower and renamed Pocha (see the renames and contested): in 618 Goguryeo presented stone-throwers captured from the Sui to Japan (Nihon Shoki), and both sides used traction engines at Gwiju in 1231 (Goryeosa). Without it Korea from 500 to c. 1400, before the hwacha, would have no throwing artillery.

Renamed from Mangonel. Pocha (砲車) is the general word of the Korean sources for the traction stone-thrower: the Goryeosa uses it for the engines of both sides at the siege of Gwiju (1231). It covered engines of every size and here names the light one, as the Khitan design’s Whirlwind Pao does (RULES 6.10); the heavy engines stay as the Traction Trebuchet. Same unit and effect.
Owner’s decision: the upgrade of the light stone-thrower, an abstraction with no distinct Korean referent (see contested).

The heavy multi-pole engines of the same pocha tradition (Gwiju, 1231, Goryeosa) replace the counterweight Trebuchet as the long-range siege weapon (RULES 6.11), beside the Bombard Cannon of late Goryeo and Joseon. Not in the owner’s sketch: added under the traction test (RULES 6.16.5), since heavy traction engines are attested at Gwiju, and for consistency with the Chinese, Japanese, Jurchen and Khitan designs, as the counterweight engine reached China only in 1273.

Renamed from Rocket Cart. The hwacha (火車, ‘fire cart’) is the Korean name of this launcher. First recorded in 1409 as a cart firing arrows from gun tubes, it took its best-known form in Munjong’s model of 1451, which could carry a frame of 100 singijeon rockets (or one of gun barrels), the form the game’s Rocket Cart shows (Joseon Wangjo Sillok; Gukjo oryeui seorye, 1474). Same unit and function (RULES 6.10); the Chinese keep the generic name.

Renamed from Heavy Rocket Cart. The improved hwacha of 1451, built under King Munjong, which could fire a hundred singijeon at once; ‘Munjong hwacha’ is the modern name for that model. Same unit, identical effect.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Leitis (Heavy Cavalry that ignores armor). From the 14th century the Grand Duchy’s heavy cavalry came from its boyars, Lithuanian and Ruthenian, who served with their retinues in banners; as the state grew over the old Rus' principalities (Polotsk, Vitebsk, Kiev, Smolensk), most of its nobility became Orthodox Ruthenian boyars. At Grunwald (1410) Vytautas led some forty banners, many raised in Ruthenian lands, among them the three Smolensk banners that held their ground beside the Poles (Długosz; Ekdahl 1982). The Rus' Boyar (cavalry with exceptional melee armour) is shared because these were the same class (RULES 6.7); the model is shared only with the Rus', and the Horodło discount sets the Lithuanian Boyar apart. It takes the slot of the Leitis (see [[dropped]]).

From the 14th century the Grand Duchy’s heavy cavalry came from its boyars, Lithuanian and Ruthenian, who served with their retinues in banners; as the state grew over the old Rus' principalities (Polotsk, Vitebsk, Kiev, Smolensk), most of its nobility became Orthodox Ruthenian boyars. The Rus' Boyar (cavalry with exceptional melee armour) is shared because these were the same class (RULES 6.7); the model is shared only with the Rus', and the Horodło discount sets the Lithuanian Boyar apart. It takes the slot of the Leitis (see [[dropped]]).

New in the codex (level 2). At Horodło (2 October 1413) Jogaila and Vytautas renewed the union and reshaped the Grand Duchy on the Polish model: palatines and castellans of Vilnius and Trakai, joint assemblies with the Polish nobility, and the privileges of the Polish nobles extended to the Lithuanian boyars, 47 of whose families were adopted into Polish heraldic clans. The privileges were at first for Catholics only; Sigismund Kęstutaitis extended them to the Orthodox boyars in 1434, and Casimir’s privilege of 1447 widened them for the whole nobility (Kiaupa et al. 2000). Cheaper Boyars translate privileges paid for by service at the boyars’ own expense, as Szlachta Privileges does for the Poles. A new tech (level 2): sharing Szlachta Privileges itself would give the Lithuanians, who have the Paladin, very cheap knights and blur the Polish and Lithuanian identities. Chosen over Jogaila’s privilege to the Catholic boyars (1387), which Horodło renewed and widened, and over Vytautas’ replacement of the appanage princes of Kiev, Podolia, Novgorod-Seversky and Vitebsk by his own lieutenants (1390s), a strengthening of the grand duke’s power that left no lasting constitution.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Tower Shields (Spearman-line and Skirmishers +2 pierce armor). After his campaigns against the Golden Horde (1397–98) Vytautas settled Tatar captives and the followers of the exiled khan Tokhtamysh around Vilnius and Trakai, and a Tatar contingent under Jalal ad-Din fought on the Polish–Lithuanian side at Grunwald (1410) (Długosz; Tyszkiewicz 1989). The Tatars served the grand duke for land rather than pay, and their horse archers explain the civ’s Cavalry Archers; a one-off spawn of horse archers stands for the settlement of one body of steppe horsemen without making Cavalry Archers a cheap, dominant late unit. The Thumb Ring stays on the same ground, given for an archery tradition the civ’s armies demonstrably used: the steppe archery, which drew with the thumb, of the Tatars in the grand duke’s service. ‘Lipka’ (from the Tatar name for Lithuania) is the community’s later name, from the 16th–17th centuries (Kryczyński 1938). Gold-free Cavalry Archers, or ‘Cavalry Archers cost -40% gold’ (Ordonnance Companies), are not used: they would make a secondary element the civ’s dominant late unit. Tower Shields is dropped: the pavise is above all Bohemian and Italian, and Lithuanian infantry was secondary; the pavise theme goes to the Bohemians’ N2 Pavéza idea, and in N1 the Magyars’ Black Army renders Matthias’ pavisiers with the Tower Shields effect, widened to Infantry and Hand Cannoneers.

No naval tradition: no gun-armed warships. The Grand Duchy’s Baltic coast was the Palanga strip (confirmed at Melno, 1422), and its Black Sea littoral under Vytautas (Kachibey, from which grain was shipped to Constantinople in 1415, according to Długosz) was a steppe frontier without a fleet.
As Cannon Galleon.

Navy (RULES 6.16.1): no war fleet of its own (see Cannon Galleon), so the civ keeps the basic navy (Galley-line to War Galley, Fire Galley and Fire Ship, Hulk and War Hulk, demolition ships and the generic Dock techs), with no substitute siege warship.
As Galleon.
No printing in the window: the first press in the Grand Duchy was Francysk Skaryna’s in Vilnius (1522).

Owner’s decision (RULES 6.16.10): the regional Genitour extends to the Lithuanians, whose light horse was the core of their raiding. Lithuanian armies relied on light horsemen riding small native horses (Ekdahl 1998), who raided fast and often dismounted to fight in forest and broken ground (Šmidtas 2019 on Lithuanian light cavalry; Peter of Dusburg and Wigand of Marburg on the raids). The javelin is inferred from the regional tradition: the sulica (the sulitsa of the Rus’ chronicles) was the short throwing spear of the light horse of the Rus’ and Polish lands, and the sources consulted do not describe Lithuanian riders throwing it (see contested). The Genitour, a javelin-throwing light horseman, is the closest existing unit. At the Archery Range from the Castle Age, as for the Berbers, Castilians and Portuguese; a regional unit, so not counted as a unique unit (RULES 6.1). It shares with the Light Cavalry the light-cavalry role of the dropped Winged Hussar. The Genitour cannot fight at close range, while the Lithuanian riders also fought hand to hand and dismounted (see ideas).

Renamed from Genitour. The regional Genitour named after the sulica, the short throwing spear of the light horse of the Rus’ and Polish lands, which the Lithuanian riders are inferred to have used (see contested); the generic name (the English and French borrowing of Spanish jinete) is foreign to Lithuania. ‘Sulica Rider’ is a modern descriptive coinage, not a troop name found in the sources, and is flagged as such on the site (RULES 6.16.15); no period name for these riders is known. The Castilians and Portuguese rename the same unit Jinete and Ginete, and the Berbers keep ‘Genitour’.
The Elite upgrade of the Sulica Rider (Archery Range), for the same light horsemen.
Renamed from Elite Genitour. Follows the Sulica Rider, for the Lithuanians only; a modern coinage, flagged (RULES 6.16.15).

Kept from the game (level 1). Hussars appear in documents from southern Hungary in the first half of the 15th century: light cavalry, probably of Serbian origin, organised on a large scale under Matthias Corvinus (Engel 2001); the game’s generic Hussar takes its name from the same Hungarian word, huszár. A 15th-century troop as a Castle Age unit is early, and ‘Strong vs. Siege Weapons’ has no particular basis. The generic Hussar stays in the tree beside it, the default for keeping both: the Scout-line Hussar is the top tier of the kingdom’s light horse across the window (the Conquest-era horsemen, the Cuman and Székely light cavalry), while the Huszar renders the 15th-century hussars of the southern frontier and of Matthias’ army.
