New in the codex (level 2). Effect revised on 18 October 2026 at the owner’s request: the earlier cheaper Town Centers only discounted a few one-time purchases. Stephen I’s counties were built around royal castles whose ispáns raised the castle warriors (várjobbágyok) and the county levies, the backbone of the early kingdom’s army, which the faster training renders. Stephen I (997–1038, crowned 1000/1001) organised the new Christian kingdom into counties (Latin comitatus, later Hungarian vármegye), each run from a royal castle by an ispán (comes) with its castle folk; until the mid-13th century these castles were earth-and-timber ramparts rather than stone (Engel 2001; Fügedi 1986). Cheaper Town Centers stand for the spread of these stone-less royal centres across the Carpathian Basin. A new tech (level 2): no existing unique tech fits a state founding. Chosen over Charles I’s mining reform of 1327, which is the gold passive, and the militia portalis of 1397/1459, part of the Huszar passive’s basis.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Corvinian Army (Magyar Huszar gold cost is replaced by additional food cost): its slot; the effect became a native bonus. Matthias Corvinus’ standing mercenary army (from the 1460s) combined heavy and light cavalry, its core, with infantry and a large artillery train. In his letter of 1481 to Gabriele Rangoni, bishop of Eger, Matthias describes common foot, armoured foot and shield-bearers with great pavises, with the handgunners placed behind the shield-bearers at the start of battle and in defence (Rázsó 1982): effect 1, the pavise. Effect 2 follows the owner’s outline: Hungarian armies took over the Hussite war wagon, though not the Hussite way of fighting with it, and used wagon forts in a secondary, mainly defensive role, as mobile fortifications, under John Hunyadi (Varna 1444, Kosovo 1448) and in Matthias’ own campaigns (Baia 1467; the Breslau campaign of 1474) (Tóth 2026), which is what the Hussite Wagon renders. Czech companies brought the expertise: Jan Jiskra, whose companies had fought in Upper Hungary since 1440, entered Matthias’ service in 1462, and the brotherhoods (bratříci) who held out were defeated at Kostoľany (1467) and their survivors hired (Engel 2001); the Bohemians’ team bonus renders these Czech companies. The Elite Hussite Wagon upgrade is at the Castle as for the Bohemians, who keep the unit. A new tech (level 2), as the owner decided.

Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): the boat tier, by vessel. The royal Danube flotilla, the kingdom’s war fleet, was made of naszáds, oared river boats whose hulls the sources consulted do not describe (see the navy note under contested). The high-seas sailing warships (Galleon, Carrack) are removed, while the Galley, Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines keep their tiers as an abstraction of the river flotilla for water maps, with the Dock techs and the ‘Galleon, Fast Fire Ship and Carrack’ upgrade kept for the Fast Fire Ship. The Cannon Galleon stays as a special warship for the naszáds’ bow guns.
See Galleon.

Owner’s decision. Matthias’ army is traditionally credited with an unusually high share of handgunners (often given as one in four infantrymen, a figure of unclear origin), Czech mercenaries had brought Hussite firearms to Hungary since the 1440s, and Hunyadi’s wagon forts used guns; a kingdom without hand firearms was the most serious gap in the regional trees.
Matthias kept a large artillery train and won by siege at Jajce (1463), Šabac (1476), Vienna (1485) and Wiener Neustadt (1487) (Engel 2001); the Magyars had no gunpowder siege weapon at all.

After 1241 stone castles multiplied across the kingdom, and in the 15th century it maintained a line of frontier fortresses (Fügedi 1986; Pálosfalvi 2018); the Keep (held by 37 of the game’s 56 civs) was missing from one of the most castle-rich kingdoms of the frontier.

After 1241 stone castles multiplied across the kingdom, and in the 15th century it maintained a line of frontier fortresses (Fügedi 1986; Pálosfalvi 2018); the Keep (held by 37 of the game’s 56 civs) was missing from one of the most castle-rich kingdoms of the frontier.
Same basis: the castle and town walls of the post-1241 kingdom and the great frontier fortresses such as Belgrade (Nándorfehérvár), which withstood Mehmed II in 1456.
Same basis: the castle and town walls of the post-1241 kingdom and the great frontier fortresses such as Belgrade (Nándorfehérvár), which withstood Mehmed II in 1456.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Karambit Warrior. Malay rulers fought with their war chiefs and champions (hulubalang), such as Hang Tuah of the Malacca tradition, and the followers they brought, armed with spear, kris and shield; warfare in the region aimed at capturing people and relied on numbers (Reid). The karambit, a small curved knife of the Minangkabau for farm work and close defence, never armed a corps of troops, so the unit takes the name of the warriors; the half-population mechanic abstracts the war chiefs’ bands of followers.

Renamed from Elite Karambit Warrior. Follows the unique unit (Karambit Warrior → Hulubalang), for the Malay only.

New in the codex (level 1). Malacca’s port was run by four harbour masters (syahbandar), each in charge of the merchants of a group of nations, from Gujarat to China and Ryūkyū: they received the captains, presented them to the bendahara, found them warehouses and dispatched their goods (Pires, Suma Oriental), under the 15th-century codes of Malacca (the Undang-Undang Melaka and the maritime Undang-Undang Laut). The syahbandars were not among the great officers of state (the bendahara, the penghulu bendahari, the temenggung and the laksamana) but served under the treasurer, the penghulu bendahari (Sejarah Melayu). Faster gold income and a lower market fee abstract an efficient, open port. At the Town Center rather than the Market because in a port-state like Malacca the administration of the port was the core of government and of the crown’s revenue; moving it to the Market and giving the Town Center the Malacca law digest (Undang-Undang Melaka, compiled under Muhammad Shah and Muzaffar Shah) as a new, level-2 tech was considered and not adopted. It also gives the civ an economic edge on land maps, where it loses the faster age-up, the free infantry armour, the Knight-line, the Arbalester and the long-range siege; that power budget is accepted without compensation (RULES 6.16.13).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Thalassocracy (Docks are upgraded to Harbors). An adopted technique: gunpowder artillery, taken up in the Straits in the 15th century by routes that are uncertain. Malacca met the Portuguese in 1511 with guns on its stockades and its waterfront, and reportedly on its ships (not confirmed at first hand), light bronze pieces such as the lela and the swivel-mounted rentaka, of which the Portuguese took a great number (about 3,000 in João de Barros, probably inflated; see contested) (Barros; Comentários of Albuquerque). The Harbor, the Malay unique building that shoots at enemies, abstracts the gun-defended waterfront; the lela, the classic light Malay cannon, gives the tech its name (RULES 6.10). At the Dock because it is the defence of the port (RULES 6.2); Castle Age, as for the game’s Thalassocracy, although the guns belong to the last century of the window. The game’s name, a modern scholarly term for the sea power that the Galley-line bonus already carries, is replaced.

Kept from the game (level 1). Malay rulers counted their power in people and called them up for war. The Sejarah Melayu tells how, when Siam attacked Malacca under Muzaffar Shah (c. 1445–56), Tun Perak, headman of Klang, brought the men of Klang with their wives and children to defend the city, saying that men fight hardest with their families beside them, and so began his rise to bendahara, the office from which he led Malacca’s expansion (chronicle tradition; see contested). Paying the levy in food rather than gold fits an infantry of levies.
The Malay world has no tradition of mounted archery.
Cavalry was marginal in Malay warfare; the heavy shock arm was the elephant (the Khmer design removes the Knight line on the same ground).
As for the Knight.

Bow and crossbow mattered little; the characteristic missile weapons were the blowpipe (sumpit), javelins and throwing spears (lembing) and later firearms. The thumb draw belongs to the steppe and East Asian archery traditions, which Malay armies did not use (RULES 6.16.4).

No evidence for the crossbow in Malay warfare, whose missile weapons were the blowpipe, javelins and later guns; under the project’s crossbow criterion (RULES 6.16.3) the Crossbowman stays as the generic bow tier (see contested).

Heavy siege guns are not attested in Malay offensive warfare: Malacca’s guns of 1511 were mostly light pieces on its stockades and waterfront, and reportedly on its ships (see contested). The Siege Ram takes the anti-building role, and Malay gunpowder stays in the Harbor (Lela), the Bombard Tower and the Cannon Galleon (RULES 6.16.5).

No stone-throwing engine is attested in Malay warfare (see contested); the counterweight trebuchet reached China only in 1273, and there is no evidence that it reached this region. The rams keep the civ able to destroy buildings (RULES 6.11).

Malacca’s defences in 1511 were timber stockades, on which its light guns stood (see Lela); no stone or brick fortifications are documented before the Portuguese built A Famosa after the conquest (1511–12), partly with stone from the city’s mosques. The Guard Tower stays as the abstraction of defended posts, as for the Muisca.

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
No printing in the window: Malay texts such as the Sejarah Melayu and the law codes of Malacca were copied by hand, and the first printed Malay books came from European presses after 1600.

The rams take the anti-building role of the removed Bombard Cannon (RULES 6.11), as for the Khmer; Malay land war against fortifications meant assaults on stockades, for which the ram is the game’s generic tool, an abstraction. The Malay have no long-range siege weapon on land (no Trebuchet, Traction Trebuchet or Bombard Cannon; the Cannon Galleon, an abstraction of the light guns reported aboard Malacca’s ships, is the only one at sea) and rely on the Siege Ram as the RULES 6.11 substitute, as RULES 6.16.5 allows where no engine is attested.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no stone-throwing engine is attested in Malay warfare (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Gbeto. Mande tradition gives Sunjata's army the tontajon, the ‘quiver-bearers’ (ton-ta-jon), sixteen clans of free warriors who formed the military arm of the Manden; archers were the mass of Mande infantry, using simple bows whose weakness they made up for with poison, and Ibn Battuta (1352) saw the mansa himself come to audience with a bow in his hand and a quiver on his back. The Blackwood Archers, cheap self-bow archers trained in pairs at half population and strong in high numbers, fit that mass archery; the Armenian Composite Bowman, the alternative, has an armour-ignoring composite bow, the opposite of the Mande self bow. The Gbeto came from the Fon kingdom of Dahomey (18th–19th centuries), far from Mali in place and time.

New in the codex (level 2). The mansas ruled subject towns and provinces through governors called farba, a word Ibn Battuta glosses as ‘deputy’: at Walata in 1352 the farba Husayn received the merchants of his caravan, speaking to them only through an interpreter (Levtzion and Hopkins, 1981). Through such governors and the local chiefs the provinces supplied the levies of an army that al-Umari's informants put at about 100,000 men (Levtzion, 1973); foot soldiers that grow cheaper with every town held translate this. Tigui (Town Centers fire arrows without garrison) had no documented referent (see dropped), and no existing tech expresses provincial governors, so this is a new tech (level 2). A tech for Mansa Musa's pilgrimage (1324) was weighed and set aside: the hajj was a royal journey, not an institution of government, and its fame already shows in the gold bonus.

Kept from the game (level 1). The name seems to come from farin, ‘brave’, a Mande title of war leaders that also lies behind the governors' title farba; the horsemen, mounted on costly horses brought across the Sahara, were the warrior aristocracy (Law, 1980). They fought with lance, javelins and sword and are carried by the generic Stable lines; the regional Genitour is not extended to the Malians (owner's decision, RULES 6.16.10). The cavalry aristocracy is a long tradition rather than a datable moment, so Farimba keeps the mandatory Castle slot as a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19(b)): no datable military reform of the mansas is documented well enough to replace it, and Kirina (1235), the founding victory, is a battle, not a reform.
Neither Mali nor its Songhay successor used firearms: Songhay's army was routed at Tondibi (1591) by Judar Pasha's Moroccan arquebusiers precisely because it had none.
As Hand Cannoneer: no gunpowder in the Western Sudan before the Moroccan invasion of 1591. Rams, Petards and infantry still destroy buildings.

No gunpowder, and the civ lacked the Galleon, so the Cannon Galleon was incoherent. The boat-tier navy that stays (see the Carrack) keeps the Galley line, on the canoe model (see the renames), the fire ships, hulks and demolition ships.

The top tier of the stone-thrower line is dropped (the tech tree audit rates it unfounded); the Mangonel and Onager stay as the generic stone-thrower and the rams as the abstraction of assault (RULES 6.16.5). Sahelian towns were taken, when at all, by blockade and assault: al-Sa'di's Tarikh al-Sudan says, with a formulaic number, that the rulers of Mali attacked Djenné ninety-nine times without taking it.

No torsion or traction artillery is attested in the Sahel (analysis; tech tree audit), so the counterweight engine never reached the civ and is removed (RULES 6.16.5); the Mangonel and Onager stay as the generic stone-thrower, and the Siege Ram becomes the late anti-building engine.
Sahelian horsemen fought with lance, javelins and sword, and the archers fought on foot (tech tree audit).
As Cavalry Archer.

No camel troops are attested in Mali's armies: al-Umari counts only horse and foot, the Massufa of Walata and Taghaza were caravaneers and guides, and the Tuareg were rivals who took Timbuktu from Mali in 1433 (analysis; tech tree audit). The Ethiopian design removes its camels on the same kind of evidence. The Halberdier replaces it as the anti-cavalry unit (RULES 6.11); the camels are not kept as an abstraction of the Saharan peoples inside or beside the empire, whose service in Mali's armies is not attested.
As Camel Rider.

No crossbow is attested in the Sahel, so the crossbow tier goes (RULES 6.16.3); the Crossbowman stays as the generic Castle Age bow upgrade until the N2 bow/crossbow split, and the Tontajon fills the elite archer role. The tech tree audit rates the Malian Arbalester unfounded.

No thumb draw or thumb rings are attested for Sahelian archery (RULES 6.16.4); the thumb draw belongs to the steppe and Asian traditions (names theme), and other designs drop the tech on the same ground (among them the Ethiopians, Malay, Maya, Inca and Muisca).

The navy is the boat tier (RULES 6.16.1), which keeps the generic lines without the Galleon and Carrack: Mali's craft were dugout canoes, on its own river, where Ibn Battuta travelled down the Niger from Timbuktu (1353) in a small boat carved from a single piece of wood (Levtzion and Hopkins, 1981), and on the empire's western fringe, where canoes of archers attacked the Portuguese on the Gambia (Cadamosto, 1455); there were no high-castled sailing warships.
Sudano-Sahelian building was in earth, and medieval Malian town walls are thinly attested (see contested); the Guard Tower stays as the abstraction of defended posts, as for the Muisca.
Sudano-Sahelian building was in earth, and medieval Malian town walls are thinly attested (see contested); the Guard Tower stays as the abstraction of defended posts, as for the Muisca.
No printing in the window: the scholarship of Timbuktu and the Sahel lived in manuscripts copied by hand.

Archers were the mass of Mande infantry (the tontajon), so the archers' Blacksmith line should be complete; the analysis lists Bracer as missing. Arrowslits, which the analysis lists with it, stays out: medieval Malian fortifications are thinly attested, and the loopholed tata walls are 19th-century (see contested).

The anti-cavalry substitute for the removed camels (RULES 6.11), as in the Mongols' and Khitans' designs: a generic top spear tier for Mali's foot soldiers, whom modern historians describe as spearmen and archers (Levtzion, 1973).

Substitute for the removed Trebuchet and Bombard Cannon as the late anti-building engine (RULES 6.11), as for the Goths and the Malay: Sahelian towns were taken, when at all, by blockade and assault (see the Siege Onager), for which the ram is the game's generic tool, an abstraction. The civ has no long-range anti-building weapon, as RULES 6.16.5 allows where none is attested.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no torsion or traction artillery is attested in the Sahel (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

Renamed from Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Mali's craft were dugout canoes: Ibn Battuta travelled down the Niger from Timbuktu (1353) in a small boat carved from a single piece of wood (Levtzion and Hopkins, 1981), and canoes of archers attacked Cadamosto's caravels on the Gambia with poisoned arrows (1455) (see the Carrack). The Scenario Editor's Canoe (RULES section 5; codex/tools/scenario-units.md), a light boat that shoots arrows like the Galley, gives the Galley the look of a dugout war canoe, which fits the boat tier far better than a Mediterranean galley; the Galley keeps its stats, and the Canoe's look and scale must be checked in game. Same rename as in the Aztec, Avar, Mapuche, Maya and Tupi designs. No Mande name for the war canoe is secure in the sources used here, so the generic English name is used.
Renamed from War Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Upgrade tier of the renamed Galley, with the same Canoe look (see Galley).

New in the codex (level 1). The long lance of colihue cane was the main Mapuche weapon when the Spaniards arrived: the early chroniclers describe lances of great length and squadrons of pikemen from the first battles (Vivar, 1558; Góngora Marmolejo, 1575). The weapon is older than the contact, so it originated inside the time frame (RULES section 2); only its use in dense squares against horses dates from the 1550s. The Inca Kamayuk, a spearman with long reach, is the nearest existing unit (shared with the Inca and with the Berbers' and Ethiopians' designs). Decision: the model is kept until N3 infantry units of the Mapuche's own exist (ideas); shared models are accepted in N1 (RULES 6.16.12).

Renamed from Elite Kamayuk. Elite tier of the renamed unit.

Changed by the codex (level 1). Kona were the young warriors in the service of a lonko. As riders they belong to the decades after c. 1560, when the Mapuche, having captured and then bred horses, fielded the cavalry that destroyed the Spaniards at Curalaba (1598). Late element (RULES section 2): it originated after 1500, so it is available at the Castle only from the Imperial Age (age-gated availability, as in the game's Italian team bonus ‘Condottiero available at the Barracks in Imperial Age’), and it is the civ's only civ-specific post-1500 element; generic post-1500 items held by most civs, such as the Petard and the demolition ships, stay as flagged abstractions and do not count as a late element (RULES 6.16.2). Decision (a historical call, RULES section 11): the pre-Hispanic recentring of the civ stands, with the Kona as its one late element; the Mapuche are not exempted from RULES section 2, and Lautaro's tactics at Tucapel (1553) and the other Arauco War content stay N2 ideas. With the cavalry an Imperial-Age late element, the label becomes ‘Infantry and Counter-Units civilization’, one of the game's categories (RULES 6.16.16).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Malon. In war the Mapuche chose a war leader, the toqui, named after the polished stone axe (toki) that was his insignia, who led the warriors of the allied lof for the length of a campaign; Lautaro and Caupolicán held the office (Rosales; Bengoa 2003). Clubs and slings were among the weapons of the weichafe. The effect abstracts the toqui's command of the raiding levies of clubmen and slingers; the Colihue Lancers are left out because the tech keeps the existing Caciques effect unchanged, which keeps it at level 1, and the lancers have their own unit role. Malon is dropped: the word belongs mostly to the later mounted raids of the pampas, and its effect (pass-through damage) had no link to it (rated stretched).

New in the codex (level 2). War and peace were decided in assemblies (koyag, koyagtun) of lonkos and warriors, which also chose the toqui; the communities then took the field at their own cost, with their own weapons and food, since there was no state to pay or arm them (Bengoa 2003; Boccara 1998). Cheaper levy troops render this. The same word later named the parliaments with the Spanish Crown (Quilín, 1641). For a people without a state the Town Center tech represents a community institution (RULES 6.3); its basis is thin, since the assemblies are known from post-1541 sources.

The crossbow was unknown in the Americas, which have neither crossbow tier (RULES 6.16.3), and nothing suggests the Mapuche adopted captured ones; their missile weapons were bows, slings and, in some accounts, bolas. Archers, Slingers and Skirmishers cover the role. In the current game the Bulgarians also lack crossbows.

Removed under the codex convention for the American civs (RULES 6.16.6, the owner's decision on their power budget): a playability line, not a historical one, since the kept Pikeman bears as European a name; the American spear line stops at the Pikeman, as the game already does for the Aztecs and Muisca. The long lance itself is the Colihue Lancer, and Spearman and Pikeman remain.

Ocean-going sailing warships were unknown; Mapuche boats were dugout canoes (wampu) and, further south, sewn-plank dalcas, and no Mapuche war fleet is documented. Basic navy (RULES 6.16.1), since the Mapuche had no war fleet of their own: the galleys (renamed Canoe), fire ships, the Hulk line, the demolition ships and the generic Dock techs stay as an abstraction for water maps, without the Galleon, Carrack, Fast Fire Ship or a siege warship; the demolition ships are generic post-1500 items kept as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.2).
See Galleon.
A sailing ship carrying a catapult: both a European ship type and a siege engine.
Removed under the basic navy (see Galleon); the Fire Ship stays.

Removed for its Byzantine name and concept (the siphon that projected Greek fire), which has no American equivalent; the Mapuche were the only American civ with it. The Fire Ship line stays as a generic abstraction for water maps.
Gunpowder towers have no Mapuche basis: arquebuses captured from the Spaniards appear at Quiapo (1558) in an unsuccessful defence, and artillery use is uncertain (tech-tree audit: stretched).
Gunpowder towers have no Mapuche basis: arquebuses captured from the Spaniards appear at Quiapo (1558) in an unsuccessful defence, and artillery use is uncertain (tech-tree audit: stretched).

The Mapuche built in wood, cane and thatch (the ruka) and raised earthwork forts, not stone buildings. The Castle itself stays for structural reasons (it trains the unique units, researches the Castle tech and is needed for the Imperial Age) until an N3 pucará replaces it (ideas).
See Architecture; in the current game the Aztecs, Byzantines and Tupi also lack Masonry (the Aztecs' design adds it).
Mapuche defences were earthworks, ditches and palisades; stone walls are removed (in the current game the Cumans and Goths also lack them; the Goths' design adds them) and Palisade Walls remain.
Removed with the Stone Wall; the Palisade Gate remains.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no siege engine of any kind existed in the pre-contact Americas (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice. The Siege Workshop stays in the tree for this engine alone. For its other units the design’s reading stands: The Mapuche built no siege engines; they took Spanish forts by assault, blockade and fire (Tucapel, 1553; the sieges of La Imperial, Villarrica and Osorno after 1599) and captured some Spanish guns (Villagra's artillery at Marihueñu, 1554) without making them a weapon of their own. The Weichafe line (strong against buildings), Arson, Sappers and Petards replace them (owner's decision, RULES 6.16.5; RULES 6.11 and section 10). Before the heavy-engine floor every Castle had to be taken by units standing in its arrow fire; the Traction Trebuchet now does it from range, as a game convention, until an N2/N3 assault unit exists (ideas), with no compensating bonus (RULES 6.16.13). The Petard, a 16th-century gunpowder charge, stays unrenamed as a flagged generic abstraction of assault parties with fire, outside the one-late-element limit (RULES 6.16.2).

Renamed from Champi Scout. Weichafe is the Mapudungun word for warrior. Champi, the Quechua name of the Andean mace, is foreign to the Mapuche, whose clubs were of wood and whose stone axe (toki) was the war leader's insignia.
Renamed from Champi Runner. Same rename as Champi Scout.
Renamed from Champi Warrior. Same rename as Champi Scout.
Renamed from Elite Champi Warrior. Same rename as Champi Scout.

Renamed from Horse Collar. There were no draft animals. Raised cultivation platforms in the wetlands of the Purén and Lumaco valleys, in use at least from AD 1000 to 1500 (Dillehay et al. 2007) and dated at the sites PU-165 and LU-69 to about 1220–1420 by later botanical studies of Dillehay's team, belong to the same landscape as the kuel ceremonial mounds. Same rename as for the Maya and the Muisca. Heavy Plow (there was no plough before contact: ploughing with hueque is reported from Spilbergen's expedition at Mocha Island in 1615, as retold by Molina) and Crop Rotation keep their generic names as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.6; see the civ-level note on generic economy items).

Renamed from Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Mapuche boats on the coast, the rivers and the lakes were dugout canoes (wampu), with the sewn-plank dalca further south (see the Galleon note). The Scenario Editor Canoe, a small warship introduced in The Forgotten (RULES section 5), gives the Galley the look of a dugout; the Galley keeps its stats, and the Canoe's look, scale, attack and role must be checked in game. The rename renders the vessel type the Mapuche had, not a documented war fleet: they are in the basic navy (see Galleon). Same rename as for the Aztecs, Maya and Tupi, and outside the Americas in the Malians' and Avars' designs.
Renamed from War Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Upgrade tier of the renamed Galley, with the same Canoe look (see Galley).

Kept from the game (level 1). No corps of ‘plumed archers’ is documented: the unit stands for the Postclassic Maya bowman, with the feathered headdresses worn as insignia by warriors of rank across Mesoamerica (Landa; the Bonampak murals, c. 790). Its high speed is a game invention. Also trainable at the Archery Range in the Imperial Age (see bonuses).

Kept from the game (level 1). Hul'che (hulche) is the Yucatec Maya name of the spear-thrower: a Yucatec specimen in the Smithsonian is catalogued as ‘(Hulche) or spear-thrower (atlatl)’; the colonial dictionaries (the Calepino de Motul; the Diccionario Maya Cordemex, 1980) have not been checked. Warriors with atlatls and darts fill the carvings and murals of Terminal Classic and Early Postclassic Chichén Itzá (Temple of the Warriors), and the Spaniards met darts or javelins at Champotón in 1517 (Bernal Díaz). The extra projectile is an abstraction of dart volleys; the Aztec Atlatl gives range and attack instead (intended overlap, RULES 6.7). As a weapon tradition it is not a datable moment: it is a kept existing tech, held as a tech by the effect-size tie-break (RULES 6.2.4), a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19 b). Castle Age, before the Late Postclassic holkan of the Imperial tech (RULES 6.4).

Kept from the game (level 1). The holkan were the soldiers of Postclassic Yucatán, paid while on campaign and led by the war captain (nacom), who was elected for three years, as Landa describes. The tech replaced the old ‘El Dorado’, a Muisca myth, with the same effect.

New in the codex (level 2). Classic Maya kingdoms were ruled by ‘holy lords’ (k'uhul ajaw) from palace and acropolis complexes at the heart of each city, such as the Central Acropolis of Tikal and the Palace of Palenque; the king led in war, performed the calendar rituals, commissioned temples and stelae and drew labour and tribute from his polity (Martin & Grube 2008; Martin 2020). Stronger and busier Town Centers render the royal seat as the hub of the city-state. Divine kingship is a state institution, so it is the Town Center tech (RULES 6.2).

The crossbow was unknown in the pre-Hispanic Americas, which have neither crossbow tier (RULES 6.16.3); Maya missile troops used bows, slings and atlatls. The Plumed Archer becomes available at the Archery Range in the Imperial Age in its place (bonus). In the current game the Bulgarians also lack crossbows (so do the current Spanish; the Castilian and Bulgarian designs restore the Crossbowman).
Removed with the Crossbowman (see there).
No thumb rings or thumb draw are attested in the Americas, so the tech goes (RULES 6.16.4); the game's Britons, the archer civ par excellence, also lack it.

Removed under the codex convention for the American civs (RULES 6.16.6, the owner's decision on their power budget): a playability line, not a historical one, since the kept Pikeman bears as European a name; the American spear line stops at the Pikeman, as the game already does for the Aztecs and Muisca. The Maya met no cavalry before the Spanish expeditions (Centla, 1519), and Spearman and Pikeman remain for the spear of Classic imagery.

Ocean-going sailing warships were unknown; Maya seafaring used large dugout canoes (the canoe seen off Guanaja in 1502; the Chontal canoe trade, Scholes & Roys 1948). Boat tier (RULES 6.16.1), resting on these dugouts: the high-seas sailing ships (Galleon, Carrack) are removed and the siege ship goes with the siege engines, while the Galley (renamed Canoe), Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines stay with their tiers as a generic abstraction of canoe fleets for water maps; the demolition ships are generic post-1500 items kept as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.2).
High-castled sailing warships were unknown (see Galleon).
A sailing ship carrying a catapult: both a European ship type and a siege engine.

There was no printing: Maya books (codices of bark paper) were painted by hand, and Landa burned many of them at Maní in 1562. With no equivalent for the function the tech is removed (18 of the game's 56 civs already lack it); the scribes are represented by the University and Monastery bonus.

No defensive Maya stone tower is documented: the four-storey tower of the Palace of Palenque was a palace lookout or observatory, and the small corner structures of the Tulum wall are shrines or watch posts, which the Watch Tower and Guard Tower stand for. Region-wide tower policy: the Keep, a stone tower, stays only where stone towers are documented, which among the American civs means the Inca (the towers of Sacsayhuamán).

No defensive Maya stone tower is documented: the four-storey tower of the Palace of Palenque was a palace lookout or observatory, and the small corner structures of the Tulum wall are shrines or watch posts, which the Watch Tower and Guard Tower stand for. Region-wide tower policy: the Keep, a stone tower, stays only where stone towers are documented, which among the American civs means the Inca (the towers of Sacsayhuamán).

Quilted cotton armour is well documented among the Maya: Landa describes jackets of cotton quilted in two layers with coarse salt as very strong, and the Spaniards met cotton-armoured warriors in 1517. The Maya have the Militia-line but lacked the tech; it is added and renamed Quilted Cotton Armor.

Renamed from Gambesons. Same effect as Gambesons. Landa describes Maya jackets of quilted cotton as very strong. The Nahuatl name ichcahuipilli used for the Aztecs is not applied to the Maya, to avoid giving one people's word to another.

The Maya who fought the first Spanish expeditions in 1517 used slings as well as bows and lances (Bernal Díaz, on Champotón). The regional Slinger, shared with the Aztecs, the Inca, the Muisca and the Mapuche, replaces part of the role of the removed crossbows.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no siege engine of any kind existed in the pre-contact Americas (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice. The Siege Workshop stays in the tree for this engine alone. For its other units the design’s reading stands: The Maya built no siege engines: cities fell to assault, fire and blockade. Infantry with the anti-building bonus, Arson, Sappers and Petards replace them (owner's decision, RULES 6.16.5; RULES 6.11 and section 10). Before the heavy-engine floor every Castle had to be taken by units standing in its arrow fire; the Traction Trebuchet now does it from range, as a game convention, until an N2/N3 assault unit exists (ideas), with no compensating bonus (RULES 6.16.13). The Petard, a 16th-century gunpowder charge, stays unrenamed as a flagged generic abstraction of assault parties with fire, outside the one-late-element limit (RULES 6.16.2).

Renamed from Horse Collar. There were no draft animals. Raised and channelised wetland fields, such as those of Pulltrouser Swamp (Turner & Harrison 1983) and the field complexes of north-western Belize mapped by LiDAR and multiproxy study (Beach et al. 2019), intensified lowland farming: the Maya counterpart of the Aztec chinampas. The same rename is used for the Muisca and the Mapuche.

Renamed from Heavy Plow. There was no plough. Agricultural terraces covered whole hillsides around Caracol, documented by ground survey and excavation (Chase & Chase 1998) and later shown in full by LiDAR. Same rename as for the Aztecs.

Renamed from Crop Rotation. Agreed rename (Crop Rotation → Milpa), applied to both Mesoamerican civs: the milpa, intercropping maize, beans and squash, is the basis of Maya farming to this day. ‘Milpa’ is Nahuatl (mīlli with -pan) but is the standard term of Mexican Spanish and of Maya scholarship, as ‘andenes’ is Spanish for Andean terraces. Decision: it is kept rather than the Yucatec kool, although the region otherwise avoids giving one people's word to another. The tier order is a game convention: historically the milpa came first, and raised fields and terraces intensified it later.

Renamed from Iron Casting. There was no iron. Maya lances, axes and arrows were tipped with knapped flint (chert), as Landa describes, and with obsidian imported from highland sources such as El Chayal and Ixtepeque (Aoyama 2005). Same effect as Iron Casting. The Aztec counterpart is Obsidian Blades. The other Blacksmith tiers keep their generic names as a flagged generic equipment level (RULES 6.16.6): Forging and Blast Furnace, although there was no iron metallurgy (metal, copper bells and axes, arrived late and mostly as imports); Bodkin Arrow, although arrows were tipped with flint and obsidian, not forged iron; Scale Mail, Chain Mail and Plate Mail Armor, although there was no metal armour (Maya warriors wore quilted cotton, which renames Gambesons, and carried flexible or hide shields); and Ring Archer Armor, beside Padded and Leather Archer Armor, which have real equivalents in cotton and hide. Chemistry stays for its +1 ranged attack as a flagged abstraction, although the Maya had no gunpowder.
Renamed from Wheelbarrow. There were no wheeled vehicles; Maya porters, like all Mesoamerican porters, carried loads with a tumpline across the forehead. Same rename as for the Aztecs.

Renamed from Hand Cart. Porters slung wooden carrying frames from the tumpline throughout Mesoamerica (Hassig 1985). Same rename as for the Aztecs. The Trade Cart keeps its generic name and look as a flagged abstraction of porter trains and the canoe trade (RULES 6.16.6), since there were no wheeled vehicles.

Renamed from Coinage. There were no coins: Landa says the Yucatec Maya traded salt, cloth and slaves for cacao and stone beads, which were their money. Same rename as for the Aztecs. Banking (tributes to other players are free) keeps its generic name as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.6), since no Maya equivalent with a period term was found.

Renamed from Guilds. Same effect as Guilds (Market trading fee reduced to 15%). The Yucatec word for merchant was p'olom (ppolom in colonial spelling), and merchant lords led the canoe trade of the Chontal of Acalan, whose ruler was its chief merchant (Scholes & Roys 1948). The Maya counterpart of the agreed Aztec Pochteca, a rename beyond the agreed list applied under RULES 6.16.6.

Renamed from Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Maya fleets were dugout canoes: off Guanaja in 1502 Columbus's men met a trading canoe ‘as long as a galley’ with some 25 paddlers (Ferdinand Columbus), the Chontal of Tabasco and Acalan carried the coastal trade in canoes (Scholes & Roys 1948), and in 1518 armed warriors in canoes met Grijalva's ships off Tabasco (Bernal Díaz, who says he sailed with him). The Scenario Editor Canoe, a small warship introduced in The Forgotten (RULES section 5), gives the Galley the look of a dugout war canoe; the Galley keeps its stats, and the Canoe's look, scale, attack and role must be checked in game. Same rename as for the Aztecs, Mapuche and Tupi, and outside the Americas in the Malians' and Avars' designs.
Renamed from War Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Upgrade tier of the renamed Galley, with the same Canoe look (see Galley).

Kept from the game (level 1). Named after the Manggud, who with the Uru'ud formed Chinggis's vanguard against the Kereyid at Qalaqaljit Elet in 1203 (Secret History §170–171); an elite horse archer is a faithful picture of the Mongol core.

Kept from the game (level 1). Named after the Manggud, who with the Uru'ud formed Chinggis's vanguard against the Kereyid at Qalaqaljit Elet in 1203 (Secret History §170–171); an elite horse archer is a faithful picture of the Mongol core.

New in the codex (level 1). The kheshig, Chinggis's guard, was created in 1204 with day guards, night guards and quiver-bearers, and expanded to 10,000 men in 1206 (Secret History §191, §224–234); it served as the school of the empire's commanders and governors and survived under the Yuan and the Ilkhans. The game gives it only to the Tatars; here the Mongols share it with them, and the gold earned in combat stands for the booty distributed through the khan's household. Decision: the unit is shared rather than made Mongol-only, since the Tatars' design keeps it for the armoured elite of the Horde's households (RULES 6.7).

New in the codex (level 1). The kheshig, Chinggis's guard, was created in 1204 with day guards, night guards and quiver-bearers, and expanded to 10,000 men in 1206 (Secret History §191, §224–234); it served as the school of the empire's commanders and governors and survived under the Yuan and the Ilkhans. The game gives it only to the Tatars; here the Mongols share it with them, and the gold earned in combat stands for the booty distributed through the khan's household. Decision: the unit is shared rather than made Mongol-only, since the Tatars' design keeps it for the armoured elite of the Horde's households (RULES 6.7).

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Nomads (Lost Houses do not decrease population space). Ögödei organised the yam, a network of relay stations with fresh horses and supplies, around 1234–1235 (Secret History §279–281). Marco Polo describes posts every 25 to 30 miles, and holders of a paiza tablet (envoys, officials and licensed merchants) could claim mounts and lodging, so that urgent orders covered in weeks journeys that took caravans months: express riders made 200 to 250 miles a day (Marco Polo; Allsen 1987; A. Silverstein, Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World, 2007). The stations are the outposts; the riders and the intelligence they carried take over the old scouting team bonus. A state institution, so the Town Center (RULES 6.2). Nomads had little effect and caught little of the moving ger camps it alluded to (see N3 idea).

Kept from the game (level 1). The Mongols kept corps of Chinese and Muslim engineers with the army: engines, ladders and stones were hauled to Nishapur in 1221 by the thousand (Juvaini); Hülegü took a thousand households of Chinese catapult men, naphtha-throwers and crossbowmen west in 1253 (Juvaini; Rashid al-Din), crews of siege crossbows such as the “ox's bow” that Khitan craftsmen built at Maymun-Diz (1256), which Juvaini says shot 2,500 paces (the Heavy Scorpion, which the Mongols keep, stands for them too); and Muslim engineers sent from the Ilkhanate built the engines that took Xiangyang for Kublai in 1273 (Yuan shi). A mobile siege train is a fair abstraction.
Bactrian camels carried the Mongols' baggage and dismantled gers; there is no record of camel-mounted combat troops.
As Camel Rider.

A power-budget decision that history tolerates: Mongol infantry came from subject levies, which the Two-Handed Swordsman and the Halberdier stand for, and the top swordsman tier is withheld to offset the second unique unit and Plate Barding.
No ship-borne guns are recorded for the Yuan fleets of 1274, 1281 or 1293; replaced by the Catapult Galleon.
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
Carpini (1247) describes armour for horses made of leather strips laid in several layers and shaped to the body; the absence of the last horse-armour upgrade contradicted the sources.

The anti-cavalry substitute for the removed camels (RULES 6.11), rather than keeping the Heavy Camel Rider as a declared abstraction. The Mongol army proper had no infantry; its foot came from subject peoples: the north Chinese “Han armies” raised from the 1230s and, under the Yuan, the Han and “newly submitted” (xinfu) troops of the former Song, heirs of Song spear and crossbow infantry (Hsiao 1978). Their polearms match the game's Halberdier (the Chinese ji); the kept Two-Handed Swordsman and Arbalester stand for the same troops, the Arbalester also for the crossbow bolts in the wreck of the 1281 fleet off Takashima (Sasaki 2015).

The khans' merchant partners (ortoq), trading with capital from the princely households (Allsen 1989), and the Yuan paper money (chao) made the Mongol courts great patrons of commerce; the absence of Guilds was odd for the empire of the Pax Mongolica.

Printing inside the window, under the Yuan: the state printed its paper money (chao), which Marco Polo describes (see Guilds), Buddhist scriptures were printed under the khans' patronage, and the Yuan official Wang Zhen described the wooden movable type with which he printed a county gazetteer (Nong shu, 1313). The same printing-date test gives Block Printing to the Khitans for Liao printing; the Persians' design does not count the Ilkhanid paper money of Tabriz (1294), which was not book printing, so the test rests here on Yuan printing.

Yuan war fleets fought with bombs and crossbows rather than guns: the wreck of the 1281 invasion fleet off Takashima yielded ceramic bombs (tetsuhō), crossbow bolts, arrowheads, spears and swords, but no cannon (Sasaki 2015). The non-gunpowder siege warship fits these ship-borne bombs, usually read as catapult-thrown, better than a gun ship and replaces the Cannon Galleon (RULES 6.11). Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, resting on the planked ships from Chinese and Korean yards of the Yuan fleets against Song China, Japan (1274, 1281) and Java (1293). The tree keeps the game's Mongol navy, without the Carrack, Dry Dock and Heated Shot that the game already withholds, and the Galleon stays as a flagged abstraction of the game's skeleton (RULES 6.16.2); special warships stay only where their type or function is documented (RULES 6.16.1).

Kept from the game (level 1). The güechas were a privileged class of frontier warriors facing the Panche, adorned with gold or tumbaga ornaments that marked the enemies they had killed; they fought with darts, slings, clubs and long shields. Regenerating when a comrade falls evokes the mummies of famous warriors carried into battle (Simón; Piedrahita). Decision: it stays the civ's only unique unit until the N2 mummy-bearer exists (ideas). Against cavalry, which the Muisca first met in 1537, they keep the Pikeman and Monks, as the current Aztecs do; no anti-cavalry bonus is added, since none would pass the relevance test (RULES 6.9). The label keeps the game's ‘Archer and Monk’, since the game's categories count skirmishers, such as the güechas and the Archery Range skirmishers, as archers (RULES 6.16.16).

Kept from the game (level 1). Chewing coca with lime increased endurance and was common practice among warriors and travellers as among the jeques; coca, which the chroniclers of New Granada call hayo, came by trade from the warmer valleys (Langebaek 2019). The speed bonus is an acceptable abstraction. Coca chewing is a structural practice with no datable moment or formalisation (RULES 6.2, 6.3): this is a current-game tech kept as an abstraction and held as a tech by the effect-size tie-break (RULES 6.2.4), a flagged fallback (RULES 6.16.19 b), because the Muisca have no datable military moment for the mandatory Castle slot. Effect unchanged; the in-game text only renames the Champi Warriors as Club Warriors. Its Archer-line target sits awkwardly with a civ whose bows were secondary (the chroniclers link the bow mainly with the Panche). Decision: the effect stays unchanged at level 1; retargeting it to Skirmishers, Slingers and Club Warriors would make a new, level-2 tech for a detail.

New in the codex (level 1). Muisca commoners paid tribute to their caciques, and the caciques to the zipa of Bacatá and the zaque of Hunza, largely in cotton mantles and gold (Langebaek 2019; Gamboa 2010). Gold income renders the tribute that flowed to the chiefs; the lower market fee renders the mantle as the measure of exchange. Tribute is a chiefly institution, so this is the Town Center tech of a people organised in chiefdoms (RULES 6.2 and 6.3). The effect is Grand Trunk Road, kept by the Hindustanis as Tanka and shared in the Anglo-Saxons', Burgundians', Khitans' and Malay designs; five more designs use its gold half, in the Arabs', Avars', Bulgarians' and Danes' techs and the Byzantines' passive (RULES 6.7; reuse is accepted in N1, RULES 6.16.12).

Counterweight artillery never existed in the Americas.
No siege engines are left to improve.

The crossbow was unknown in the Americas, which have neither crossbow tier (RULES 6.16.3). Muisca missile weapons were darts, slings and, to a lesser degree, bows (associated mainly with the Panche); the Guecha Warrior, Slingers and Skirmishers cover the role, and the Archer stays. In the current game the Bulgarians also lack crossbows.
Removed with the Crossbowman (see there).
No thumb rings or thumb draw are attested in the Americas, so the tech goes (RULES 6.16.4).

An ocean navy is absurd for an inland plateau people; Muisca boats were reed rafts on the lakes. Basic navy (RULES 6.16.1), since the Muisca had no war fleet of their own: the Galley-line to War Galley, the Fire Galley and Fire Ship, the Hulk and War Hulk, the demolition ships and the generic Dock techs stay as an abstraction for water maps, with no Galleon, Carrack or siege warship; the demolition ships are generic post-1500 items kept as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.2). The Scenario Editor Canoe is not used, since the look follows the vessel type, not the navy tier: it renders a dugout, and Muisca craft were reed rafts on the lakes (the Inca, with balsa and reed rafts, leave it aside for the same reason, while the Mapuche, also in the basic navy, take it for their dugouts).
See Galleon.
A sailing ship carrying a catapult: both a European ship type and a siege engine.
There was no printing or writing. With no equivalent for the function the tech is removed (18 of the game's 56 civs already lack it).

Region-wide tower policy: only the Keep, a stone tower, needs documented stone towers, so it stays only where they are documented (the Inca); the Guard Tower stays as a generic tier wherever the game gives it (the Mapuche, who lack it in the game, stay without it). The Muisca built in wood, cane and wattle-and-daub and had no towers, so their Guard Towers are an abstraction of wooden frontier posts. The Castle itself stays for structural reasons (it trains the unique unit, researches the Castle tech and is needed for the Imperial Age) until an N3 cercado replaces it (ideas).

Muisca defences were palisades around the enclosures of the caciques; stone walls are removed (in the current game the Cumans and Goths also lack them; the Goths' design adds them) and Palisade Walls remain.
Removed with the Stone Wall; the Palisade Gate remains.

There was no stone masonry tradition (the Temple of the Sun at Sugamuxi was of wood); the Muisca already lacked Architecture, and in the current game the Aztecs, Byzantines and Tupi lack Masonry too (the Aztecs' design adds it).

With the Temple Guard dropped, the Muisca need another way to destroy buildings (RULES 6.11). Houses and cacique enclosures were of wood, cane and thatch, so fire is a plausible abstraction, though no chronicle passage on Muisca fire attacks was found. In the current game only the Goths, Romans and Muisca lack Arson.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no siege engine of any kind existed in the pre-contact Americas (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice. The Siege Workshop stays in the tree for this engine alone. For its other units the design’s reading stands: The Muisca built no siege engines; their defences were palisaded enclosures. The Club line (strong against buildings), Arson and Petards replace them (owner's decision, RULES 6.16.5; RULES 6.11 and section 10). The Muisca have no Sappers; before the heavy-engine floor every Castle had to be taken by units standing in its arrow fire, and the Traction Trebuchet now does it from range, as a game convention, until an N2/N3 assault unit exists (ideas), with no compensating bonus (RULES 6.16.13). The Petard, a 16th-century gunpowder charge, stays unrenamed as a flagged generic abstraction of assault parties with fire, outside the one-late-element limit (RULES 6.16.2).

Renamed from Champi Scout. Champi is the Quechua name of the Andean stone or bronze mace, and macana, the chroniclers' word for the Muisca clubs of hard palm wood, is Taíno: both are foreign to the Muisca. No muysccubun term for the club was found in the sources used (the colonial grammars and vocabularies of the language, c. 1612 and 1619, could not be checked), so a neutral English name is given. Decision: it is kept rather than the chroniclers' loanword ‘macana’, which would also have opened the Taíno ‘cacique’ to the Tupi.
Renamed from Champi Runner. Same rename as Champi Scout.
Renamed from Champi Warrior. Same rename as Champi Scout.
Renamed from Elite Champi Warrior. Same rename as Champi Scout.

Renamed from Horse Collar. There were no draft animals. Ridged fields (camellones) separated by drainage ditches covered the flood plains of the Sabana de Bogotá from the Herrera period to the Late Muisca period (Broadbent 1968; Rodríguez-Gallo 2018). Same rename as for the Maya and the Mapuche. Heavy Plow and Crop Rotation keep their generic names as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.6; see the civ-level note on generic economy items).

Kept from the game (level 1). Sasanian armies brought Indian elephants to Avarayr (451), the Battle of the Bridge (634) and Qadisiyya (636/637), where they at first frightened the Arab horses (al-Tabari); later rulers of Iran used them too, from the Ghaznavids to Timur, who fought with elephants taken from Delhi at Ankara (1402). Trample damage is a reasonable abstraction. The Burmese design shares the unit, each on its own history (RULES 6.16.12).

Kept from the game (level 1). Savār means ‘horseman’ in Persian; the asvaran were the armoured noble cavalry of the Sasanians, the clibanarii of Roman sources. Heavy cavalry strong against ranged units is a reasonable role; these horsemen also used the bow. The game's own Persian unit fits better than the Scenario Editor's Sogdian Cataphract, a Central Asian heavy horseman.

New in the codex (level 1). Kavad I began and Khosrow I (531–579) completed a survey of the cultivated land and fixed the land tax (Middle Persian harāg) in silver per jarib according to the crop (wheat and barley, vines, date palms), collected in instalments; it paid a standing army, and the Arab conquerors kept it as the kharāj of Iraq and Iran (al-Tabari, trans. Bosworth, 1999; Daryaee, 2009). Farmers whose fields yield coin to the treasury translate it directly. The tech takes the Arabic name, under which the tax ran through the whole Islamic part of the window. Neither Kamandaran nor Citadels fits the Town Center, so another civ's existing tech is shared (level 1).

Kept from the game (level 1). Hasan-i Sabbah's seizure of Alamut (1090) began the Nizari Ismaili castle network of Iran (Alamut, Lamasar, Girdkuh and the forts of Quhistan). Its mountain strongholds largely held out against the Seljuks for generations, though Muhammad Tapar took Shahdiz near Isfahan in 1107, until the Mongol conquest (Alamut, 1256) (Daftary, 1990). It continues the Sasanian tradition of fortress cities and frontier forts (Nisibis, Persian from 363; the forts of Khosrow I's Derbent walls). Keep, Fortified Wall and Arrowslits now enter the tree, removing the contradiction the analysis noted.

The window ends with the Timurids (1507). Light guns are reported for Timurid and Aq Qoyunlu armies, but thinly: Uzun Hasan lost at Otlukbeli (1473) to Ottoman guns (Woods, 1999), and Ismail I's army fought at Chaldiran (1514), after the window, without significant firearms (Matthee, 1996; the reason is contested). The window is not stretched to the early Safavids (to 1524) to bring the Hand Cannoneer back as a late element: Safavid firearms were thin before Chaldiran, and the Safavids are an N3 civ idea.
As Hand Cannoneer. Trebuchet, Onager, Siege Ram, Petard and the War Elephant (strong against buildings) still destroy buildings (RULES 6.11).

The navy is a fleet of ships (RULES 6.16.1). The Sasanian navy guarded the sea lanes of the Persian Gulf and supported Iranian influence across the northern Indian Ocean; it was most active under Khosrow I (531–579), whose fleet helped take Yemen (Dmitriev, 2017). As the land routes suffered from the Roman–Persian rivalry, the sea trade of the Persian Gulf grew in the 5th and 6th centuries, and Persian merchants and settlements reached as far as Sri Lanka (Daryaee, 2003). The tier rests on these vessels: the eight ships in which Khosrow I sent Wahriz with an expeditionary force of about 800 men to Yemen (c. 570; al-Tabari, trans. Bosworth, 1999), whose victory brought Yemen under Sasanian suzerainty, and, in the Islamic part of the window, the armed fleets of the Gulf's Iranian side, such as that of the island principality of Kish (Qays), whose ships attacked Aden in 1135 (Goitein, 1954). So the generic tiers stay, the Galleon as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2). But no gun-armed warship is documented for Iran inside the window, and even the Safavids needed English East India Company ships to take Hormuz from the Portuguese in 1622, so the Cannon Galleon goes.
As Cannon Galleon.
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

No printing in the window: the paper money that the Ilkhan Geikhatu had block-printed at Tabriz on the Chinese model (1294) was withdrawn within months and was not book printing, and printed amulets (tarsh) survive mostly from Egypt (see the Arabs' design).
Archery was the Persian arm par excellence (Procopius; the Strategikon), so the archers' Blacksmith line should be complete, as the analysis asks.

The project gives the Arbalester, the crossbow tier, only where crossbows are attested, keeping the Crossbowman as the generic Castle Age bow upgrade until the N2 bow/crossbow split (RULES 6.16.3). The crossbow (charkh) was known in the Persianate east: Fakhr-i Mudabbir's manual of war (Adab al-harb wa'l-shaja'a, early 13th century), written in the Ghaznavid–Ghurid tradition for the Delhi sultan Iltutmish, describes it; it belongs to the Indian side of the Ghaznavid split and is also the basis of the Hindustanis' Arbalester, so for Iran it is indirect evidence (see contested). With it the Persians' archery gets the full line, as the analysis asks.

The Wall of Gorgan (c. 195 km with more than 30 forts; Sauer et al., 2013), the Tammisha wall and the walls of Derbent (Khosrow I, 6th century) were among the largest fortification works of late antiquity; Citadels without Keeps was incoherent. With Keep, Fortified Wall, Arrowslits and Citadels carrying the fortification theme, the frontier walls get no fifth passive (such as ‘Walls and Watch Tower-line +30% HP’, the Chinese Great Wall without the Bombard Towers, as the Japanese design's Genko Borui has it).

As Keep: the great Sasanian barrier walls against the northern nomads (Gorgan, Tammisha, Derbent).
As Keep: the great Sasanian barrier walls against the northern nomads (Gorgan, Tammisha, Derbent).
The analysis lists it with Keep and Fortified Wall: the towers of the Derbent walls and the forts of the Gorgan wall were garrisoned firing points of an archer army.

Apostasy from Zoroastrianism was a capital crime in Sasanian law: Mihr-Mah-Gushnasp, a noble baptised as Giwargis, was executed under Khosrow II in 615 (Babai the Great, Life of Giwargis); the charge was pressed during a quarrel between Christian factions at court (Payne, 2015). Its absence was ironic.

The region's one reading of the tech (the Arabs, Persians, Turks, Berbers, Malians and Ethiopians; see the Arabs' design): no treadwheel crane is attested in medieval Iran in the sources used here, so the tech is a generic abstraction of faster building, as in the Hindustani, Tamil and Bengali designs, added where large building programmes raised in stone or fired brick are a documented trait (here and for the Arabs; kept where the game gives it, for the Turks and Berbers and, as a flagged abstraction, for the Malians; not added for the Ethiopians). Iran's are among the largest of the window: the Seljuk domes of the Friday Mosque of Isfahan (1086–1089), the dome of Öljeitü's mausoleum at Sultaniyya (1302–1312) and Timur's Samarkand, and perhaps the vault of the Taq Kasra at Ctesiphon, attributed to Khosrow I, though some date it to Shapur I, before the window.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Obuch (Infantry). Late-medieval Polish cavalry fought in banners (chorągwie) made up of ‘lances’ (kopie): an armoured knight with his retainers. Registers of the royal court banner distinguish heavily armed riders in kopijnik armour (zbroja kopijnicza, arma plena) from medium ‘shooters’ and light horse; in the register drawn up after the Moldavian campaign of 1497 only about 13% of 288 riders had kopijnik armour (Kałużny 2019; 2023), and Jan Ostroróg required a kopijnik to have full armour (cited in Kałużny 2023). At Grunwald (1410) Długosz lists about fifty Polish banners. The Monaspa profile (heavy cavalry that becomes stronger when other Kopijniks or Knight-line units are nearby) translates banner fighting. It takes the slot of the Obuch, a nobleman’s war hammer of the 16th–17th centuries above all, never an infantry type, so the Obuch is not kept as a second unique unit either. The Monaspa model is shared with the Georgians and the Castilians’ Freire (RULES 6.7).

Renamed from Elite Monaspa. Follows the unique unit (Monaspa → Kopijnik), for the Poles only; the Georgians keep the Monaspa.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Szlachta Privileges (Castle unique tech, same effect). The privilege of Košice (1374) freed the nobility from almost all taxes and bound the king to pay compensation for service beyond the borders; Czerwińsk (1422) and Jedlnia–Kraków (1430/1433) protected noble property and person; and in 1454 the nobles mustered for the Thirteen Years’ War extorted the privileges of Cerekwica and Nieszawa, by which no levy could be called without the land assemblies (Davies 1981). The Buda privilege of 1355, granted for the Angevin succession, prefigured Košice (Knoll 1972). In exchange the nobles owed mounted service at their own expense within the realm in the general levy (pospolite ruszenie), mustered for Grunwald (1410) and for the Thirteen Years’ War. The levy belongs to this tech, not to a tech of its own: it was a standing obligation (RULES 6.2) and the other side of the same bargain (RULES 6.3). Cheaper knights translate the bargain; the tech moves to the Town Center because the privileges were the constitution of the noble state.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Lechitic Legacy (Scout Cavalry-line deals trample damage). The noble levy was beaten at Chojnice (1454), and in the Thirteen Years’ War (1454–66) the crown turned to hired companies (roty) of horse and foot, Polish, Silesian, Moravian and Czech, raised by captains (rotmistrze) under contract and paid from taxes the nobles voted and from loans; in 1457 it even bought Marienburg from the Order’s own unpaid mercenaries, and a hired army under Piotr Dunin won at Świecino (1462), which turned the war (Długosz; Davies 1981). At sea the war was fought by the ships of Gdańsk and Elbląg (see the navy note under contested). By the 1490s a small standing force of hired horse (obrona potoczna) guarded the south-eastern border against the Tatars, while the levy failed again in the Bukovina forest (1497). Faster Stables abstract the companies of horse that a paying crown could raise. Chosen for the Castle over the Union of Krewo (1385), an alliance and so team-bonus material (RULES 6.2), and over the general levy as a tech of its own, which is the other side of Szlachta Privileges (RULES 6.3). Lechitic Legacy is dropped: Kadłubek already called the Poles ‘Lechitae’, but nothing links that name to trampling light cavalry.

Under RULES 6.16.4 the Thumb Ring is given where the thumb draw is attested for a civ’s own archers or for an archery tradition its armies demonstrably used (the steppe, Islamic and East Asian traditions); civs whose archers used the European draw, or whose missile troops were crossbowmen, do not get it. Poland does not: its archers used the European draw and its missile troops the crossbow.

Western-style armoured knights (Zawisza the Black of Garbów) formed the core of the Polish army at Grunwald. For a cavalry civilization, lacking the last cavalry armour upgrade (held by 36 of the game’s 56 civs) was the most significant gap in the tree, while the Lithuanians had it.

Guns are recorded in Poland from 1383 and the first handgun in 1410, at Kraków (Grabarczyk 2021), and in the 15th century towns such as Kraków kept hook guns (hakownice) in their arsenals. In 1433 the Hussite Orphans fought beside the Polish army against the Order, and in the Thirteen Years’ War (1454–66) the crown hired foot, many of them Czech, who fought with wagons and some handguns (Świecino, 1462). Crossbows still prevailed among the hired foot, and the handgun’s breakthrough among them came only in the 1490s: under 1% of the hired foot of the 1470s had firearms, against 27% of the shooters in the lists of 1496 and most of them by 1500 (Grabarczyk 2000, on the armament of the hired companies; 2021), so the generic Imperial Age Hand Cannoneer, not an earlier one, fits. The Poles already had the Bombard Cannon.
Casimir III’s building programme and the brick Gothic of Kraków, Toruń and Gdańsk, the last two under the Polish crown from 1454 (confirmed in 1466).

Light horsemen equipped ‘in the Rascian or Tatar manner’ already served in the royal court banner in the second half of the 15th century (Kałużny 2023), and hussar banners of Rascian (Serbian) horse appear by name in the crown’s pay registers from c. 1500–03; they stayed light cavalry until the reign of Stephen Báthory (1576–86). The type originated inside the time frame, so it is not a late element under RULES section 2. Added to replace the light cavalry upgrade the Winged Hussar used to provide.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Organ Gun. The municipal crossbowmen of the quotas (contos): each concelho had to keep a fixed number of enrolled crossbowmen, mostly artisans, who trained, mustered under an anadel-mor and enjoyed privileges in return (Monteiro, 1998); they fought at Atoleiros (1384) and Aljubarrota (1385) (Fernão Lopes). The Genoese Crossbowman, strong against cavalry, is the closest existing unit; it is shared with the Italians and renamed (owner's decision). Since the Italians' team bonus also gives the Genoese Crossbowman to their allies, a Portuguese–Italian team fields the same unit under two names, which the design accepts (level-1 review decision; RULES 6.16.12). The Scenario Editor's Heavy Crossbowman (RULES section 5), a foot crossbowman with high attack and range (base 10 attack and range 6 in the extracted game data, codex/tools/scenario-units-stats.md), would avoid the double and suit the N2 idea of a hard-hitting besteiro, but it has no anti-cavalry role, its play is untested, and the owner chose the Genoese model, so it is not adopted. The Organ Gun it replaces was the pan-European ribaudequin (England 1339, Flanders 1382, Burgundy, Italy), with no Portuguese speciality.
