Renamed from Elite Genoese Crossbowman. Follows the unique unit (Genoese Crossbowman → Besteiro do Conto), for the Portuguese only; the Italians keep the Genoese Crossbowman.

Kept from the game (level 1). The lateen caravel was refined in Portugal through the 15th century and carried the Guinea voyages and Bartolomeu Dias (1487–1488); it also served as an armed patrol ship in the Strait and off Morocco (Diffie and Winius, 1977). It was mainly a light exploration ship; the armed 'caravela redonda' is the closest war version.

Kept from the game (level 1). The lateen caravel was refined in Portugal through the 15th century and carried the Guinea voyages and Bartolomeu Dias (1487–1488); it also served as an armed patrol ship in the Strait and off Morocco (Diffie and Winius, 1977). It was mainly a light exploration ship; the armed 'caravela redonda' is the closest war version.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Arquebus. Nuno Álvares Pereira's defensive battles of the crisis of 1383–1385: at Atoleiros (6 April 1384) his men fought on foot and broke a larger Castilian cavalry force; at Aljubarrota (14 August 1385) the Portuguese and their English allies held a chosen position, with dismounted men-at-arms in the centre and crossbowmen and archers on the wings, strengthened with ditches, pits and abatis, and defeated the Franco-Castilian army; Valverde (October 1385) followed (Fernão Lopes; Monteiro, 2003 and 2009). The tech stands for this defensive system, usually linked to English practice, which Portugal could have known through the alliance of 1373 and the Earl of Cambridge's expedition (1381–1382), and which English archers joined at Aljubarrota (see contested): armour for infantry and foot archers abstracts a prepared position, whether it was attacked on horse or on foot. The Arquebus tech it replaces had no Portuguese specificity: the arquebus was a German and Burgundian weapon that Portugal spread rather than developed.

New in the codex (level 2). King Fernando I's law of 1375, issued when the Black Death had left land untilled, obliged owners to cultivate their land or have it cultivated, on pain of losing it to others, and put the idle to work in the fields (Rau, 1946; Oliveira Marques, 1972). Owner's decision, as in the agreed example (RULES section 8).

New in the codex (level 2). At King Dinis' request, Pope John XXII founded the Order of Christ by the bull of 14 March 1319 and gave it the Portuguese property of the suppressed Templars, with its seat at Castro Marim and later Tomar. Prince Henry governed the order from 1420 and used its revenues for the Atlantic and African voyages; in 1456 the papacy gave it spiritual jurisdiction over the new lands, and its red cross was carried on the sails (Russell, 2000; Disney, 2009). The relic-driven attack is an abstraction, not a documented practice: it stands for the crusading frame the papacy gave the African enterprise and the order, the indulgences of Dum diversas (1452) and Romanus pontifex (1455) and the order's spiritual jurisdiction (1456). Owner's decision, as is its scope: the relic attack goes to the Galley-line only, at most +2 (level-1 review, section 3.1; owner's decision of section 9). The Galley-line stands here for the royal war fleet as a whole: the galleys of the admiralty that Manuel Pessanha held from 1317, the galleys and ships of the Ceuta armada (1415) and the armed ships that held the Strait and the Moroccan coast afterwards. The Caravel, which also patrolled the Strait (see the unit), the fire ships and the other warship lines are left out by the magnitude ceiling, not because history excludes them: at +4 on every warship the tech would have doubled or tripled the attack of the light ships (Caravel 4 to 8, Fire Galley 2 to 6, firing every 0.25 s) from the Castle Age and stacked with the ship-HP passive, Volta do Mar and the team's faster ships.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Circumnavigation. The Portuguese way home from Guinea: instead of beating against the trade winds along the African coast, ships stood out into the open Atlantic towards the Azores to pick up the westerlies, a route worked out on the West African voyages of the 15th century. Its South Atlantic form opened the Cape route: Dias was carried out to sea round the Cape (1487–1488), and Gama made the first deliberate great arc through the South Atlantic (1497), helped by solar tables and the astrolabe (Diffie and Winius, 1977). The faster ship production is mechanical, loosely the royal shipyard of Lisbon (the Ribeira das Naus) that fitted out the yearly India fleets from 1500. Circumnavigation honoured the Castilian expedition of Magellan and Elcano (1519–1522), which Portugal tried to stop.

The Thumb Ring is given where the thumb draw is attested for a civ's own archers or for an archery tradition its armies demonstrably used (the steppe, Islamic and East Asian traditions); civs whose archers used the European draw, or whose missile troops were crossbowmen, do not get it. Portugal does not: its archers used the European draw and its missile troops the crossbow (see the Besteiro do Conto) (RULES 6.16.4).

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ. The Portuguese keep the fleet-of-ships tier (RULES 6.16.1): the royal war galleys of the 14th century, the caravels and the gun-armed naus of the India fleets (Diffie and Winius, 1977), with the Galleon as the skeleton's flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2).

Portugal kept a dense network of frontier castles, rebuilt under D. Dinis (1279–1325) and his successors with tall keeps, machicolations and loopholes (Monteiro, 1999). Owner's decision in the agreed example.
Same castle network: wooden and later stone galleries on the walls of the castles of D. Dinis and his successors (Monteiro, 1999). Owner's decision in the agreed example.

Riding à gineta (short stirrups, light lance, javelins and leather adarga), taken from the Zenata and Granadan horsemen, was one of the two riding styles of Portuguese cavalry: King Duarte's Livro da Ensinança de Bem Cavalgar Toda Sela (c. 1434–1438) teaches both à brida and à gineta. Ginetes were central to the raiding war around the Moroccan strongholds (Ceuta from 1415, Alcácer Ceguer from 1458, Arzila and Tangier from 1471), which Zurara's chronicles of the Meneses (Ceuta and Alcácer Ceguer, to 1464) and Rui de Pina's chronicle of Afonso V narrate (Ricard, 1955). The ginete's main weapon was the short lance, with javelins secondary; the Genitour, a javelin horseman that cannot fight at close range, is the closest existing unit. A regional unit (owner's decision; RULES 6.16.10) that does not count as a unique unit (RULES 6.1), trained at the Archery Range from the Castle Age as for the Berbers' allies, and renamed Ginete.

Renamed from Genitour. Ginete is the Portuguese name (from Zenata) of the light horseman the Castilians call jinete: the same regional unit, named in each language. The rename meets RULES 6.16.15: the same function inside the window, a period term (à gineta in King Duarte's Livro da Ensinança), and 'genitour' is the English and French borrowing of the same word. The Berbers keep 'Genitour', and the Lithuanians, to whom RULES 6.16.10 extends the regional unit, name it in their own design.
The Elite upgrade of the Ginete (Archery Range), for the same light horsemen.
Renamed from Elite Genitour. Same rename for the Elite upgrade.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Mameluke. Mamluks were slave soldiers bought young and trained as the elite of the Ayyubid and Mamluk armies; al-Salih Ayyub's Bahriyya (1240s) and the early Mamluk sultans' troops were mostly Kipchak Turks from the steppe (from 1382 mostly Circassians). They stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) and Homs (1281) and took Acre (1291), fighting above all as horse archers trained to shoot rapidly in volleys (Ayalon; Amitai-Preiss, 1995; Latham and Paterson, 1970). The Cuman Kipchak, a horse archer who looses several arrows at once, is the same people and the nearest existing unit; the game's camel-riding Mameluke with a thrown scimitar had the depiction wrong (analysis: ‘wrong’). The unit takes the spelling of modern scholarship, ‘Mamluk’, not the game's ‘Mameluke’.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Mameluke. Mamluks were slave soldiers bought young and trained as the elite of the Ayyubid and Mamluk armies; al-Salih Ayyub's Bahriyya (1240s) and the early Mamluk sultans' troops were mostly Kipchak Turks from the steppe (from 1382 mostly Circassians). They stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) and Homs (1281) and took Acre (1291), fighting above all as horse archers trained to shoot rapidly in volleys (Ayalon; Amitai-Preiss, 1995; Latham and Paterson, 1970). The Cuman Kipchak, a horse archer who looses several arrows at once, is the same people and the nearest existing unit; the game's camel-riding Mameluke with a thrown scimitar had the depiction wrong (analysis: ‘wrong’). The unit takes the spelling of modern scholarship, ‘Mamluk’, not the game's ‘Mameluke’.
Renamed from Elite Kipchak. Follows the unique unit (Kipchak → Mamluk) for the Arabs only.

Kept from the game (level 1). Murda al-Tarsusi's treatise for Saladin (c. 1187) contains one of the earliest clear descriptions of counterweight trebuchets, and the Mamluks massed them against the Crusader fortresses, above all Acre (1291). The technique also travelled east: Muslim engineers sent by the Ilkhan Abaqa built such engines for Kublai at Xiangyang (1273), where they were called huihui pao, ‘Muslim trebuchets’ (a secondary illustration, also used in the Mongols' design).

New in the codex (level 2). Abd al-Malik (685–705) gave the caliphate its own money and its own language of government. In 696/697 (AH 77) his mint struck the first purely epigraphic gold dinars, with the profession of faith in place of the Byzantine and caliphal images and a lighter weight standard (the mithqal of about 4.25 g), followed by reformed silver dirhams (AH 78–79); in the same years the registers of the treasury (diwan) were turned into Arabic, in Iraq from Persian on al-Hajjaj's orders (697) and in Syria from Greek under Sulayman ibn Sa'd (700) (al-Baladhuri; Robinson, 2005; Bacharach, 2010). Arab coin and Arab clerks replaced the Byzantine and Sasanian systems the conquerors had inherited, and the dinar became the gold coin of the Islamic world. Gold income that comes in faster translates a state that collected and paid in its own coin. The tech gives the early caliphate (632 to c. 1050), otherwise carried by passives and the team bonus, a datable moment of its own.

Changed by the codex (level 1). The bimaristan (Persian bimar ‘sick’ + stan ‘place’) was the great Islamic hospital: Dols (1987) places the first in Baghdad in the early 9th century, where al-Razi later practised; Nur al-Din's in Damascus (1154) and Qalawun's al-Mansuri in Cairo (1284–1285) followed with specialised wards and medical teaching. They were pious foundations endowed as waqf and often joined to a mosque or madrasa: the al-Mansuri hospital stood in one complex with Qalawun's madrasa and mausoleum. As a charitable religious foundation whose effect works through Monks, the tech sits at the Monastery (RULES 6.2).

The Mamluks used cannon in sieges from the 1360s (the Bombard Cannon stays), but their cavalry elite refused hand firearms: a corps of black slaves armed with arquebuses under al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qaytbay was attacked by the royal mamluks and broken up (1498), and the arquebusier corps raised under al-Ghawri (c. 1510) stayed small, low-status and outside the mamluk elite (Ayalon, 1956). Tumanbay still had guns and arquebusiers at Raydaniyya (1517), so the removal models the elite's refusal, not a lack of handguns (see contested). It also sets the Arabs apart from the Turks.

The navy is a fleet of ships (RULES 6.16.1): the planked war galleys (shini, shalandi) and fire ships (harraqa) built in the caliphal arsenals keep the generic tiers, the Galleon as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2), except the Fast Fire Ship, which the game's Saracens lack and which is not added, for the power budget (see dropped). Siphons and Incendiaries stay, as in the game, unlike in the Persians', Turks' and Berbers' designs, whose removal rests on the Byzantine fire siphon: the harraqa carried naphtha throwers (naffatun) in the caliphal, Fatimid and Ayyubid fleets (Picard, 2015), so a ship-borne fire weapon is documented for this civ, although whether the naphtha was projected through tubes like the Byzantine siphon or thrown in pots is uncertain. The Cannon Galleon needs gun-armed warships inside the window, and gun-armed Mamluk warships are attested only for the Red Sea fleets of the sultanate's last years (from 1505: Chaul 1508, Diu 1509). It would be a post-1500 element whose fame is that of the Portuguese victory at Diu, while the Mamluks are known for their reluctance to adopt firearms (Ayalon 1956), so it fails the clear-fame test of RULES section 2. Without it the civ has no siege warship, as the navy rule allows.
As Cannon Galleon.

Heavy mail-clad cavalry with lance and sword, sometimes on armoured horses (tijfaf), was the core of Ayyubid and Mamluk armies and an important arm of the Fatimids, whose armies also relied on Kutama Berber cavalry, black infantry ('abid) and Turkish and Armenian contingents (Yaacov Lev, State and Society in Fatimid Egypt, 1991). Stopping at the Knight contradicted the civ's best-documented military identity. The Paladin stays out.
Renamed Dar al-Sina'a (see the rename): the state arsenals of Tunis (c. 698), Alexandria and Rawda island at Fustat built the caliphal fleets. Its absence was ironic in a naval civ.

Renamed from Shipwright. Dār al-ṣināʿa, ‘house of manufacture’, the state naval arsenal (Tunis, Alexandria, Rawda); through Venetian it gave European languages the word ‘arsenal’. The function (a state shipyard that builds ships faster and cheaper) is a real equivalent inside the window, the name is the period term, and the effect is identical (RULES 6.16.15).

Monumental building from the Dome of the Rock (691/692) and the Great Mosque of Damascus (705–715) to Samarra (836–892), al-Azhar (970–972) and Mamluk Cairo (Sultan Hasan, 1356–1363), and military works such as Saladin's Citadel of Cairo (from 1176).

One reading for the region (the Arabs, Persians, Turks, Berbers, Malians and Ethiopians). Lifting machines were known in the Islamic world: Hero of Alexandria's Mechanics, whose third book describes cranes and other devices for raising heavy loads, survives complete only in the Arabic translation by Qusta ibn Luqa (9th century), and Ibn Khaldun counts the lifting of heavy weights by machines (jarr al-athqal) among the arts that builders need (Muqaddimah, ch. V, on building). The treadwheel crane itself is not attested at medieval Islamic building sites in the sources used here (the device is Roman, and in medieval Europe it is attested again from c. 1225; A. L. Matthies, ‘Medieval Treadwheels’, Technology and Culture 33, 1992). So the tech is a generic abstraction of faster building, as in the Hindustani, Tamil and Bengali designs. The reading governs additions: the tech is added only where large building programmes raised in stone or fired brick are a documented trait of the civ, here and for the Persians, and not for the Ethiopians, who lack it in the game and whose core left few raised monuments. Where the game already gives it, it stays, as in the other codex designs whose civs built without cranes (the Maya, Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi designs flag it as an abstraction, and the Inca design renames it Mit'a): for the Turks and Berbers on their stone building, and for the Malians as a flagged abstraction of earthen (banco) building raised by hand. Here it rests on the caliphal and sultanic building listed under Architecture, from Umayyad Jerusalem and Damascus and Abbasid Samarra, a new capital raised within a few decades, to Mamluk Cairo.

Kept from the game (level 1). Old English heorðwerod, the lord’s household troop (The Battle of Maldon, l. 24, where Byrhtnoth’s retinue dies with him in 991; Beowulf’s word for Hygelac’s men is heorðgeneatas, l. 261). It stands for the spear-and-javelin retinues of the 10th-century lords, while the Housecarl (the renamed Varangian Guard) is the axe-armed guard of the Anglo-Danish kings (1016–1066). Throwing before melee is attested: Maldon mentions darts, and William of Poitiers describes the English at Hastings throwing spears, axes and stones.

Kept from the game (level 1). Old English heorðwerod, the lord’s household troop (The Battle of Maldon, l. 24, where Byrhtnoth’s retinue dies with him in 991; Beowulf’s word for Hygelac’s men is heorðgeneatas, l. 261). It stands for the spear-and-javelin retinues of the 10th-century lords, while the Housecarl (the renamed Varangian Guard) is the axe-armed guard of the Anglo-Danish kings (1016–1066). New in the codex (level 1). In 893 Alfred divided his levy so that half its men were always at home and half on service, apart from the men who held the burhs (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 893). Service was owed by land: Domesday’s Berkshire custom (1086) sent one man from every five hides, who received four shillings from each hide for his food or pay for two months (Abels 1988). The effect renders a levy kept by the land that owed it rather than paid from the king’s purse. A datable military reform, so at the Castle (RULES 6.2); it takes the slot the shield wall, a long tradition, held in the game. Imperial Age, the game age of Forced Levy (RULES 6.16.11); Edgar's Recoinage and Clerical Recruitment, later in date, are Castle Age techs at other buildings, which the chronological rule allows, since it binds only two Castle techs (RULES 6.16.19(a)).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Clerical Recruitment (Castle unique tech, same effect). Based on the Church at home, since the continental missions are the team bonus: the conversion of the Danish settlers (Guthrum baptised in 878 with Alfred as his sponsor; Oda, son of a Danish settler, archbishop of Canterbury 941–958) and the 10th-century Benedictine reform of Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald, which refounded dozens of monasteries and was codified in the Regularis Concordia (c. 973). Conversion range renders the conversion of the Danelaw, faster training the refounded houses. At the Monastery, where religion belongs (RULES 6.2).

New in the codex (level 1). Æthelstan’s Grately code (c. 926–930) decreed one coinage throughout the king’s realm and minting only in a market town, and Edgar’s reform (c. 973) gave the kingdom a single silver penny of one type, struck in dozens of burh mints and periodically called in and reissued with new types; the system let the late Anglo-Saxon kings raise the great gelds of 991–1018 (Dolley and Metcalf 1961; Molyneaux 2015). Gold income renders the gelds and the profits of the mints, the lower trading fee a single trusted coin in the burh markets. A state reform, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2).

The counterweight trebuchet appears only in the later 12th century, a century after the end of the civ. No Anglo-Saxon siege engine of any kind is attested either, so the traction test gives no Traction Trebuchet (RULES 6.16.5): English siege warfare was blockade, assault and counter-fortification (Alfred’s two forts on the Lea, 895; Edward’s burhs on both banks at Buckingham, 914; the storming of Tempsford and Derby, 917; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). The rams, Mangonel, Onager and Scorpions stay only as the engine’s minimum abstraction of siege warfare (RULES 6.11, 6.14), not as evidence of Anglo-Saxon engines. The civ has no long-range anti-building weapon, as RULES 6.16.5 allows where none is attested, and relies on the Siege Ram, which it keeps; no other compensation is added for the items the tree loses, mostly later than 1066 (RULES 6.16.13).

The crossbow was practically unknown in Anglo-Saxon England; at Hastings the crossbowmen were on the Norman side (William of Poitiers). The Crossbowman tier is kept as the generic ranged upgrade (RULES 6.16.3).

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. Here it is anachronistic and foreign to an army that rode to battle and fought on foot (Maldon, 991; Hereford, 1055; Hastings, 1066).
Same reason as the Mounted Crossbowman.
A 15th-century continental crossbow fitting.

The English did not fight as heavy cavalry: in 1055 near Hereford they fled ‘because they were on horseback’ (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle), and John of Worcester adds that Earl Ralph had made them fight mounted against their custom. The Knight is kept, without upgrades, as the abstraction of thegns who rode to war.
Hungarian and Serbian light cavalry of the 15th century; Light Cavalry is kept for scouts and mounted thegns.
Horse-breeding upgrades belong to cavalry armies; the English rode to battle and fought on foot, so the mounted thegns keep the plain Knight and Light Cavalry.

No evidence of ship-borne catapults in North Sea warfare; Longships keep the role of attacking coasts and shore buildings. Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, resting on Alfred’s long ships of 896, Æthelred’s ship levy of 1008 and Harold II’s fleet of 1066. The Carrack, a 14th–15th-century type, stays as a generic tier of a fleet of ships (RULES 6.16.1) and the Galleon as a flagged post-1500 abstraction (RULES 6.16.2); both are anachronistic for this civ and flagged as abstractions. The civ has no Cannon Galleon.

Castles and their great towers were the Norman novelty (Orderic Vitalis); the burh was a communal earthwork held by its garrison. The Watch Tower and Guard Tower stay as the abstraction of the burh gate tower (burh-geat), which an early 11th-century text on ranks (Geþyncðo) counts among the marks of a thegn.

Castles and their great towers were the Norman novelty (Orderic Vitalis); the burh was a communal earthwork held by its garrison. The Watch Tower and Guard Tower stay as the abstraction of the burh gate tower (burh-geat), which an early 11th-century text on ranks (Geþyncðo) counts among the marks of a thegn.
Archery from towers belongs to the stone castles of the Normans and later; archery was marginal in Anglo-Saxon warfare, and the old tower-arrow bonus is dropped for the same reason.
The timber galleries of 12th–13th-century stone castles; the civ has no castles in that sense (Orderic Vitalis).
The thumb draw belongs to the steppe and Asian archery traditions, and Anglo-Saxon archery was marginal and European (RULES 6.16.4). The English design, the codex’s archer civ, also lacks the tech.

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, the projector of Greek fire, a state secret never to be given to another nation (De Administrando Imperio 13); its game effect, an explosive charge for fire ships, has no Anglo-Saxon equivalent. The Fire Galley and Fire Ship stay as the engine’s convention for close-range incendiary warships.

European block printing dates only from c. 1400, centuries after the civ ends; Anglo-Saxon book culture was manuscript copying (the Lindisfarne Gospels, the scriptoria of the Benedictine reform). The Gaels’ design also leaves the tech out, since the Gaelic world printed nothing before 1567.
The Sutton Hoo ship (c. 625) is the classic clinker-built hull; in the game the Saxons were the only civ without this tech.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no Anglo-Saxon siege engine of any kind is attested (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice.

Renamed from Varangian Guard. The housecarls (Old Norse húskarlar) were the household troops of Cnut and his successors, from 1016 to Harold II’s guard at Hastings (1066), armed with the two-handed Dane axe that the Bayeux Tapestry shows (Hooper 1985); whether they were paid from the heregeld (levied 1012–1051) or rewarded with land is debated (see contested). The rename keeps the model inside the civ’s window; the Danes rename the same model the same way, and the Varangian Guard itself stays Byzantine (RULES section 4; a renamed regional unit, which does not count as a unique unit, RULES 6.16.10).
Renamed from Elite Varangian Guard. Same as the Varangian Guard rename.

Kept from the game (level 1). Servientes, non-noble soldiers on foot or on horseback, are counted beside the milites in the kingdom's register of military service (the Catalogus Baronum, c. 1150–1168); building Donjons is an abstraction of their garrison role.

Kept from the game (level 1). Servientes, non-noble soldiers on foot or on horseback, are counted beside the milites in the kingdom's register of military service (the Catalogus Baronum, c. 1150–1168); building Donjons is an abstraction of their garrison role.

Kept from the game (level 1). Servientes, non-noble soldiers on foot or on horseback, are counted beside the milites in the kingdom's register of military service (the Catalogus Baronum, c. 1150–1168); building Donjons is an abstraction of their garrison role.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces First Crusade. Roger II's government recorded the service that each fief of the mainland provinces of Apulia and Capua owed to the general levy, the 'great expedition' (Quaternus magne expeditionis, c. 1150–1151, revised under William II in 1167–1168, preserved in the 14th-century compilation known as the Catalogus Baronum): for every fief, the knights and serjeants (servientes) it had to send (Jamison, 1972; Cuozzo, 1984). Town Centers that raise Serjeants stand for this levy of the kingdom's lordships; resistance to conversion, for the crown's control of the Church through the apostolic legation that Urban II granted Roger I in 1098 (Houben, 2002). The effect is First Crusade's, whose name inverted history: Count Roger I's Sicily stayed out of the crusade, and when Bohemond's men took the cross at the siege of Amalfi (1096) Roger saw his army melt away and went home (Malaterra).

New in the codex (level 2). Roger II's kingdom was governed through a royal diwan on Fatimid lines, staffed by Arabic- and Greek-writing officials: from the 1140s its offices kept Arabic registers of the villeins attached to each estate (jarāʾid) and of estate boundaries, confirmed grants and collected the king's revenues, and the royal administration issued documents in Arabic, Greek and Latin (Johns, 2002; Takayama, 1993). Ibn Jubayr (1184–1185) still found Muslim officials and pages in William II's palace. A Town Center that works faster abstracts a government that knew its lands and men; no other Latin kingdom had an Arabic-language administration. The tech structure follows RULES 6.2 (level-1 review decision): Magna Expeditio, a royal levy of feudal service, keeps First Crusade's place at the Castle, and the diwan takes the Town Center, rather than the Assizes of Ariano (conventionally 1140) or al-Idrisi's Tabula Rogeriana (1154); with it the civ has 6 passive bonuses and 3 unique techs, the cap of 9 (RULES 6.1).

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Hauberk (Knight-line +1 melee/+2 pierce armor): dropped for relevance (RULES 6.9), since the long mail shirt was standard for all Western cavalry, a detail with no Sicilian specificity. Muslim troops served the Hauteville from the conquest onwards (Malaterra; Metcalfe, 2009). During the long revolt of the Muslims of western Sicily (from 1189–1190 to c. 1246), Frederick II deported them in large numbers to Lucera in Apulia, from c. 1224; the colony's lightly armed archers were a loyal royal corps at Cortenuova (1237) and Benevento (1266) until Lucera was destroyed in 1300 (Taylor, 2003).

No gunpowder in the window: the earliest European records of cannon date from 1326, sixty years after Benevento (1266), and the civ already lacks Bombard Cannon and Hand Cannoneer. Under RULES 6.11 the anti-ship role at sea stays with the Galley and Fire Ship lines and the anti-building role with the single-use Heavy Demolition Ship, and on land with the Trebuchet; no substitute siege warship is added (RULES 6.16.1).

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. No mounted crossbowmen are documented in the kingdom before 1266 in the sources checked for this design: the kingdom's crossbowmen (Frederick II's balistarii) are evidence for the crossbow, not for crossbowmen on horseback, and the generic Crossbowman carries them (RULES 6.16.3); the tech tree audit justified mounted crossbowmen for the Sicilians by the Angevin and Aragonese kingdom, after the window. Removed; nothing the civ needs to play is lost (RULES 6.11): the foot Archer and crossbow lines, with the Lucera tech, keep the missile role, the Light Cavalry and the Cavalier the mounted one.
Same reason as the Mounted Crossbowman, and later still (14th–15th centuries).

The cranequin, a rack-and-pinion winder for heavy crossbows, belongs to the late 14th and 15th centuries, after the window (1266) (names theme of the analysis); RULES 6.10 forbids renaming it to hide the anachronism, and no 13th-century equivalent is attested in the kingdom. The mounted crossbow line it improves also leaves the tree (see the Mounted Crossbowman), and the civ does not need it to play (RULES 6.11).

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ. The Sicilians keep the fleet-of-ships tier (RULES 6.16.1): the galley fleets of Christodulus, George of Antioch and Margaritus of Brindisi (Stanton, 2011), with the Galleon, a 16th-century type, as the skeleton's flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2).

Given for an archery tradition the kingdom's armies demonstrably used, the Islamic one, rather than for an attested draw of their own: Muslim troops served the Hauteville from the conquest onwards, and the Muslim archers of Lucera were a royal corps under Frederick II and Manfred. The Islamic tradition drew with the thumb, as its Arabic manuals teach, from Taybugha's Mamluk manual (c. 1368; Latham and Paterson, Saracen Archery, 1970) to an anonymous manual of c. 1500 thought to be North African (Faris and Elmer, Arab Archery, 1945); that the archers of Sicily and Lucera drew the same way is an inference from that tradition, since no source specific to them describes their draw (RULES 6.16.4). It supports the Lucera tech.

The kingdom was a great builder: Cefalù cathedral (from 1131), the Palatine Chapel (consecrated 1140), La Zisa (begun c. 1164–1165) and Monreale (from 1174), which the civ's own history text praises; the lack of building techs contradicted it.

The treadwheel crane is first attested in medieval Europe c. 1225 (France) and first illustrated c. 1240 (A. L. Matthies, 'Medieval Treadwheels', Technology and Culture 33, 1992). No source documents it at Frederick II's building sites, but it fits their date rather than the 12th-century churches: Castello Maniace at Syracuse (c. 1232–1240), Castello Ursino at Catania (1239–1250) and Castel del Monte (c. 1240).

In 1098 Urban II granted Roger I the apostolic legation, the root of the 'Monarchia Sicula' through which the kings controlled the island's church, and the Martorana mosaic shows Roger II crowned by Christ (Houben, 2002). The name fits; the effect is the generic one.

The towns of the kingdom were walled (Palermo, Bari, Salerno), and Frederick II's castles enclose their courtyards with stone curtain walls and corner towers (Castello Maniace, Castello Ursino). The Donjon replaces only the tower line, so the stone walls of a civ of castle-builders should reach the generic top tier.

The towns of the kingdom were walled (Palermo, Bari, Salerno), and Frederick II's castles enclose their courtyards with stone curtain walls and corner towers (Castello Maniace, Castello Ursino). The Donjon replaces only the tower line, so the stone walls of a civ of castle-builders should reach the generic top tier.

Kept from the game (level 1). The boyars were the landed aristocracy and the senior members of the prince's retinue (druzhina), fighting as armoured horsemen in Kiev, Novgorod and Galicia alike; turning a social class into a unit is an abstraction, but its heavy armour is well founded (Kirpichnikov). The model is shared only with the Lithuanians, whose Boyar renders the Ruthenian boyars of the Grand Duchy, the same class under a new ruler (RULES 6.7); the Rus' Boyar is set apart by Druzhina, which gives it trample.

Kept from the game (level 1). The boyars were the landed aristocracy and the senior members of the prince's retinue (druzhina), fighting as armoured horsemen in Kiev, Novgorod and Galicia alike; turning a social class into a unit is an abstraction, but its heavy armour is well founded (Kirpichnikov). The model is shared only with the Lithuanians, whose Boyar renders the Ruthenian boyars of the Grand Duchy, the same class under a new ruler (RULES 6.7); the Rus' Boyar is set apart by Druzhina, which gives it trample.

Changed by the codex (level 2); replaces Druzhina (Infantry deals trample damage). The druzhina was the prince's retinue, the core of every Rus' army from the 10th century to the 13th. Vladimir valued it above treasure: when his men complained of eating with wooden spoons he had silver ones made, saying that silver and gold would not find him a druzhina, but with a druzhina he would find silver and gold, as his father and grandfather had (Primary Chronicle s.a. 996). From the 11th century it fought as armoured horsemen: Rus' finds combine mail with lamellar plates, taken from Byzantine and steppe models, and tall spheroconical helmets, some with face masks (Kirpichnikov, Drevnerusskoe oruzhie, vol. 3, 1971); 10th-century chamber graves already hold horses and riding gear. Its battle was the lance charge, the emblem of the warrior in the Tale of Igor's Campaign, where Igor wishes ‘to break a lance at the end of the Polovtsian field’. Trample renders that shock charge, for the retinue (Knight line) and its senior boyars (Boyar); the 10th-century foot phase is left to the generic infantry, and the trample itself is a game abstraction. Royal and military, so at the Castle (RULES 6.2).

New in the codex (level 1). Ivan I of Moscow (1325–1340), called Kalita, ‘money-bag’, became grand prince of Vladimir in 1328, sharing the title with Alexander of Suzdal until 1331, after helping the Horde crush the rising at Tver (1327). As grand prince he answered for the Horde's tribute (vykhod) from the principalities of north-eastern Rus'. The tribute was a levy on the people of the land, most of them farmers: in 1257 the census-takers counted the land of Suzdal, Ryazan and Murom and set up tens, hundreds, thousands and tümens (Laurentian Chronicle), and in Novgorod in 1259 they rode through the streets writing down the houses (Novgorod First Chronicle); the khans' patents to the Church name a plough tax among the levies they spared, and the plough (sokha) became the unit by which Novgorod assessed its black tribute (chernyi bor) and Muscovy its taxes. The grand prince apportioned the sum among the principalities and collected it in silver. Ivan pressed the other lands for their share, as in 1332, when he took Torzhok and Bezhetsky Verkh to force Novgorod to hand over its ‘silver from beyond the Kama’ (Novgorod First Chronicle); in 1384 a great tribute was raised across the grand principality at half a ruble from every village (Simeonov Chronicle); and his grandson Dmitry's testament (1389) divides each thousand rubles of the vykhod among the appanages, each son to keep the tribute of his own lands if God should change the Horde. Moscow profited from what passed through its prince's hands: it grew rich, bought up villages and, by tradition, whole principalities (the ‘purchases’ of Uglich, Beloozero and Galich named in the same testament), and drew the metropolitan of all Rus' to live there. Farmers who slowly generate gold render that levy: a farming population, counted by household and plough, paying silver that Moscow gathered for the khan. The silver itself was earned above all with the produce of the forest, furs first, then wax and honey (Martin 1986), which the hunting passive renders: the passive gives the source of the silver, the tech its collection. The Tatars' design renders the same tribute from the Horde's side with the same effect (Yarlyk, Castle Age): the khans imposed it from the census of the 1250s and Moscow collected it from 1328, hence the later age here. A state revenue, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2).

New in the codex (level 2). Effect revised on 18 October 2026 at the owner’s request: the earlier cheaper Monastery technologies only discounted one-time purchases. After his baptism Vladimir brought the relics of Pope Clement I and his disciple Phoebus from Korsun (Chersonesos) to Kiev and placed them in his Tithe Church (Primary Chronicle, 988–989); relics and icons from Byzantium made Kiev a holy city, which the Relic income renders. Vladimir took Christianity from Byzantium: his baptism, traditionally dated 988 and tied to the capture of Chersonesos (Korsun) and his marriage to the emperor's sister Anna, was followed by the baptism of the people of Kiev in the Dnieper, the building of the Church of the Tithes (consecrated 996), endowed with a tenth of his revenues, and the taking of children of the leading families to be taught book learning (Primary Chronicle s.a. 988–996). Rus' received a Church already formed: Greek bishops under a metropolitan of Kiev subject to Constantinople, the Byzantine liturgy and canon law, and the Slavonic books and clergy of Bulgaria, so that it had no need to create its own church language or institutions (Franklin and Shepard 1996). Cheaper Monastery technologies render institutions received ready-made. Religion, so at the Monastery (RULES 6.2).

New in the codex (level 2). Ivan III made gun-founding a work of the Muscovite state. Aristotele Fioravanti, the Bolognese engineer who came to Moscow in 1475 to build the Dormition Cathedral, also directed the guns on Ivan III's campaigns until his last mention (1485); older works credit him with founding gun-casting in Moscow on his arrival, which the sources used for this design do not confirm. A cannon house (pushechnaya izba) is first documented in Moscow in 1488, not in 1475 as older works held (O. G. Ulyanov 2015), the forerunner of the Cannon Yard (Pushechny dvor) where Andrey Chokhov cast the Tsar Cannon in 1586. The tech is named after the Cannon Yard that grew from the cannon house of 1488, as RULES section 2 allows for an element that originated inside the time frame and took its later name. Cheaper guns made faster render a state foundry that cast them in series. Gunpowder production at the building that makes the guns, so at the Siege Workshop (RULES 6.2).

Navy tier (RULES 6.16.1): the boat tier. Rus' fleets were fleets of boats, not of ships, from the monoxyla, dugout hulls that the Slavs cut in winter and the Rus' fitted out with oars and, for the sea, with masts, sails and rudders (De Administrando Imperio 9), in which the Rus' crossed the Black Sea against Constantinople in 860, 941 and 1043, to the ushkui of the Novgorodian river raiders in the 14th century. The boat tier keeps the generic Galley, Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines as the game gives them (without the Heavy Demolition Ship) as an abstraction for water maps, the ‘Galleon, Fast Fire Ship and Carrack’ upgrade staying for the Fast Fire Ship, and removes the high-seas sailing warships (Galleon, Carrack). The Scenario Editor's Canoe (RULES section 5), which several boat-tier designs use as the Galley's look, the Avars' among them for the Slav dugouts of 626, was weighed and not adopted: in the game it is a light boat (70 HP; codex/tools/scenario-units-stats.md), while the Rus' monoxyla, rigged for the sea, carried some forty men each by the Primary Chronicle's reckoning (s.a. 907), nearer in scale and role to the Galley, which keeps its look.
See Galleon.

The Rus' had no purpose-built warships and no gun-armed ships: their fleets were river-sea boats (monoxyla, lod'i), which nonetheless crossed the Black Sea against Constantinople in 860, 941 and 1043. The Cannon Galleon needs gun-armed warships inside the window (RULES 6.16.1).
Hungarian and Serbian light cavalry of the 15th century; Rus' light horsemen fought as mounted archers in the steppe manner, rendered by the Cavalry Archer, and Light Cavalry stays.

Dropped with the original ‘Infantry and Siege’ identity and its siege discount, whose top tier it was; the Mangonel and Onager stay as the generic light stone-thrower (RULES 6.16.5), and Muscovy's late siege power is represented by the Bombard Cannon. The Trebuchet stays on Rus' evidence: Rus' armies built stone-throwing engines (poroki), as when Novgorod had poroki made at the archbishop's court for the campaign against Rakvere (Novgorod First Chronicle s.a. 1268), and Kirpichnikov (Voennoe delo, 1976) traces their use through the 13th–14th centuries. The chronicles do not describe their mechanism, and porok is sometimes read as a ram (see the Tatars' design); the design reads the Rus' poroki of the counterweight era as heavy counterweight engines, a flagged inference (see contested), with the Traction Trebuchet as the fallback if they were man-powered (RULES 6.16.5, 6.11).

No printing in the window (to 1505): Moscow's first press worked anonymously from the 1550s, and the first dated Moscow book, Ivan Fedorov's Apostol, appeared in 1564. The same printing-date test keeps Block Printing for the Danes (Odense, 1482) and gives it to the Swedes (Stockholm, 1483).

The unit stands for the firearm infantry of late-15th-century Muscovy, inside the window: the tree follows the period the design represents (RULES 6.16.19(d)), and Muscovy's late 15th century is part of it. The chronicles say that on the Ugra (1480) the Muscovites drove back the Tatars with arrows and pishchali, and firearms had been in Rus' use since 1382 and spread through the 15th century (Kirpichnikov, Voennoe delo na Rusi v XIII–XV vv., 1976). The word pishchal' then also covered light guns, so the reading is flagged in the civ-level notes, with the late-element fallback.
Ivan III's Italian engineer Aristotele Fioravanti (in Moscow from 1475) directed his guns on campaign, and a cannon house in Moscow is first documented in 1488 (Ulyanov 2015); see Pushechny Dvor.
In 1382 the defenders of Moscow fired tyufyaki and pushki from the Kremlin walls against Tokhtamysh, the first firearms in Rus' hands that the chronicles name (see contested).
In 1382 the defenders of Moscow fired tyufyaki and pushki from the Kremlin walls against Tokhtamysh, the first firearms in Rus' hands that the chronicles name (see contested).

Given for the steppe archery tradition that Rus' armies demonstrably used (RULES 6.16.4); the draw of the Rus' archers themselves is not documented. Rus' bows and quivers followed steppe models; the Black Hoods, Turkic nomads settled on the Ros, served Kiev as frontier troops; and the Muscovite cavalry fought in the Tatar manner with bow and sabre (see the horse-archer bonus).

Rus' archery followed steppe models: Rus' bows and quivers are of steppe types (Medvedev 1966), the Black Hoods, Turkic nomads settled on the Ros, served Kiev as frontier horse archers, and the Muscovite cavalry fought in the Tatar manner with bow and sabre (Ostrowski 1998). The Bracer, the last archery upgrade, renders that tradition for the horse archers of the Cavalry Archer passive, as the Thumb Ring renders their draw; without it the passive's unit would also lack an upgrade most civs have.
Stone and brick building of the later window: the white-stone churches of Vladimir-Suzdal (12th century) and the brick Kremlin of Moscow (1485–1495), built by Italian architects.

Crossbows (samostrely) were secondary to the bow in field armies but a regular weapon in the defence of Rus' towns: crossbow bolts are common in 13th–14th-century finds (Medvedev 1966), and in the tale of Tokhtamysh's siege of Moscow (1382) the defenders shot crossbows from the walls, where the clothier Adam killed the son of a Horde prince with a crossbow bolt from the Frolov gate. The top tier suits a civ labelled defensive (RULES 6.16.3).

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Conquistador and Missionary (their unique-unit slots; both in [[dropped]]). The professed knights (freires caballeros) of the military orders of Calatrava (1158, under the Cistercian rule), Santiago (founded 1170, approved by the pope in 1175) and Alcántara (c. 1176 as San Julián del Pereiro, named Alcántara from 1218) garrisoned frontier castles and held lordships from La Mancha to Extremadura, and fought at Alarcos (1195), Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) and in the conquest of Andalusia (O'Callaghan, 1975; Lomax, 1965). The Monaspa, heavy cavalry that grows stronger beside other Monaspas or Knight-line units, abstracts a sworn brotherhood fighting beside the royal and noble knights; it is shared with the Georgians (and the Poles' Kopijnik) and renamed (owner's decision). The name 'Freire', the orders' own word for a professed brother (freires caballeros beside freires clérigos), is kept rather than 'Caballero de Calatrava' or 'Caballero de Santiago', which would single out one order (level-1 review decision). The orders keep the unique unit while the Castle tech goes to the caballería de cuantía: the freires were a distinct, professed troop that fought as a body under their masters, which a unit renders, and a tech for the orders as well would spend two high slots on one institution (RULES 6.3). The Scenario Editor's Crusader Knight (RULES section 5) is not used as the model, although its white mantle is close to the Cistercian habit of Calatrava and Alcántara: its black cross is the Teutonic Order's, while the Castilian orders bore red crosses (the sword-cross of Santiago; the cross fleury of Calatrava) or, at Alcántara, a green cross fleury; and the Monaspa's aura renders the brotherhood fighting beside the knights better than a lone heavy horseman would.

Renamed from Elite Monaspa. Follows the unique unit (Monaspa → Freire), for the Castilians only; the Georgians keep the Monaspa.

New in the codex (level 2). Alfonso XI tied the keeping of a war horse to wealth. After a reform of the crown's paid vassals and their soldadas at Burgos (1338), a precursor, the Cortes of Alcalá (1348) obliged householders whose property reached a set amount (cuantía), reckoned in maravedís, to keep a horse and arms and to show them at the musters (alardes) (Agrait, 2005; Pérez-Prendes, 1960; González Jiménez, 1985). The institution took root above all in Andalusia and Murcia, where the caballeros de cuantía, or cuantiosos, became the core of the town cavalry; they served in the frontier war and the war of Granada. Faster Stables abstract a body of horsemen kept ready at home at their own cost and called out at once. The tech speeds what the Stable trains, the Knight-line for the horsemen a la brida and the Light Cavalry line for the lighter horse; the Jinete, the rider a la jineta typical of the Granada frontier (see the tree), trains at the Archery Range and stays outside the effect, a limit of the game's buildings rather than a claim that the cuantiosos did not ride a la jineta. The game's Chivalry, a name for an ethos rather than an institution, gives the effect at twice the magnitude but only in the Imperial Age (see the precedent).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Supremacy. At the Cortes of Madrigal (1476) Isabella and Ferdinand set up the Santa Hermandad, a crown-controlled league of the towns of Castile, paid for by their contributions, with its own judges (alcaldes de hermandad) and paid squads (cuadrilleros) that policed roads and countryside; it raised men and money for the war of Granada, and its general organisation was wound up in 1498 (Lunenfeld, 1970). It grew out of the town brotherhoods (hermandades) that had policed roads and defended town rights since the 13th century (the Hermandad Vieja of Toledo, Talavera and Ciudad Real; the general hermandades of 1282–1315 and of the 1460s), and drew on the towns' long armed tradition under the frontier fueros (the Latin fuero of Sepúlveda, 1076; the Fuero de Cuenca, late 12th century), which obliged householders to serve in the town host (Powers, 1988; The Code of Cuenca, tr. Powers, 2000). The townsmen who served on horseback belong to the Caballería de Cuantía; this tech keeps the brotherhoods, their policing and the armed town community. Armed townsmen fit the effect on Villagers; 'Supremacy' named nothing historical.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Inquisition. Crusade privileges framed and paid for the Reconquista: popes granted crusade indulgences for the Spanish wars from the 12th century and a share of church tithes for the conquest of Seville (the tercias reales, 1247), and in 1482 Sixtus IV granted the crusade bull for the war of Granada, preached throughout Castile, whose sale of indulgences, with the subsidies of the clergy, became a major source of the war's funds (Goñi Gaztambide, 1958; Ladero Quesada, 1967). Owner's decision, which ties the tech to the war of Granada: it stays in the Imperial Age for the bull of 1482, although the older crusade privileges would also justify the Castle Age (level-1 review decision). The -15% also stays: the level-1 review accepts the civ's power as it stands (against the game's Spanish it gains a sixth passive, a third unique tech, the foot crossbow line, Siege Engineers and the Jinete, and loses the builders, the gold per technology, the Cannon Galleon accuracy, two unique units, Thumb Ring, Siphons and the Mounted Crossbowman line); a -10% Bula would be the counterweight if play required one. The Inquisition it replaces (1478) judged only the baptised and converted no one; the forced conversions came from royal decrees (1492, 1499–1526) (Kamen, The Spanish Inquisition, 1997).

The Thumb Ring is given where the thumb draw is attested for a civ's own archers or for an archery tradition its armies demonstrably used (the steppe, Islamic and East Asian traditions); civs whose archers used the European draw, or whose missile troops were crossbowmen, do not get it. Castile does not: its archers used the European draw and its missile troops the crossbow (see the Crossbowman) (RULES 6.16.4).

Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ. The fire arrows and pots of burning grease and oil that the Castilian galleys used against the English fleet at La Rochelle (1372), in the account of the Chronique des quatre premiers Valois, were ordinary incendiaries, which the generic Fire Ship line already abstracts. The Castilians keep the fleet-of-ships tier (RULES 6.16.1): war galleys from the royal shipyard of Seville (1252) and the naos and carracks of the Cantabrian and Andalusian coasts, with the Galleon as the skeleton's flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2). The Cannon Galleon rests on guns carried aboard Castilian ships inside the window: Columbus's ships of 1492 carried lombards, and a lombard shot was the agreed signal for land: the Niña fired one on 7 October, and the Pinta gave the agreed signal when land was sighted on 12 October (Diario, in Las Casas's abstract). That shows ships armed with guns, not a documented fight between gun-armed Castilian warships, so the Cannon Galleon line is a thinly grounded abstraction and is flagged as such.

The crossbow was a central weapon of Christian Iberia: the frontier fueros gave privileges to the crossbowmen (ballesteros) of the concejo militias (Powers, 1988), and the Crown kept enrolled royal crossbowmen (ballesteros de nómina) in the 15th century, who served in the war of Granada; just after the window, Cortés still had 32 crossbowmen against 13 handgunners (1519, Bernal Díaz). In the game only the Spanish and the Bulgarians lack it, though the Spanish already have mounted crossbowmen. Owner's decision.
Same basis as the Crossbowman: the foot crossbowman stayed central in Castilian armies and fleets until the end of the 15th century.

The war of Granada was a war of sieges (Ronda 1485, Loja 1486, Málaga 1487) with a large royal artillery train under Francisco Ramírez de Madrid (Cook, 1993). At the end of the window, in Ferdinand's war for Naples, Pedro Navarro, serving Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, used gunpowder mines decisively at the Castel Nuovo of Naples (1503), building on Italian experiments of 1487–1495 and on his own mine at Cephalonia (1500). Owner's decision; its absence contradicted the civ's history.

The jinete, the light horseman riding a la jineta (short stirrups, light lance, javelins and leather adarga), was the typical cavalry of the Granada frontier and a large part of the Catholic Monarchs' horse in the war of Granada (Ladero Quesada, 1967); 'genet' and 'genitour' passed into English and French. The style and the word came from the Zenata horsemen of Granada and North Africa (zenete > jinete). The jinete's main weapon was the lance, with javelins secondary; the Genitour, a javelin horseman that cannot fight at close range, is the closest existing unit. A regional unit (owner's decision; RULES 6.16.10) that does not count as a unique unit (RULES 6.1), trained at the Archery Range from the Castle Age as for the Berbers' allies, and renamed Jinete.

Renamed from Genitour. Jinete (from zenete, 'Zenata') is the Castilian name of the light horseman the Portuguese call ginete: the same regional unit, named in each language. The rename meets RULES 6.16.15: the same function inside the window, a period term (Castilian ginete, jinete), and 'genitour' is the English and French borrowing of the same word. The Berbers keep 'Genitour', and the Lithuanians, to whom RULES 6.16.10 extends the regional unit, name it in their own design.
The Elite upgrade of the Jinete (Archery Range), for the same light horsemen.
Renamed from Elite Genitour. Same rename for the Elite upgrade.

Kept from the game (level 1). The armoured horsemen of the khans' and begs' households fought beside the Kipchak horse archers. Carpini, who crossed Batu's lands in 1246–1247, describes the lancers and the lamellar armour of hardened leather or iron that protected the richer warriors and their horses, a description that covers the Horde's founding army; the khans kept a Mongol military elite of princes (oghlans) and begs over the Kipchak levies for two centuries (Vásáry 2005). The name is that of the Chinggisid guard (kheshig), documented for the Yuan and the Ilkhans; a Jochid guard is likely but not directly documented, so the name stands for the institution's model rather than a recorded Jochid corps. Shared with the Mongols; the gold earned in combat stands for booty.

New in the codex (level 1). The khan's patent (yarlyk) made and unmade the princes of Rus': Yaroslav Vsevolodovich received the seniority from Batu in 1243 and Alexander Nevsky the throne of Vladimir in 1252, while princes who displeased the khan were put to death at his camp (Mikhail of Chernigov 1246, Mikhail of Tver 1318). In return the khans took the tribute (vykhod): the censuses of 1257–1259 registered the population for tribute and levy (Laurentian and Novgorod chronicles); Muslim tax-farmers collected it until the risings of 1262 and baskaks oversaw it into the early 14th century, after which the grand princes delivered it themselves, which made the fortune of Moscow (Halperin 1985; Ostrowski 1998). The khans' patents to the Church, known from Russian translations from Mengu-Temür's onwards, list a plough tax among the levies they spared: gold from farmers abstracts tribute raised from a farming population. Government and taxation of the subject principalities, so the Town Center (RULES 6.2), where the project's other tribute and land-tax techs also sit.

New in the codex (level 2). The tamga was the Mongol tax on commerce. In the Horde it was levied at Sarai and on the trade of the ports where the khans let the Italians hold colonies and quarters (Caffa, traditionally from the 1260s; Tana from 1332), and the khans' patents to the Church, from Mengu-Temür's onwards, name it among the levies the clergy were spared. Pegolotti (c. 1340), relaying merchants' reports, called the road from Tana to Cathay safe by day and by night, and even its worst stretch, Tana to Sarai, safe for a company of about sixty men (trans. Yule, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. III, 1914); the Russian word for customs, tamozhnya, comes from tamga (Favereau 2021). A state revenue levied on trade, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2), like the Danes' Øresundstold, and an institution distinct from the Rus' tribute, so a third tech (RULES 6.3) and the civ's second at the Town Center; Imperial Age for the trade boom of the 14th century.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Silk Armor (Scout Cavalry-line, Steppe Lancers and Cavalry Archers +1 melee/+1 pierce armor), the game's Castle Age unique tech. Quyaq is the Mongol and Turkic word for armour (Middle Mongol quyaɣ, modern Mongolian khuyag; Turkic qujaq), used above all for armour of plates laced in rows, and it passed into Russian as kuyak, the name later Muscovite usage gave to armour of plates on a cloth or leather base. The Horde's horsemen wore it as the Mongol armies did: Carpini, who crossed Batu's lands in 1246–1247, says that every rider had to carry two or three bows, while the richer also had helmets and cuirasses, and he describes lamellar made of strips of hardened hide and of thin iron plates laced together, which some riders also put on their horses (Ystoria Mongalorum). Finds from the ulus agree: fragments of laminar armour lay with birch-bark quivers and arrowheads in the graves of Mongol warriors at Karasuyr in the Ulytau, in the Jochid lands of Central Kazakhstan (late 13th–early 14th century; Usmanova et al. 2018), and Gorelik's studies of Mongol arms reconstruct the lamellar and laminar armour of the Mongol world from such plates and from images (Gorelik 2002). Better-protected Scout Cavalry, Steppe Lancers and Cavalry Archers render the armoured riders of the Horde's hosts, horse archers among them; most of the Kipchak levy rode lighter, so the effect is an abstraction, said openly. The game's name rested on a modern myth, silk shirts that helped draw out arrows, first found in M. Prawdin, Tschingis-Chan: der Sturm aus Asien (1934); the tech now takes the armour's own name, as the level-1 review first suggested (section 3.3) and the owner decided (19 October 2026: if the effect gives armour, it can be the armour's name). In the 14th century the hosts that wore it were raised and led by four great begs, the first of whom, the beglerbeg (‘bey of beys’, Arabic amir al-umara), commanded the army (Schamiloglu 1984); after Berdibeg's death (1359) beglerbegs ruled through khans of their own choosing: Mamai, whom the Rus' chronicles call a temnik, sent Begich to the Vozha (1378) and led the Horde at Kulikovo (1380), and Edigu, with Temür Qutlugh, won the Vorskla (1399) and besieged Moscow (1408) (Vásáry 2005; Favereau 2021). The earlier design named the tech after that office. A military tech, so at the Castle, where the game has Silk Armor (RULES 6.2); Imperial Age for the 14th century, the century of the beglerbegs' great hosts.
Camels carried baggage and caravan goods in the Horde and Khwarazm; there is no record of camel cavalry.
As Camel Rider.

No firearms are securely recorded in the Horde's own armies: the “thunder” of Bolghar (1376) is a disputed reading, the first reliable firearms in Rus' were Moscow's, against Tokhtamysh in 1382, and the guns of Kazan and Crimea belong to successor khanates outside the entity (RULES 6.16.19(d)), while none are securely recorded for the Great Horde (at the Ugra in 1480 the guns were Muscovy's).
As Hand Cannoneer: no gun towers are recorded in the Horde's towns.
As Hand Cannoneer: no gun towers are recorded in the Horde's towns.

The counterweight trebuchet is not attested in the Horde's own armies: the chronicles do not say what kind Batu's poroki were, the one reading of the type, for Caffa (1344), is of man-powered engines (Zanders; see Traction Trebuchet), and besieging Moscow in 1408 Edigu ordered the prince of Tver to bring his artillery, which never arrived (Rus' chronicles). Its absence is an argument from silence (civ-level contested list); on the evidence as it stands it is removed under the codex rule for engines that never reached a civ (RULES 6.16.5) and replaced by the Traction Trebuchet (RULES 6.11); the Mangonel and Onager stay as the generic stone-thrower.

The Horde defended its realm with field armies rather than fortresses, and most of its towns were unwalled until the troubles of the later 14th century, when some received ramparts (Fedorov-Davydov 1984). The Stone Wall and the Guard Tower stand for those late defences; the top tiers, the Fortified Wall and the Keep (which the Tatars already lack), are left out.

The Stone Wall and the Guard Tower stand for those late defences; the top tiers, the Fortified Wall and the Keep (which the Tatars already lack), are left out.
No printing in the window: in the Horde's lands documents and books, from the khans' yarlyks to the Codex Cumanicus, were written by hand.

The Horde had no war fleet: the khans let Genoese and Venetians hold colonies and quarters in their ports (Caffa, Tana) and kept their own customs officials there, and its wars were fought on land and across rivers. So the basic navy only, under the codex navy rule (RULES 6.16.1): the Galley-line to War Galley, the Fire Galley and Fire Ship, the Hulk-line as the game's generic melee warship, the demolition ships and the Dock techs, with no Galleon, Carrack, Fast Fire Ship or siege warship.
As Galleon.
As Galleon: no ocean-going ships.
No naval artillery is recorded for the Horde.
As Cannon Galleon.

Added and renamed Araba (see the bonus): the Horde's wagon camps. It stands beside the Lumber and Mining Camps instead of replacing them; the Tatars are one of the Mule Cart's four holders (RULES 6.16.7).

Renamed from Mule Cart, with the look of the Ox Wagon. Ibn Battuta's word (ʿaraba) for the wagons of the Kipchak steppe, which carried felt tents and goods; araba is still the Turkic word for a cart. The look is the Scenario Editor's Ox Wagon (The Last Khans), existing game content (RULES section 5), which fits Rubruck's ox-drawn house-carts better than the mule of the Armenian and Georgian cart; only the look is used, so the cart keeps the Mule Cart's function, and the Ox Wagon's art must be checked in the game.

Islam became the Horde's state religion under Özbeg (from 1313), after Berke's personal conversion before his reign (1257–1266); the khans also protected the Orthodox Church, with a bishopric at Sarai from 1261.
As Faith: the mosques, madrasas and Sufi lodges of Sarai, Bolghar and Solkhat, where Özbeg's mosque was built in 1314.

The Horde built and rebuilt cities: Sarai and Sarai al-Jadid on the lower Volga, a revived Bolghar, Azak, Hajji Tarkhan and Solkhat, with palaces and mosques of fired brick and glazed tile at Sarai and Urgench and of cut stone at Bolghar and Solkhat (G. A. Fedorov-Davydov, The Culture of the Golden Horde Cities, 1984); Architecture stands for this urban building.

Heavy stone-throwers are attested for the Horde and its founding campaign, and the counterweight type is not. Batu's army, the Horde's founding host, set up poroki (the chronicles' word for siege engines, usually read as stone-throwers; the chronicles do not record their type) against Vladimir (February 1238; Laurentian Chronicle) and at the Polish Gate of Kiev, where they battered the walls day and night until they broke them (December 1240; Hypatian Chronicle), both just before the window, in the campaign that founded the Horde. Janibeg besieged Genoese Caffa with engines that an Italian relief force destroyed in February 1344 (M. Wheelis, “Biological Warfare at the 1346 Siege of Caffa”, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8, 2002); J. P. Zanders, who has studied the siege, takes them for man-powered engines, the one reading of the type of a Horde engine (Zanders 2021, as reported by Field 2023, both in the sources; the man-powered reading is not confirmed at first hand in Zanders' paper). On that reading the Traction Trebuchet is the Horde's long-range siege weapon and replaces the counterweight Trebuchet (RULES 6.16.5, 6.11), as for the Avars; the type rests on one reading and on the silence of the other sources (civ-level contested list). Trained at the Siege Workshop in the Imperial Age.

Changed by the codex (level 2); replaces Teutonic Knight (Infantry): slow infantry with exceptional melee armor, resistant to conversion. The brother-knights of the Order fought mounted, as heavy cavalry: at Durbe (1260) and at Grunwald (1410) a few hundred brothers per campaign led sergeants, guest crusaders and Prussian auxiliaries (Christiansen 1997; Urban 2003); making them infantry inverted their role and fitted at most dismounted knights in sieges and garrisons. The brethren rode heavy warhorses bred in the Order’s own studs, beside the small native horses of its Prussian light horsemen (Ekdahl 1998), and were armed and armoured from the stores of their convents, whose inventories (Das große Ämterbuch des Deutschen Ordens, ed. Ziesemer 1921) record horses and weapons office by office. Owner’s decisions: the look is the Scenario Editor Crusader Knight (Dawn of the Dukes), a mounted knight in the white mantle with the black cross of the Teutonic Order (RULES section 5); and, on 19 October 2026, the unit is the game’s Teutonic Knight with that art, faster on horseback and with two points less attack to compensate (level 2: existing art with adapted stats, RULES section 5; see stats). It moves at the art’s own speed of 1.2, slower than the Knight’s 1.35, for heavily armoured brethren on heavy horses. Mounted, it is a cavalry unit for the counter system: the Spearman-line and the camels counter it, as they counter the Knight. It keeps the game’s other values, its 7/2 armour (Elite 8/2) and its cost of 85 food and 30 gold among them. The attack it gives up (12, Elite 15, against the game’s 14 and 17) keeps it below the Elite Leitis’ 16, the highest attack the game gives a mounted melee unit other than the elephants (Paladin 14), so its attack stays within the class ceiling (RULES 6.16.11). Its armour does not: fully upgraded, with the Germans’ melee-armour passive (+2 in the Imperial Age) and the barding upgrades (+3/+4), the Elite tier has 13/6, the armour of the game’s fully upgraded Elite Teutonic Knight (8 + 2 + 3 melee with the Teutons’ passive and mail armour, 2 + 4 pierce), and a melee armour above that of every other mounted unit in the game (a fully upgraded Elite Boyar, the most armoured of them, has 11/7, a fully upgraded Paladin 5/7), while its pierce armour stays below theirs. This is an exception to the class ceiling (RULES 6.16.11) by the owner’s decision of 19 October 2026, for the heavily armoured brother knights (realism first, RULES 6.14). The Crusader Knight’s own campaign values (codex/tools/scenario-units-stats.md: 100 HP, 18 attack, 4/4 armour, 80 food and 50 gold, no Elite version) are not used, and neither is the campaign unit’s immunity to conversion: the unit can be converted, like the game’s Teutonic Knight, and the Germans’ conversion-resistance passive covers it, for the professed brethren. It is trained at the Castle from the Castle Age, like the game’s unit, and the game’s Elite Teutonic Knight upgrade at the Castle leads to its Elite tier. Its in-game role must still be checked in the game. The name and the data stay the game’s own; only the look, the speed, the attack and the class change, which the site notes (RULES 6.16.15); the site keys units by model.
