New in the codex (level 2). From about 1486–87 Maximilian I, King of the Romans, raised German foot on the Swiss model, the Landsknechte: a block of pikemen, with halberdiers and two-handed swordsmen (the double-pay Doppelsöldner) in the front ranks and, more and more, handgunners. Captains recruited them under contract, mustered them, swore them to articles of war and paid them by the month, so that a prince with money could raise thousands of foot within weeks; within a few years they fought for Maximilian in the Low Countries, in Hungary (1490) and in Italy (1496), and other princes hired them too (Baumann 1994). Not a late element (RULES section 2): the Landsknechte originate inside the window, in its last fifteen years. As a troop of the 1480s–90s the design makes the unit available only in the Imperial Age, a design choice rather than a requirement of section 2. Owner’s decision: the Landsknecht is a unit. The model is the Scenario Editor Heavy Pikeman (The Forgotten), a pikeman with its own look, whose art is edited from the Pikeman’s, and its stats are adapted (level 2, RULES section 5; see stats). As it is, the model has the Pikeman’s values with +20 HP and +2 against cavalry (codex/tools/scenario-units-stats.md: 75 HP, 4 attack, 0/0 armour, speed 1.0, 35 food and 25 wood, +24 against cavalry, +25 against war elephants, +18 against camels and +16 against ships), which would make the civ’s second unique unit weaker in its own role than the Halberdier the Germans train beside it at the same cost (60 HP, 6 attack, +32 against cavalry), an absurdity of the kind RULES 6.14 rules out. The adapted values are anchored on the Elite Kamayuk, the game’s long-spear unique infantry (80 HP, 8 attack, 1/1 armour), and on the Halberdier’s bonus table: 36 damage per hit against cavalry (8 + 28) stays just below the Halberdier’s 38, while the higher base attack renders the halberds and two-handed swords of the double-pay men in the front ranks, the first to meet the enemy’s pikes; the unit has no bonus against the Spearman-line, which no melee unit in the game has. The measure is the game’s anti-cavalry infantry (RULES 6.16.11), checked fully upgraded: the base armour is 0/1, so that with the Germans’ melee-armour passive (+2 in the Imperial Age, the only age in which the unit exists) and the Blacksmith’s infantry armour (+3/+4) it reaches 5/5, the melee armour of the Teutons’ fully upgraded Halberdier (0 + 2 + 3) and of the Incas’ Elite Kamayuk with Fabric Shields (1 + 3 + 1), with a pierce armour below the latter’s 6 (1 + 4 + 1); its 80 HP and its fully upgraded 12 attack (8 + 4) equal the Elite Kamayuk’s. No value goes beyond what the game gives anti-cavalry infantry. The cost is that of the game’s Condottiero, its Imperial Age mercenary infantry at the Barracks (50 food and 35 gold), for foot paid by the month: a tougher pikeman paid in gold, so a choice beside the Halberdier rather than a strict upgrade. Its in-game role must still be checked in the game. Trained at the Barracks, as mustered foot rather than a castle garrison, as the game’s Condottiero is for the Italians’ allies (Condottiero available at the Barracks in Imperial Age, Italians team bonus, which the Italians’ design replaces with the Genoese Crossbowman). The model has no Elite version, and the unit, which arrives only in the Imperial Age, has no Elite tier either, like the game’s Condottiero.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Crenellations (Castles +3 range, garrisoned Infantry fires arrows). The ministeriales were unfree knights: legally the servants of a lord, bound by written service customs (Dienstrechte, the earliest Bamberg’s of the mid-11th century), yet armed, enfeoffed with service fiefs and employed as household knights, castellans and officials. By the later 12th century they made up most of the knighthood of the German kings, bishops and princes, at once unfree and noble, professional warriors in a kingdom where violence for political ends prevailed (Arnold 1985); the Salians and the Staufen built their power on the imperial ministeriales (Reichsministerialen), who held royal castles and estates (Bosl 1950–51), and one of them, Markward of Annweiler, was a leading commander of Henry VI’s conquest of the Kingdom of Sicily (1194). Faster Stables abstract a lord’s own hereditary household of knights, raised and replaced without bargaining with free vassals. The kingdom’s own knighthood had no element in the game’s design; the tech takes the Castle slot of Crenellations (see [[dropped]]), while the Landsknechte are a unit rather than a tech. A new tech (level 2): no existing unique tech renders an unfree knighthood.

New in the codex (level 2). Effect revised on 18 October 2026 at the owner’s request: the earlier cheaper Imperial Age advance only discounted a one-time purchase, paid for with Town Center time. Chapters IX and X of the Golden Bull granted the electors the regalian rights over every mine (gold, silver, tin, copper, lead, iron) and salt in their lands and the right to coin money, which the faster miners render. The Golden Bull of Charles IV, issued at the diets of Nuremberg (January 1356) and Metz (December 1356), fixed the election of the King of the Romans, who was still to be crowned emperor, by seven electors (the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, the King of Bohemia, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg) by majority vote at Frankfurt, made the secular electorates indivisible, confirmed the electors’ regalian rights (mines, tolls, coinage) and banned urban leagues; it remained a fundamental law of the Empire until 1806 (Golden Bull, ed. Fritz 1972; Scales 2012; Wilson 2016). It fixed the procedure to prevent double elections such as those of 1198, 1257 and 1314, the wars between rival kings that followed the first and the last (Philip of Swabia against Otto IV; Louis IV against Frederick the Fair, to Mühldorf, 1322), and rival kingships such as Charles IV’s own election at Rhens (1346) against Louis IV. It did not end every dispute (Wenceslas deposed in 1400; the double election of 1410, see contested), but from 1411 the elections followed it until the Empire’s end. A cheaper advance to the Imperial Age stands for a settled royal election, the gateway to the imperial crown: an abstraction, and the link with the game’s ‘Imperial’ Age is a play on the word. Henry I’s burgs (926–933), the other candidate, stay as the root of the garrison passive: the Town Center slot goes to the Golden Bull, the weightier state moment (level-1 review, section 3.1), and whether Henry issued a systematic ordinance is debated (Bachrach 2012). Tigui’s effect (Town Centers fire arrows without garrison) stays with the Italians’ Comune. A state constitution, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2); Castle Age, so that it precedes the advance it eases. A new tech (level 2): no existing unique tech renders an electoral constitution.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Ironclad (Siege Weapons +4 melee armor). The Hanse (c. 1250–1500; first general diet 1356) linked Lübeck, Hamburg, Cologne, Danzig and dozens of other German towns, with Kontore at Novgorod, Bergen, London and Bruges; its cogs and later hulks (the ship type that gives the game’s Hulk-line its name) also fought: the towns’ Cologne Confederation forced Denmark to the Peace of Stralsund (1370), the Teutonic Order took Gotland from the Victual Brothers in 1398, and the towns fought England at sea in 1470–74 (Dollinger 1964). Its trade also served its partners, as the Rus’, Norwegians’, Swedes’, Danes’ and Lithuanians’ designs note (furs, stockfish, copper and iron, herring and wax sold to Hanseatic merchants), but a civ has one team bonus and the German sketch gives it to the miners (see the team bonus); as a datable institution the Hanse becomes a unique tech (RULES 6.2). At the Dock, as in the German sketch, because its power rested on its ships; the effect is narrowed to sea trade. Ironclad is dropped: it is the mid-19th-century term for armoured warships (La Gloire 1859, Monitor 1862), and covering siege engines with hides and boards was universal.

New in the codex (level 2). In Mainz Johann Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type around 1450; the 42-line Bible was finished by about 1454–55. German printers carried the technique across Europe within a generation: Sweynheym and Pannartz at Subiaco (1465), Johann of Speyer at Venice (1469), Gering, Friburger and Crantz at Paris (1470), Andreas Hess at Buda and Kasper Straube at Kraków (1473); by 1500 presses had worked in more than two hundred towns (Febvre and Martin 1958; Eisenstein 1979). Print also served learning at home: at Nuremberg Regiomontanus set up a press in his own house (1471) for mathematical and astronomical works, printing Peurbach’s Theoricae novae planetarum and his own Ephemerides (1474), whose tables and diagrams print reproduced without the copyists’ errors (Eisenstein 1979). Cheaper University technologies stand for knowledge made cheap by print: an abstraction. Placement (RULES 6.2): the spread of printing abroad benefited the neighbours and is team-bonus material, but a civ has one team bonus and the German sketch gives it to the miners (see the team bonus); the invention itself is datable and bears a proper name, so it becomes a unique tech at the University, where knowledge and writing belong, as the Hanse, whose trade also served its partners, becomes the Dock tech. Imperial Age: the press belongs to the last half-century of the window. A new tech (level 2): no existing unique tech represents printing, and the generic Block Printing, a Monastery tech for the Monks’ conversion range, stays in the tree, since printing falls inside the window (the printing-date test of the Danes’, Swedes’ and Norwegians’ designs). Owner’s decision of 19 October 2026, ‘for now’: Gutenberg's Press is the fourth tech beside the fifth passive (Monks +100% healing range), so the civ has 5 passives and 4 techs, 9 in all, the cap of RULES 6.1; the earlier design had kept it as an N2 idea to stay at 8.

Removed to offset the additions. There is no specific German basis for the top tier of the stone-thrower line (held by only 15 of the game’s 56 civs); the Germans keep the Onager, Capped Ram, Trebuchet and Bombard Cannon.
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.

Crossbowmen were central to the Order’s garrisons and arsenals in Prussia (Ekdahl 1998) and to the urban militias of the German towns, whose shooting guilds (Schützengilden) appear from the 14th century. The Germans already have the Heavy Mounted Crossbowman; the foot upgrade completes the crossbow line.

The Order used native Prussian light horsemen, riding the small native horses beside the brothers’ heavy warhorses, on its raids (Reisen) through the wilderness against Lithuania (Ekdahl 1998; Christiansen 1997).
Romanesque Speyer, Gothic Cologne, the brick Gothic of the Baltic towns and the Order’s castles (Marienburg) make the absence hard to justify for a defensive civilization.

The medieval treadwheel crane is almost a German emblem: the crane of Cologne cathedral stood on the unfinished south tower from the 15th century until 1868, and the Krantor of Danzig (1442–44) was built under the Order.
Germany was the mining heart of medieval Europe (Rammelsberg, Freiberg, the Harz and the Erzgebirge, Schwaz in Tyrol) (Bartlett 1993); lacking the late mining upgrade contradicted that.

Navy (RULES 6.16.1): a fleet of ships, resting on the Hanse’s cogs and hulks and later carvel-built ships, which dominated the Baltic and the North Sea, defeated Denmark (1367–70) and carried the Order to Gotland (1398) (Dollinger 1964); a weak navy contradicted this. The Galleon stays as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2), and the Carrack and Fast Fire Ship as generic tiers that a fleet of ships keeps (RULES 6.16.1). The Cannon Galleon stays for a documented gun-armed Hanseatic warship: the great caravel Peter von Danzig, a French ship left at Danzig in 1462 and taken over by the town, was fitted out with guns for the Hanse’s war against England (1470–74), cruised the North Sea in 1471–73 and under Paul Beneke took a galley carrying Memling’s Last Judgment (1473) (Możejko 2020). Danzig was then a city of the Polish crown (from 1454, confirmed in 1466), and the ship served the Hanse’s war rather than the crown’s, so it counts for the Hanse first; the Poles’ design also cites it for Gdańsk, a city of the crown (shared evidence, RULES 6.7).

The Hanseatic towns built their own cogs and hulks in town shipyards (the Lastadie of Lübeck and Danzig), and the hulk and the carvel-built ship were adopted in the Baltic in the 15th century (Dollinger 1964); the Dock upgrade completes the Hanseatic navy.

Kept from the game (level 1). The chroniclers describe bows taller than European ones, made of hard dark woods (the airi palm, pau-d'arco), and massed archery was central to Tupinambá war (Léry 1578; Métraux 1928). Training the Blackwood Archers in pairs at half population abstracts these masses. Also trainable at the Archery Range in the Imperial Age (see bonuses). The model is shared with the Malians' Tontajon.

Kept from the game (level 1). The ibirapema, a decorated wooden club, is the most iconic Tupinambá object: it served in the ritual execution of captives and also in battle (Staden; Léry). The frontal area attack is an acceptable abstraction of the heavy two-handed club.

Kept from the game (level 1). The ibirapema, a decorated wooden club, is the most iconic Tupinambá object: it served in the ritual execution of captives and also in battle (Staden; Léry). The frontal area attack is an acceptable abstraction of the heavy two-handed club.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Caciques. ‘Cacique’ is a Taíno word from the Antilles; the Tupi called their chiefs morubixaba, like Cunhambebe, whose authority was greatest in war and rested on prestige won in combat (Staden; Thevet; Fernandes 1949). That prestige came from enemies killed and captives taken: the warrior who killed a captive in the ritual execution took a new name, and the tacape and the ibirapema were the instruments of capture and execution (Fernandes 1952; Carneiro da Cunha & Viveiros de Castro 1985). The effect keeps the kind of Caciques but applies it to the Tupi club fighters instead of the Andean mace and the sling, which the Tupi did not use; it carries capture warfare in N1 until the N2 renaming mechanic exists (see ideas).

New in the codex (level 2). Village men cleared the forest together for new manioc gardens and built the great longhouses and the palisades in common work parties, and villages were moved and rebuilt every few years (Métraux 1928; Fernandes 1949); Old Tupi motyrõ, ‘work in common’, is the source of Brazilian Portuguese ‘mutirão’. Faster building renders the work parties that raised and rebuilt the villages; the clearing of the gardens already carries the Coivara rename, and a wood-gathering effect would stack a second gathering bonus on manioc farming (RULES 6.14). For a people without a state the Town Center tech represents a community institution (RULES 6.3); its basis is thin, since the 16th-century sources describe the communal clearing and building but not the institution's name, which is known from colonial Tupi. Decision: Motyrõ is kept rather than a level-2 tech for the council of elders and principal men that decided war, village moves and the fate of captives (Léry 1578; Thevet 1557; Fernandes 1949), which is better attested but has no fitting existing effect.
Removed with the Siege Workshop: there were no rams and no wheeled vehicles.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Battering Ram).
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Battering Ram).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: no torsion or traction artillery existed in the Americas.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Mangonel).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: no bolt-throwers existed in the Americas.
Removed with the Siege Workshop (see Scorpion).
Removed with the Siege Workshop: a wheeled assault tower.
Counterweight artillery never existed in the Americas.

The crossbow was unknown in Brazil, and the Americas have neither crossbow tier (RULES 6.16.3); Tupi warfare rested on great bows. The Blackwood Archers become available at the Archery Range in the Imperial Age in its place (bonus). In the current game the Bulgarians also lack crossbows.
Removed with the Crossbowman (see there).

Removed under the codex convention for the American civs (RULES 6.16.6, the owner's decision on their power budget): a playability line, not a historical one, since the kept Pikeman bears as European a name; the American spear line stops at the Pikeman, as the game already does for the Aztecs and Muisca. The Tupi fought with bows and clubs, and Spearman and Pikeman remain as a generic abstraction.
The sling is not a characteristic Tupinambá weapon in the 16th-century sources, and the Andean slinger belongs to the Inca world (analysis: wrong).

Ocean-going sailing warships were unknown; the Tupi navy was a fleet of bark and dugout canoes (see the warships bonus). Boat tier (RULES 6.16.1), resting on these canoes: the high-seas sailing ships (the Galleon; the Tupi never had the Carrack) are removed and the siege ship goes with the siege engines, while the Galley (renamed Canoe), Fire Ship, Demolition and Hulk lines stay with their tiers as a generic abstraction of canoe fleets for water maps; the demolition ships are generic post-1500 items kept as flagged abstractions (RULES 6.16.2).
A sailing ship carrying a catapult: both a European ship type and a siege engine.

Region-wide tower policy: only the Keep, a stone tower, needs documented stone towers, so it stays only where they are documented (the Inca); the Guard Tower stays as a generic tier wherever the game gives it (the Mapuche, who lack it in the game, stay without it). The Tupi built no towers: their defences were palisades and stakes (Staden's woodcuts), and their Watch Tower and Guard Tower are abstractions of a defended village. The Castle itself stays for structural reasons (it trains the unique unit, researches the Castle tech and is needed for the Imperial Age) until an N3 caiçara replaces it (ideas).

There was no stone building; palisades, sometimes double, were the Tupi fortification. Stone walls are removed (in the current game the Cumans and Goths also lack them; the Goths' design adds them) and Palisade Walls remain.
Removed with the Stone Wall; the Palisade Gate remains.

Game convention (RULES 6.16.5, the heavy-engine floor; owner’s decision of 20 October 2026), not a historical claim: no siege engine of any kind existed in the pre-contact Americas (see the Trebuchet). Every civ keeps one heavy engine so that it can answer an enemy’s trebuchets, and the traction trebuchet, a man-powered engine known across Eurasia and North Africa from the late 6th century, is the oldest and most widespread of the three heavy engines, so the least anachronistic choice. The Siege Workshop stays in the tree for this engine alone. For its other units the design’s reading stands: The Tupi built no siege engines: villages were attacked by surprise, by assault on the palisade and with fire. At the siege of the Portuguese settlement of Igarassu in 1548 Staden saw the native besiegers, on a coast held by Tupi-speaking peoples, shoot burning arrows of cotton and wax at the houses; Staden does not call them Caeté, an identification that comes from Richard Burton's footnote to the Hakluyt Society edition (1874). The Tacape line (strong against buildings), Arson, Sappers and Petards replace them (owner's decision, RULES 6.16.5; RULES 6.11 and section 10). Before the heavy-engine floor every Castle had to be taken by units standing in its arrow fire; the Traction Trebuchet now does it from range, as a game convention, until an N2/N3 assault unit exists, with no compensating bonus (RULES 6.16.13). The Petard, a 16th-century gunpowder charge, stays unrenamed as a flagged generic abstraction of assault parties with fire, outside the one-late-element limit (RULES 6.16.2).
Renamed from Champi Scout. The tacape was the Tupi wooden war club. Champi is the Quechua name of the Andean stone or bronze mace, and the Tupi had no metal before contact (analysis: wrong).
Renamed from Champi Runner. Same rename as Champi Scout.
Renamed from Champi Warrior. Same rename as Champi Scout.
Renamed from Elite Champi Warrior. Same rename as Champi Scout.

Renamed from Horse Collar. There were no draft animals. Fields were cleared by felling and burning the forest (coivara, a word of Tupi origin), and the ash fertilised each new plot: a real equivalent of ‘new Farms provide more food’. Heavy Plow keeps its generic name as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.6; see the civ-level note on generic items); the Tupi already lacked Crop Rotation.

Renamed from Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Tupi war parties travelled in fleets of bark and dugout canoes (igara, ubá), each carrying many warriors (Staden; see the warships bonus). The Scenario Editor Canoe, a small warship introduced in The Forgotten (RULES section 5), gives the Galley the look of a war canoe; the Galley keeps its stats, and the Canoe's look, scale, attack and role must be checked in game. Same rename as for the Aztecs, Maya and Mapuche, and outside the Americas in the Malians' and Avars' designs; the igara war-canoe line proper is an N3 idea.
Renamed from War Galley, with the look of the Canoe. Upgrade tier of the renamed Galley, with the same Canoe look (see Galley).

Kept from the game (level 1). The yeniçeri (‘new troops’) were formed under Murad I (c. 1363–1380) from the sultan's fifth of war captives (pençik) and later from the devşirme levy of Christian boys; they began as archers and took up firearms from the mid-15th century. The unit represents the Janissary of c. 1450–1600 well; the Scenario Editor's Royal Janissary, a stronger variant, adds nothing the game's unit lacks. The wagon fort (tabur) behind which the Janissaries fought, most famously at Chaldiran (1514) and Mohács (1526), on Hungarian and Hussite models, is not added through the Bohemians' Hussite Wagon: it was a field-fortification tactic rather than a troop type, the Hussite Wagon, whether as a second unique unit or unlocked by a Castle tech (as in the Magyars' design), would render a Bohemian institution, and its Ottoman fame rests on battles after 1500 (on when the Ottomans adopted it, see contested).

Kept from the game (level 1). The unit represents the Janissary of c. 1450–1600 well; the Scenario Editor's Royal Janissary, a stronger variant, adds nothing the game's unit lacks. The wagon fort (tabur) behind which the Janissaries fought, most famously at Chaldiran (1514) and Mohács (1526), on Hungarian and Hussite models, is not added through the Bohemians' Hussite Wagon: it was a field-fortification tactic rather than a troop type, the Hussite Wagon, whether as a second unique unit or unlocked by a Castle tech (as in the Magyars' design), would render a Bohemian institution, and its Ottoman fame rests on battles after 1500 (on when the Ottomans adopted it, see contested).

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Sipahi (Mounted Archers +20 HP). The timar assigned the revenue of a district, recorded in the state's survey registers (tahrir defterleri, from the 1430s), to a provincial cavalryman (sipahi) who served with bow, lance and mace and brought armed retainers in proportion to his income (İnalcık, 1973). The Town Center fits the institution, a land-revenue system run by the central government; sturdier mounted archers translate the equipped timariot cavalry. The tech is named after the institution rather than after the soldiers (Sipahi), and the codex reads it as grown out of the Seljuk and Ilkhanid iqta' (see contested on its origin).

Kept from the game (level 1). Ottoman superiority in siege artillery is well documented: Orban's great bombard at Constantinople (1453), Munir Ali's Dardanelles Gun (1464), the sieges of Rhodes (1480, 1522) and Belgrade (1521). Siege Engineers stays out of the tree, as in the game: with Artillery it would give Bombard Cannons a range of 15, beyond the highest value the game gives the class (RULES 6.16.11); Sappers, already in the tree, carries the Ottoman miners (lağımcı).
Named after the Byzantine fire siphon, a state secret never given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13); no ship-borne liquid-fire weapon is documented for this civ.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.

Seljuk-era Anatolian rulers and the Ottomans founded great hospitals (darüşşifa): Gevher Nesibe in Kayseri (Kaykhusraw I, 1205–1206), the Mengujekid hospital of Turan Malik at Divriği (1228–1229) and the hospital of Bayezid II's complex at Edirne (1488). The absence was ironic.

Granted by the Caravanserai bonus (the Seljuk sultan hans and the Ottoman hans; see there) and added so that the tree shows the building, as in the Khmer design (the Persians and Hindustanis have it in the game).

Renamed from Hussar. The akıncı (‘raider’) were the Ottoman light horsemen who raided ahead of the army into Hungary, Austria and Italy (Friuli, 1477–1499); the word hussar itself probably comes, through Serbian, from a word for raider. Same function, identical effect.

Renamed from Shipwright. The Ottoman state arsenals (tersane), at Gallipoli from c. 1390 and on the Golden Horn after 1453, enlarged by Selim I from 1515; the word itself comes, through Italian darsena, from the Arabic dār al-ṣināʿa, which the Arabs' renamed Shipwright uses. Same function (a state shipyard), identical effect. The navy is a fleet of ships (RULES 6.16.1): the galleys of Gallipoli and the Golden Horn and the gun-carrying göke of Kemal Reis at Zonchio (1499) keep the game's generic tiers, the Galleon as a flagged abstraction (RULES 6.16.2), and the Cannon Galleon. The game's lack of the Fast Fire Ship stands and no naval bonus is added: the fleet fought inside the window (Negroponte 1470, the Otranto landing 1480, Zonchio 1499, Modon 1500), but its peak (Rhodes 1522, Preveza 1538, Djerba 1560) comes after it.

Kept from the game (level 1). The mounted aristocracy of the medieval kingdom: the knights and squires of the Erikskrönikan (c. 1320s–1330s), the frälse who served the crown on horseback under the Alsnö statute. The name follows the Rígsþula, a West Norse poem, whose Jarl, ancestor of the nobles, learns to ride, bend the bow and throw the spear; and jarl was the title of the realm's first officer, held by Birger Jarl (1248–1266), who founded Stockholm (first named in 1252). The reach of its attack renders the lance.

Kept from the game (level 1). The mounted aristocracy of the medieval kingdom: the knights and squires of the Erikskrönikan (c. 1320s–1330s), the frälse who served the crown on horseback under the Alsnö statute. The name follows the Rígsþula, a West Norse poem, whose Jarl, ancestor of the nobles, learns to ride, bend the bow and throw the spear; and jarl was the title of the realm's first officer, held by Birger Jarl (1248–1266), who founded Stockholm (first named in 1252). The reach of its attack renders the lance.

New in the codex (level 1). At Alsnö (1279 or 1280) King Magnus Ladulås exempted from taxes everyone who served the crown with a war horse (rusttjänst), creating the secular frälse, the Swedish nobility, and forbade the great men's forced hospitality (gästning) on the peasants, the protection traditionally linked to his byname Ladulås, ‘barn-lock’. Cheaper knights render mounted service paid for by tax exemption, as with the Polish privileges. A royal statute on taxation and estates, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2); the earlier of the civ's two datable moments, so the Castle Age tech.

New in the codex (level 1); replaces Vendel Legacy (Knight-line deals trample damage). The peasant armies of the 15th century decided Sweden's struggle with the Kalmar kings. In the summer of 1434 the mine owner Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson led the miners and peasants of Bergslagen and Dalarna against Erik of Pomerania's bailiffs; within a few months the rising had spread across Svealand and Götaland and taken most of the royal castles, and in January 1435 an assembly at Arboga made Engelbrekt captain of the realm (rikshövitsman), before his murder in 1436 (Engelbrektskrönikan). A generation later the regent Sten Sture the Elder called out the peasant levies again and, with the burghers of Stockholm and the horsemen of his noble allies, routed Christian I's army at Brunkeberg outside Stockholm (10 October 1471), a victory commemorated by the St George group in Stockholm's great church, commonly attributed to Bernt Notke (1489). Barracks that work twice as fast render levies of armed peasants called out within weeks. A military moment, so at the Castle (RULES 6.2); the later of the civ's two datable moments, so the Imperial Age tech.

The Varangian Guard stays with the Byzantines (RULES section 4): it was an institution of the Byzantine state, though some thirty runestones, most of them in Uppland, name Swedes who went to or died in ‘Greece’. The Champion takes over its heavy infantry role.
Same as the Varangian Guard.
Hungarian and Serbian light cavalry of the 15th century, a type medieval Sweden never fielded; Light Cavalry stays as its top light cavalry.

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. No Swedish mounted crossbowmen are recorded as a troop type in the sources consulted; Swedish crossbowmen are represented by the Arbalester, and the Danes' and Norwegians' designs drop the line on the same test.
As for the Mounted Crossbowman, and later still (15th century).
A 15th-century spanning device for the mounted crossbow line, which the Swedes no longer have.
Requires Siphons, which this design removes.
The fire siphon was a Byzantine state secret never to be given to other nations (De Administrando Imperio 13).
No ship-borne catapults are known in Scandinavian fleets; the Longship (strong vs buildings) keeps the anti-building naval role, as for the Norwegians and Danes.
Substitute for the removed Varangian Guard as heavy infantry (RULES 6.11); the top swordsman tier is a generic abstraction.

The crossbow was the common missile weapon of 14th–15th-century Scandinavian warfare, in castle garrisons and in the armies of the Union wars; lacking the top tier was incoherent for a civ whose window runs to 1500 (RULES 6.16.3).
Stone castles of the medieval kingdom: Stockholm (from the 1250s), Kalmar, Stegeborg and Nyköpingshus, scene of the Nyköping Banquet (1317); Engelbrekt's men took the royal castles in 1434–1436.
Stone castles of the medieval kingdom: Stockholm (from the 1250s), Kalmar, Stegeborg and Nyköpingshus, scene of the Nyköping Banquet (1317); Engelbrekt's men took the royal castles in 1434–1436.
Sweden's medieval mines: the copper of Falun (Stora Kopparberg, first recorded in 1288) and the iron of Bergslagen, whose miners rose with Engelbrekt in 1434.
The cults of St Erik (king, d. 1160) at Uppsala and of St Birgitta (d. 1373, canonised 1391), whose order was founded at Vadstena (consecrated 1384).

The unit stands for the handguns of the Sture armies. Firearms were in Swedish hands by the Sture period: in the Swedish tradition of Brunkeberg (1471), a battle the rhymed Sture Chronicle narrates, a shot from the Swedish side struck Christian I in the mouth and broke several of his teeth, the weapon, a hook gun (hakebössa) in the usual retelling, resting on later tradition (see contested). Under RULES 6.16.19(d) the tree follows the represented period, and the struggle with the Union kings to 1500 is part of it, so the Imperial Age unit enters. Further gun items (Bombard Cannon, Bombard Tower, Cannon Galleon) are left out: the Swedish cases weighed for them, the defence of Vyborg against the Muscovite siege of 1495 under Knut Posse and the Swedish storming of Ivangorod (1496), could not be tied to documented Swedish guns in this design. The Danes' guns rest on cases of 1495–1500, and the Norwegians, whose window ends in 1469, have none.

Johann Snell printed the first book in Sweden at Stockholm, the Dialogus creaturarum (dated 20 December 1483), and then the Missale Upsalense for the archbishop of Uppsala (1484). The same printing-date test keeps Block Printing for the Danes, for whom Snell had printed at Odense in 1482, and removes it from the Norwegians (to 1469) and the Rus' (to 1505).

Kept from the game (level 1). Shields and protection of rattan and wicker were common in Southeast Asia and southern China (the rattan-shield troops, tengpai, of the Ming), which justifies the high pierce armour. The same model also serves the Bengali design’s Paik, renamed, until the Paik gets its own art (N3); the Vietnamese unique unit is shared on that footing.

Kept from the game (level 1). Shields and protection of rattan and wicker were common in Southeast Asia and southern China (the rattan-shield troops, tengpai, of the Ming), which justifies the high pierce armour. The same model also serves the Bengali design’s Paik, renamed, until the Paik gets its own art (N3); the Vietnamese unique unit is shared on that footing.

Changed by the codex (level 1); replaces Chatras (Battle Elephants +100 HP). War elephants served Đại Việt’s rulers across the period, though as a secondary arm: Song accounts of the war of 1076–77 report Lý elephants against the Song advance; in 1258 Trần Thái Tông drew up his elephant troops and infantry across the river against Uriyangqadai’s Mongols (Yuan shi, biography of Uriyangqadai); the Hồ fielded elephants against the Ming at Đa Bang (1407), where, by the Ming accounts, they were routed by cavalry in lion masks and by guns, and Lê Lợi’s insurgents used them in the 1420s; Đại Việt fought its southern wars against the elephant armies of Champa. The game’s Chatras (+100 HP) gave the largest Battle Elephant buff in the game to an arm that was secondary in Đại Việt, while the Khmer, for whom elephants were the royal arm, keep in their design only the +10% speed passive (their design gives Tusk Swords’ slot to Arogyashala); the tech therefore takes the lighter effect of the Burmese Howdah (a tech the Burmese design drops; the effect stays a Burmese passive), and stays level 1. Chatras was a Castle Age tech and Howdah an Imperial Age one, and a reused effect keeps the game’s age or a later one (RULES 6.16.11, a game constraint), so Tượng Binh moves to the Imperial Age; as the civ’s only Castle tech, it is not bound by the order of RULES 6.4. The armour is an abstraction of trained elephant troops, not a recorded harness. The elephants are a long-standing arm, which RULES 6.2 would make a passive; they stay a Castle tech as a flagged fallback for a long tradition (RULES 6.16.19(b)), because the Castle needs a military tech and no datable Lý–Trần military moment has a fitting existing effect (a new tech for Trần Hưng Đạo’s proclamation to his officers, Hịch tướng sĩ, 1284, with a modest elephant passive beside it, was considered and not adopted). The Sanskrit chattra (royal parasol) belongs to the Indianised courts of Champa and Angkor; tượng binh, ‘elephant troops’, is the Sino-Vietnamese term.

New in the codex (level 2); replaces Paper Money (Lumberjacks slowly generate gold in addition to wood). The Lý founded the Temple of Literature (Văn Miếu) in 1070, held the first examination in 1075 and set up the Imperial Academy (Quốc Tử Giám) in 1076; the Trần made the examinations regular, with the three top laureates (tam khôi) from 1247; and under the Lê, above all Lê Thánh Tông (1460–97), examination-recruited Confucian officials ran the state, their names carved from 1484 on the doctors’ stelae of the Văn Miếu (Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư; Taylor 2013). Faster research abstracts an administration of trained literati. At the Town Center because the examinations recruited the state’s officials (RULES 6.2). Castle Age, as the institution dates from the Lý.
No Vietnamese tradition of mounted archery is known.
As for the Cavalry Archer.

The counterweight trebuchet reached China only in 1273 (Xiangyang), and no Vietnamese source for it is known; the Chinese, Japanese and Korean designs, among others, make the same change (RULES 6.16.5).

No gun-armed Đại Việt warship is documented inside the window in the sources used for this design: the guns of Hải Triều (1390) may have been fired from the bank (see contested). RULES 6.16.1 admits a special warship only where the type is documented.
See Cannon Galleon.

In 1390 the Cham king Chế Bồng Nga was killed by Vietnamese gunfire; the Ming took the Vietnamese gun-making method after 1407 (see the team bonus), and the Lê used firearms against Champa (1471) and Lan Xang (1479–80) (Sun Laichen 2003). The civ had Bombard Cannon and Fire Lancer but no hand-held gun, against its own game history text.

An inference, flagged (see contested): Đại Việt’s pre-gunpowder heavy artillery would have been the traction stone-thrower (pao) of the Chinese military tradition on which it modelled its armies, the engine of both its neighbours, Song China and Champa (Yuan shi 210, for the Cham in 1283); no Vietnamese source names one, and the Song accounts of Yongzhou (1076) record towers and ramps instead. Kept as a flagged inference, which the level-1 review admits beside the traction test (RULES 6.16.5), it replaces the counterweight Trebuchet as the long-range siege weapon (RULES 6.11), beside the Bombard Cannon of the 15th-century Hồ and Lê (Sun Laichen 2003, 2006).

Renamed from Conscription. Same effect. ‘Conscription’ evokes modern compulsory service (France, 1798); the Vietnamese equivalent is the rotating levy of trained reserves who farmed between turns of service, which later historians call ngụ binh ư nông (see contested), well attested under Lê Lợi (1429). The name is a later historiographical label rather than a Lý–Trần term, kept and flagged as such (RULES 6.16.15; see contested); Vietnamese is written in the Latin script, so it keeps its diacritics.

Kept from the game (level 1). Berserkir appear among Harald Fairhair's warriors at Hafrsfjord in near-contemporary skaldic verse (Þorbjǫrn hornklofi, Haraldskvæði, c. 900), and Snorri describes warriors without mail who bit their shields and were hurt by neither fire nor iron (Ynglinga saga 6); regeneration renders that legendary invulnerability.

Kept from the game (level 1). Berserkir appear among Harald Fairhair's warriors at Hafrsfjord in near-contemporary skaldic verse (Þorbjǫrn hornklofi, Haraldskvæði, c. 900), and Snorri describes warriors without mail who bit their shields and were hurt by neither fire nor iron (Ynglinga saga 6); regeneration renders that legendary invulnerability.

New in the codex (level 2). The naval levy of the Norwegian kings: each ship district (skipreiða) had to build, man and provision a warship when the king called out the leiðangr, as the laws of the Gulaþing and Frostaþing assemblies (12th–13th centuries) and Magnus Lagabøte's national law (Landslov, 1274) set out in detail. It was a civil institution as much as a military one: the skipreiða was also a district of local administration and taxation, and by the 13th century the levy was commonly paid as a fixed yearly tax in kind, the leidang, which outlived the fleet. Faster ships and dock population render crews and hulls called up by district. A public obligation fixed in law and administered as a tax, so at the Town Center (RULES 6.2) rather than at the Dock, which would render only its sea side; Magnus Lagabøte's Landslov (1274), the first law code for a whole Scandinavian kingdom, is part of its basis rather than a tech of its own.

Kept from the game (level 1). Old Norse bogsveigir, ‘bow-bender’. Norse sea fights opened with an exchange of missiles before boarding, and the levy laws armed the ships for it: the Gulaþing law required a bow and two dozen arrows for each rowing bench (sessrúm) of a levy ship (trans. Larson 1935). Einarr Þambarskelfir is the famous archer of Olaf Tryggvason's last battle at Svolder (c. 1000, Heimskringla), and the King's Mirror (c. 1250) says that at sea crossbows and longbows are useful, as are all other shooting weapons.

The Varangian Guard stays with the Byzantines (RULES section 4). Norwegians served in it (Harald Hardrada, 1034–1043), but as individuals, not as an institution of the kingdom. The Danes rename the model Housecarl for their kings' household troops; the Norwegian kings' hirð could justify the same, but the model is left out here to keep the two civs distinct, and Berserk, Champion and Halberdier cover its roles. The Norse Warrior (Scenario Editor, RULES section 5) was weighed as the look of the hirð and not used: its base stats make it a light swordsman rather than an armoured retainer (to be checked in game), and the Berserk already gives the civ its Norse look.
Same as the Varangian Guard.
Norway never fielded a large knightly cavalry; the small mounted hirð of the 13th-century kings, whose retainers took knightly titles under Magnus Lagabøte, is represented by the Knight.

Shared basis (level-1 review, section 11): the Mounted Crossbowman line stays only where mounted crossbowmen are documented as a regular troop type of the civ’s armies. No Norwegian mounted crossbowmen are recorded; the line came with a generic ‘Western European’ block, and the Norwegian crossbow, which the King's Mirror (c. 1250) recommends at sea, is rendered by the Crossbowman and Arbalester.
The siphon for liquid fire was a Byzantine state secret that Constantine VII ordered never to be given to another nation (De Administrando Imperio 13).
There is no evidence of ship-borne catapults in Norse fleets; the Longship (strong vs buildings) keeps the role of attacking coastal buildings.

No printing in the window (to 1469): Norway's first press was set up only in 1643, by Tyge Nielssøn at Christiania. The same printing-date test keeps Block Printing for the Danes (Odense, 1482) and gives it to the Swedes (Stockholm, 1483).
Norway built royal stone castles from the late 12th century: Sverresborg in Trondheim and Bergen (1180s), Bergenhus with Håkonshallen (c. 1261), Tunsberghus (mid-13th century) and Akershus (c. 1299).
Norway built royal stone castles from the late 12th century: Sverresborg in Trondheim and Bergen (1180s), Bergenhus with Håkonshallen (c. 1261), Tunsberghus (mid-13th century) and Akershus (c. 1299).

Norway was Christian from c. 1030 (St Olaf, Stiklestad), with an archbishopric at Nidaros from 1152/53 whose province reached Iceland, Greenland, the Faroes, Orkney and Man; a pagan Monastery to the end of the window is anachronistic.
The cult of St Olaf made Nidaros the main pilgrimage centre of the North.
Monastic houses and hospitals spread with the 12th-century church; a generic Monastery tech held by most civs.

Substitute for Chieftains and the removed Varangian Guard as anti-cavalry infantry (RULES 6.11); the top spear tier is a generic abstraction, and pole weapons were in use in the late-medieval peasant levies of the window.
